## 1. Core Concept Overview & Intuition

Physical quantities fall into two broad classes. A **scalar** is a quantity possessing magnitude only: mass, length, time, temperature, and any real number are scalars. A **vector** is a quantity possessing both magnitude and direction: displacement, velocity, force, and acceleration are vectors. The distinction is not cosmetic — scalars combine by ordinary arithmetic, whereas vectors combine by a geometry that respects direction.

The intuition for vector addition is the **chain rule of displacements**. To add two vectors $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$, draw them as a chain, starting the second where the first ends; the sum $\mathbf{c}$ is the single vector joining the start of the first to the end of the second. If a body is displaced from $A$ to $B$ and then from $B$ to $C$, the net displacement is the single vector from $A$ to $C$, written $\overrightarrow{AB}+\overrightarrow{BC}=\overrightarrow{AC}$, or $\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}=\mathbf{c}$. Extending the chain to four vectors $\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b},\mathbf{c},\mathbf{d}$ drawn head-to-tail, the successive partial sums are $\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}=\overrightarrow{AC}$, then $\overrightarrow{AC}+\mathbf{c}=\overrightarrow{AD}$, then $\overrightarrow{AD}+\mathbf{d}=\overrightarrow{AE}$; the total is the single vector joining the start of the first to the end of the last, namely $\overrightarrow{AE}$. If the chain closes on itself — the end of the last vector coincides with the beginning of the first — the resultant has no magnitude.

A vector is represented graphically by a line whose length denotes magnitude according to a stated vector scale and whose direction, marked by an arrowhead, denotes the direction of action. The vector $\overrightarrow{OP}$ has initial point $O$ and final point $P$ and is written analytically as $\mathbf{A}$; its magnitude is denoted $\lvert \mathbf{A} \rvert$. The reversed vector $\overrightarrow{PO}$ has the same magnitude but opposite sense, and is written $-\mathbf{A}$. Two vectors $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ are **equal** if they have the same magnitude and the same direction, regardless of the position of their initial points.

The central computational idea of this unit is **resolution into components**. Any vector in three dimensions can be placed with its initial point at the origin $O$ of a rectangular coordinate system. If $(A_1,A_2,A_3)$ are the rectangular coordinates of its terminal point, the vectors $A_1\hat{\imath}$, $A_2\hat{\jmath}$, $A_3\hat{k}$ are the component vectors of $\mathbf{A}$ in the $x$, $y$, and $z$ directions respectively, and their resultant is $\mathbf{A}$ itself. Once a vector is in component form, its magnitude follows from the three-dimensional Pythagorean relation, and its direction is captured by the direction cosines. These two constructions — magnitude and direction cosines — are the computational backbone of the entire unit.

## 2. Mathematical Formalization & Core Definitions

> **Definition (Vector and Scalar).** A vector is a quantity having both magnitude and direction, such as displacement, velocity, force, and acceleration. A scalar is a quantity having magnitude but no direction, e.g. mass, length, time, temperature, and any real number.

> **Definition (Vector Representation).** A vector quantity is represented graphically by a line drawn so that the length of the line denotes the magnitude of the quantity according to some stated vector scale, and the direction of the line denotes the direction in which the vector quantity acts. An arrowhead indicates the sense of the direction.

> **Definition (Equality of Vectors).** Two vectors $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ are equal if they have the same magnitude and direction regardless of the position of their initial points; thus $\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{B}$.

> **Definition (Addition of Vectors).** The sum of two vectors $\overrightarrow{AB}$ and $\overrightarrow{BC}$ is the single, equivalent, or resultant vector $\overrightarrow{AC}$; that is, $\overrightarrow{AB}+\overrightarrow{BC}=\overrightarrow{AC}$, or $\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}=\mathbf{c}$.

> **Definition (Components of a Vector).** Let $\mathbf{A}$ have initial point at the origin $O$ of a rectangular coordinate system and terminal point with coordinates $(A_1,A_2,A_3)$. The vectors $A_1\hat{\imath}$, $A_2\hat{\jmath}$, $A_3\hat{k}$ are the component vectors of $\mathbf{A}$ in the $x$, $y$, and $z$ directions respectively, and
> 

$$
\mathbf{A}=A_1\hat{\imath}+A_2\hat{\jmath}+A_3\hat{k}.
$$

> **Definition (Position Vector).** The position vector or radius vector $\mathbf{r}$ from $O$ to the point $(x,y,z)$ is
> 

$$
\mathbf{r}=x\hat{\imath}+y\hat{\jmath}+z\hat{k},
$$

> and has magnitude
> 

$$
\lvert \mathbf{r} \rvert=r=\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}}.
$$

> **Definition (Unit Vector).** A unit vector is a vector having unit magnitude. If $\mathbf{A}$ is a vector with magnitude $A\neq 0$, then
> 

$$
\hat{\mathbf{a}}=\frac{\mathbf{A}}{A}
$$

> is a unit vector having the same direction as $\mathbf{A}$.

> **Definition (Direction Cosines).** The direction of a vector in three dimensions is determined by the angles it makes with the three axes of reference. For $\overrightarrow{OP}=\mathbf{r}=a\hat{\imath}+b\hat{\jmath}+c\hat{k}$, let $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ be the angles the vector makes with the $x$, $y$, and $z$ axes. Then
> 

$$
l=\cos\alpha=\frac{a}{r},\qquad m=\cos\beta=\frac{b}{r},\qquad n=\cos\gamma=\frac{c}{r},
$$

> where $r=\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}}$. The triple $[l,m,n]$, written in square brackets, is called the direction cosines of $\overrightarrow{OP}$.

### 2.1 Magnitude of a Vector

The magnitude of a vector is shown by two vertical bars on either side of the vector, $\lvert \mathbf{a} \rvert$, and is computed using Pythagoras' theorem. For $\mathbf{A}=A_1\hat{\imath}+A_2\hat{\jmath}+A_3\hat{k}$,

$$
\lvert \mathbf{A} \rvert=A=\sqrt{A_1^{2}+A_2^{2}+A_3^{2}}.
$$

In two dimensions this reduces to $\sqrt{A_1^{2}+A_2^{2}}$, the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs $A_1$ and $A_2$. The magnitude is always non-negative and is zero only for the zero vector.

### 2.2 The Unit Vector

Dividing a nonzero vector by its own magnitude produces a vector of unit length pointing in the same direction:

$$
\hat{\mathbf{a}}=\frac{\mathbf{A}}{\lvert \mathbf{A} \rvert}.
$$

The verification that $\hat{\mathbf{a}}$ has unit magnitude is immediate, since scaling a vector by $1/\lvert \mathbf{A} \rvert$ scales its magnitude by the same positive factor. A unit vector is the standard device for isolating *direction* from *magnitude*: any vector may be reconstructed as $\mathbf{A}=\lvert \mathbf{A} \rvert\,\hat{\mathbf{a}}$.

### 2.3 The Resultant of a Number of Vectors

The resultant of vectors $\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}+\mathbf{c}+\mathbf{d}+\cdots$ is obtained by drawing the vectors as a chain and taking the single vector joining the start of the first to the end of the last. In component form, addition is performed coordinatewise:

$$
\mathbf{R}=\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}+\mathbf{c}+\cdots=\left(\sum a_1\right)\hat{\imath}+\left(\sum a_2\right)\hat{\jmath}+\left(\sum a_3\right)\hat{k},
$$

where $a_1,a_2,a_3$ denote the $x$, $y$, $z$ components of each summand. The magnitude of the resultant is then $\lvert \mathbf{R} \rvert=\sqrt{R_1^{2}+R_2^{2}+R_3^{2}}$.

### 2.4 Vector from One Point to Another

Given $P(x_1,y_1,z_1)$ and $Q(x_2,y_2,z_2)$ with position vectors $\mathbf{r}_1=x_1\hat{\imath}+y_1\hat{\jmath}+z_1\hat{k}$ and $\mathbf{r}_2=x_2\hat{\imath}+y_2\hat{\jmath}+z_2\hat{k}$, the relation $\mathbf{r}_1+\overrightarrow{PQ}=\mathbf{r}_2$ gives

$$
\overrightarrow{PQ}=\mathbf{r}_2-\mathbf{r}_1=(x_2-x_1)\hat{\imath}+(y_2-y_1)\hat{\jmath}+(z_2-z_1)\hat{k},
$$

with magnitude

$$
\lvert \overrightarrow{PQ} \rvert=\sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^{2}+(y_2-y_1)^{2}+(z_2-z_1)^{2}},
$$

which is precisely the distance between $P$ and $Q$.

### 2.5 Direction Cosines and the Fundamental Identity

From $a=r\cos\alpha$, $b=r\cos\beta$, $c=r\cos\gamma$ and $a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}=r^{2}$, substituting the cosine expressions yields

$$
r^{2}\cos^{2}\alpha+r^{2}\cos^{2}\beta+r^{2}\cos^{2}\gamma=r^{2}.
$$

Dividing by $r^{2}\neq 0$ gives the fundamental identity

$$
\cos^{2}\alpha+\cos^{2}\beta+\cos^{2}\gamma=1,
$$

equivalently

$$
l^{2}+m^{2}+n^{2}=1.
$$

This identity is the standard consistency check on any computed triple of direction cosines, and it is the reason a direction in space has only two independent degrees of freedom.

## 3. Key Theorems & Essential Results

> **Theorem (Commutative Law of Addition).** If $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ are vectors, then

$$
\mathbf{A}+\mathbf{B}=\mathbf{B}+\mathbf{A}.
$$

> *Proof.* Construct the parallelogram with adjacent sides $\mathbf{A}=\overrightarrow{OP}$ and $\mathbf{B}=\overrightarrow{PQ}$, so that $\overrightarrow{OP}+\overrightarrow{PQ}=\overrightarrow{OQ}$, i.e. $\mathbf{A}+\mathbf{B}=\mathbf{C}$. Reading the same parallelogram along the other route, $\overrightarrow{OR}+\overrightarrow{RQ}=\overrightarrow{OQ}$, i.e. $\mathbf{B}+\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{C}$. Since both routes terminate at the same point $Q$, the two sums coincide. $\blacksquare$

> **Theorem (Associative Law of Addition).** If $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{B}$, $\mathbf{C}$ are vectors, then

$$
\mathbf{A}+(\mathbf{B}+\mathbf{C})=(\mathbf{A}+\mathbf{B})+\mathbf{C}.
$$

> *Proof.* Take points $O,P,Q,R$ with $\overrightarrow{OP}=\mathbf{A}$, $\overrightarrow{PQ}=\mathbf{B}$, $\overrightarrow{QR}=\mathbf{C}$. Then $\overrightarrow{OP}+\overrightarrow{PQ}=\overrightarrow{OQ}=\mathbf{A}+\mathbf{B}$ and $\overrightarrow{PQ}+\overrightarrow{QR}=\overrightarrow{PR}=\mathbf{B}+\mathbf{C}$. Grouping the first way, $\overrightarrow{OP}+\overrightarrow{PR}=\overrightarrow{OR}=\mathbf{D}$, i.e. $\mathbf{A}+(\mathbf{B}+\mathbf{C})=\mathbf{D}$. Grouping the second way, $\overrightarrow{OQ}+\overrightarrow{QR}=\overrightarrow{OR}=\mathbf{D}$, i.e. $(\mathbf{A}+\mathbf{B})+\mathbf{C}=\mathbf{D}$. Hence the two groupings agree. $\blacksquare$

> **Corollary.** The order of addition of any number of vectors is immaterial.

> **Theorem (Magnitude of a Component Vector).** For $\mathbf{A}=A_1\hat{\imath}+A_2\hat{\jmath}+A_3\hat{k}$,

$$
\lvert \mathbf{A} \rvert=\sqrt{A_1^{2}+A_2^{2}+A_3^{2}}.
$$

> **Theorem (Direction Cosine Identity).** For any nonzero vector with direction cosines $[l,m,n]$,

$$
l^{2}+m^{2}+n^{2}=1.
$$

> **Theorem (Unit Vector Normalization).** If $\mathbf{A}\neq \mathbf{0}$, then $\hat{\mathbf{a}}=\mathbf{A}/\lvert \mathbf{A} \rvert$ satisfies $\lvert \hat{\mathbf{a}} \rvert=1$ and points in the direction of $\mathbf{A}$.

> **Theorem (Diagonal Bisection in a Parallelogram).** The diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other.
> *Proof.* Let the parallelogram have adjacent sides $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$, so that $\overrightarrow{AC}=\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}$ and $\overrightarrow{BD}=\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a}$. Let $P$ be the intersection of the diagonals and write $\overrightarrow{AP}=x\,\overrightarrow{AC}$ and $\overrightarrow{BP}=y\,\overrightarrow{BD}$. Since $\overrightarrow{AB}+\overrightarrow{BP}=\overrightarrow{AP}$, we obtain $\mathbf{a}+y(\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a})=x(\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b})$. Comparing coefficients of $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ on the left and right gives $x=y=\tfrac{1}{2}$, so $P$ is the midpoint of both diagonals. $\blacksquare$

> **Theorem (Equation of a Straight Line).** The line through points with position vectors $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ consists of all points with position vector

$$
\mathbf{r}=\mathbf{a}+t(\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a}),
$$

> where $t$ is a scalar.
> *Proof.* For any point $P$ on the line, $\overrightarrow{OA}+\overrightarrow{AP}=\overrightarrow{OP}$ with $\overrightarrow{AP}=t\,\overrightarrow{AB}$ for some scalar $t$. Hence $\overrightarrow{OP}=\overrightarrow{OA}+t(\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a})$. $\blacksquare$

> **Remark (Coefficient Sum Condition).** The line equation may be rewritten as

$$
\mathbf{r}=(1-t)\mathbf{a}+t\mathbf{b},
$$

> or equivalently as

$$
(1-t)\mathbf{a}+t\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{r}=\mathbf{0}.
$$

> In this form the sum of the coefficients of the position vectors is $(1-t)+t+(-1)=0$. This vanishing coefficient sum is the standard test that a linear relation among position vectors represents a straight line.

> **Theorem (Expansion in Two Non-Collinear Vectors).** Given two non-collinear vectors $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$, any vector $\mathbf{r}$ lying in their plane can be expressed as

$$
\mathbf{r}=x\mathbf{a}+y\mathbf{b}
$$

> for scalars $x,y$; in three-dimensional space, any vector can be expressed as $\mathbf{r}=x\mathbf{a}+y\mathbf{b}+z\mathbf{c}$ for scalars $x,y,z$.

## 4. Worked Exemplar Problem with Step-by-Step Solution

**Problem.** Find the unit vector parallel to the resultant of the vectors

$$
\mathbf{r}_1=2\hat{\imath}+4\hat{\jmath}-5\hat{k},\qquad \mathbf{r}_2=\hat{\imath}+2\hat{\jmath}+3\hat{k}.
$$

**Step 1 — Form the resultant by coordinatewise addition.**

$$
\mathbf{R}=\mathbf{r}_1+\mathbf{r}_2=(2+1)\hat{\imath}+(4+2)\hat{\jmath}+(-5+3)\hat{k}=3\hat{\imath}+6\hat{\jmath}-2\hat{k}.
$$

**Step 2 — Compute the magnitude of the resultant.**

$$
\lvert \mathbf{R} \rvert=\sqrt{3^{2}+6^{2}+(-2)^{2}}=\sqrt{9+36+4}=\sqrt{49}=7.
$$

**Step 3 — Normalize to obtain the unit vector.**

$$
\hat{\mathbf{r}}=\frac{\mathbf{R}}{\lvert \mathbf{R} \rvert}=\frac{1}{7}\left(3\hat{\imath}+6\hat{\jmath}-2\hat{k}\right)=\frac{3}{7}\hat{\imath}+\frac{6}{7}\hat{\jmath}-\frac{2}{7}\hat{k}.
$$

**Step 4 — Verify unit magnitude.**

$$
\lvert \hat{\mathbf{r}} \rvert=\sqrt{\left(\frac{3}{7}\right)^{2}+\left(\frac{6}{7}\right)^{2}+\left(-\frac{2}{7}\right)^{2}}=\sqrt{\frac{9+36+4}{49}}=\sqrt{\frac{49}{49}}=1.
$$

The verification confirms the normalization is correct.

**Supplementary exemplar (direction cosines).** For $\mathbf{r}=3\hat{\imath}-2\hat{\jmath}+6\hat{k}$ we have $a=3$, $b=-2$, $c=6$, and

$$
r=\sqrt{9+4+36}=\sqrt{49}=7.
$$

Hence

$$
l=\frac{3}{7},\qquad m=-\frac{2}{7},\qquad n=\frac{6}{7},
$$

and the check $l^{2}+m^{2}+n^{2}=\frac{9+4+36}{49}=1$ holds.

**Supplementary exemplar (resultant of displacements).** Let $\mathbf{A}$ be $10$ m Northwest, $\mathbf{B}$ be $20$ m at $30^{\circ}$ north of east, and $\mathbf{C}$ be $35$ m due south. The resultant is $\mathbf{D}=\mathbf{A}+\mathbf{B}+\mathbf{C}$, formed by joining the initial point of $\mathbf{A}$ to the terminal point of $\mathbf{C}$. Working graphically on a scale of $5$ m per unit, the resultant measures $4.1$ units, i.e. a magnitude of $20.5$ m, in a direction $60^{\circ}$ south of east.

**Supplementary exemplar (right-angle forces).** Let $\mathbf{P}$ be a force of $5$ N acting due East and $\mathbf{Q}$ a force of $12$ N acting due North. Since the two directions are perpendicular, the magnitude of the resultant $\mathbf{r}$ follows from the Pythagorean relation $p^{2}+q^{2}=r^{2}$:

$$
25+144=169\quad\Longrightarrow\quad r=\sqrt{169}=13\ \text{N}.
$$

## 5. High-Yield Exam Takeaways & Common Pitfalls

**High-yield takeaways.**

- A vector carries magnitude *and* direction; a scalar carries magnitude only. State both attributes when defining a vector quantity.
- The resultant of a chain of vectors is the single vector from the start of the first to the end of the last; a closed chain has zero resultant.
- Addition is commutative and associative, so the order and grouping of any number of summands is immaterial.
- Component form converts vector geometry into coordinatewise arithmetic: add or subtract component by component, then take the square root of the sum of squares for magnitude.
- The vector from $P$ to $Q$ is $\mathbf{r}_2-\mathbf{r}_1$, and its magnitude is the distance between the points.
- The unit vector is $\mathbf{A}/\lvert \mathbf{A} \rvert$; always verify that the result has magnitude $1$.
- Direction cosines are $l=a/r$, $m=b/r$, $n=c/r$, and they must satisfy $l^{2}+m^{2}+n^{2}=1$.
- The line through position vectors $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ is $\mathbf{r}=\mathbf{a}+t(\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a})$; the coefficient-sum condition identifies straight-line relations among position vectors.

**Common pitfalls.**

- Reversing the order of subtraction when forming $\overrightarrow{PQ}$: the correct vector is terminal minus initial, $\mathbf{r}_2-\mathbf{r}_1$, not $\mathbf{r}_1-\mathbf{r}_2$.
- Forgetting that the negative of a vector reverses its sense but preserves its magnitude.
- Dividing by a zero magnitude when normalizing; the unit vector is defined only for $\mathbf{A}\neq \mathbf{0}$.
- Sign errors in the components, especially when squaring negative components — the square removes the sign, so $(-2)^{2}=4$.
- Reporting direction cosines that fail the identity $l^{2}+m^{2}+n^{2}=1$; this check should always be performed.
- Treating the magnitude of a sum as the sum of magnitudes; in general $\lvert \mathbf{A}+\mathbf{B} \rvert\neq \lvert \mathbf{A} \rvert+\lvert \mathbf{B} \rvert$ unless the vectors are parallel and similarly directed.
- Confusing the graphical scale with the physical magnitude: the measured length must be multiplied by the stated scale factor to recover the physical result.
- Assuming that a vector's position in space matters for equality; equal vectors may have different initial points provided magnitude and direction agree.

**Assessment guidance.** Assessment in this unit targets the ability to (i) distinguish scalar from vector quantities, (ii) represent vectors graphically and in component form, (iii) compute magnitudes, unit vectors, and resultants of several vectors, (iv) compute the vector joining two points and the distance between them, and (v) determine and verify direction cosines. Worked problems should be presented with the resultant formed first, the magnitude computed second, and the normalization or direction-cosine check performed last.

**Recommended reading.** The standard references supporting this unit are the texts by Davis, H.; Lewis, P.; Spiegel, M.; and Tai, C., which treat vector representation, addition, components, magnitude, unit vectors, and direction cosines in the same sequence developed here.

## 1. Core Concept Overview & Intuition

### 1.1 Lesson Learning Outcomes

By the end of this unit, a learner should be able to:

- Explain, in plain words, the difference between a scalar quantity and a vector quantity.
- Represent a vector graphically by a directed line segment, and read its magnitude and direction from that line.
- Add two or more vectors by the chain (tip-to-tail) method and identify the resultant.
- State and use the commutative and associative laws of vector addition.
- Resolve a vector into components along the $x$, $y$ and $z$ axes and write it in the form $A = A_1\hat{i} + A_2\hat{j} + A_3\hat{k}$.
- Compute the magnitude of a vector using the three-dimensional form of Pythagoras' theorem.
- Construct a unit vector in the direction of any given non-zero vector.
- Find the vector joining two given points and compute the distance between those points.
- Compute the direction cosines of a vector and verify the identity $l^2 + m^2 + n^2 = 1$.

### 1.2 The Everyday Idea Behind a Vector

Imagine you are giving a friend directions to a shop. It is not enough to say "walk $500$ metres." Your friend also needs to know which way to walk. The distance alone is a **scalar**: it has size but no direction. The instruction "walk $500$ metres due north" is a **vector**: it has both size and direction.

The same distinction appears everywhere. Mass, length, time and temperature are scalars — you can state them with a single number and a unit. Displacement, velocity, force and acceleration are vectors — a single number is not enough; a direction must accompany it.

Where the analogy stops being exact: in mathematics a vector is not tied to a physical journey. It is an abstract object with a length and a direction, and we are free to slide it anywhere in space without changing it, as long as we do not rotate it or stretch it.

### 1.3 Drawing a Vector

A vector is drawn as a straight line with an arrowhead. Three things are encoded in the drawing:

- The **length** of the line gives the magnitude, measured against some stated scale (for example, $1$ cm on paper represents $5$ m in reality).
- The **direction** of the line gives the line along which the vector acts.
- The **arrowhead** gives the sense — which of the two opposite ways along that line the vector points.

The point where the arrow starts is the **initial point**; the point where the arrowhead sits is the **terminal point**. A vector from $O$ to $P$ is written $\overrightarrow{OP}$ or simply $A$, and its magnitude is written $\lvert A \rvert$ or $A$. Reversing the arrow gives $\overrightarrow{PO}$, which has the same magnitude but the opposite sense, and is written $-A$.

Two vectors are **equal** if they have the same magnitude and the same direction, no matter where in space they are drawn. This is why we may slide a vector around freely when adding vectors.

### 1.4 Adding Vectors by Chaining

To add two vectors $a$ and $b$, draw $a$, then start $b$ where $a$ ends. The **resultant** $c$ is the single vector from the start of $a$ to the end of $b$. In symbols, if $a = \overrightarrow{AB}$ and $b = \overrightarrow{BC}$, then

$$
\overrightarrow{AB} + \overrightarrow{BC} = \overrightarrow{AC}
$$

or, more briefly, $a + b = c$.

For several vectors $a, b, c, d$, chain them one after another. The resultant is the single vector joining the start of the first to the end of the last. If the chain closes up into a closed figure — the end of the last vector coincides with the start of the first — then the resultant has no magnitude; it is the zero vector.

A useful special case: if two forces act at right angles, the size of their resultant is found by Pythagoras' theorem. A force of $5$ N due east and a force of $12$ N due north combine to give a resultant of size $13$ N, because $5^2 + 12^2 = 25 + 144 = 169$ and $\sqrt{169} = 13$.

### 1.5 Components: Breaking a Vector into Three Pieces

Any vector in three dimensions can be placed with its initial point at the origin $O$ of a rectangular coordinate system. If the terminal point has coordinates $(A_1, A_2, A_3)$, then the vector can be written as the sum of three pieces, one along each axis:

$$
A = A_1\hat{i} + A_2\hat{j} + A_3\hat{k}
$$

Here $\hat{i}$, $\hat{j}$ and $\hat{k}$ are the unit vectors along the $x$, $y$ and $z$ axes respectively. The numbers $A_1$, $A_2$, $A_3$ are called the **components** of $A$, and the three vectors $A_1\hat{i}$, $A_2\hat{j}$, $A_3\hat{k}$ are called the **component vectors**.

The special vector from the origin to the point $(x, y, z)$ is called the **position vector** (or radius vector):

$$
r = x\hat{i} + y\hat{j} + z\hat{k}
$$

### 1.6 Magnitude, Unit Vector and Resultant — the Three Central Tools

These three ideas are the working tools of the whole unit, so it is worth stating each in one plain sentence before formalising them.

- The **magnitude** answers the question "how long is this vector?" It is a single non-negative number.
- A **unit vector** answers the question "which way does this vector point?" It is a vector of length exactly $1$ in the same direction.
- The **resultant** answers the question "what single vector has the same effect as all these vectors together?" It is the sum.

The rest of these notes builds each tool carefully, then shows them working together in a fully worked example.

## 2. Mathematical Formalization & Core Definitions

### 2.1 Scalars and Vectors

> **Definition (Vector).** A vector is a quantity having both magnitude and direction, such as displacement, velocity, force and acceleration.

> **Definition (Scalar).** A scalar is a quantity having magnitude but no direction, for example mass, length, time, temperature, and any real number.

### 2.2 Vector Representation and Equality

A vector quantity is represented graphically by a line drawn so that:

- the length of the line denotes the magnitude of the quantity, according to some stated vector scale;
- the direction of the line denotes the direction in which the vector quantity acts;
- an arrowhead indicates the sense of the direction.

The vector $\overrightarrow{OP}$ has initial point $O$ and terminal point $P$, and is written analytically as $A$. Its magnitude is denoted by $\lvert A \rvert$ or $A$. The vector $\overrightarrow{PO}$ has the same magnitude but the opposite sense, and is written $-A$.

> **Definition (Equal vectors).** Two vectors $A$ and $B$ are equal if they have the same magnitude and the same direction, regardless of the position of their initial points. Thus $A = B$.

### 2.3 Addition of Vectors

> **Definition (Sum of two vectors).** The sum of two vectors $\overrightarrow{AB}$ and $\overrightarrow{BC}$ is the single, equivalent, or resultant vector $\overrightarrow{AC}$:

> 

$$
> \overrightarrow{AB} + \overrightarrow{BC} = \overrightarrow{AC}
>
$$

> or, in letters, $a + b = c$.

To find the sum of two vectors $a$ and $b$, draw them as a chain, starting the second where the first ends; the sum $c$ is the single vector joining the start of the first to the end of the second.

For a chain of several vectors $a + b + c + d$, proceed step by step:

$$
\begin{aligned}
a + b &= \overrightarrow{AC} \\
\overrightarrow{AC} + c &= \overrightarrow{AD} \\
\overrightarrow{AD} + d &= \overrightarrow{AE}
\end{aligned}
$$

so that $a + b + c + d = \overrightarrow{AE}$. The sum of all the vectors is the single vector joining the start of the first to the end of the last. If the vector diagram is a closed figure — the end of the last vector coincides with the beginning of the first — the resultant sum is a vector with no magnitude.

### 2.4 The Laws of Vector Algebra

If $A$, $B$ and $C$ are vectors and $m$ and $n$ are scalars, then:

> **Law 1 (Commutative law of addition).** $A + B = B + A$.

The justification is direct. With $O$, $P$, $Q$, $R$ forming a parallelogram, $\overrightarrow{OP} + \overrightarrow{PQ} = \overrightarrow{OQ}$, that is $A + B = C$; and $\overrightarrow{OR} + \overrightarrow{RQ} = \overrightarrow{OQ}$, that is $B + A = C$. Since both sums equal the same vector $C$, we have $A + B = B + A$.

> **Law 2 (Associative law of addition).** $A + (B + C) = (A + B) + C$.

The justification again uses a chain. With points $O$, $P$, $Q$, $R$ and $D$ arranged so that $\overrightarrow{OP} = A$, $\overrightarrow{PQ} = B$, $\overrightarrow{QR} = C$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\overrightarrow{OP} + \overrightarrow{PQ} &= \overrightarrow{OQ} = A + B \\
\overrightarrow{PQ} + \overrightarrow{QR} &= \overrightarrow{PR} = B + C \\
\overrightarrow{OP} + \overrightarrow{PR} &= \overrightarrow{OR} = D \quad \text{so} \quad A + (B + C) = D \\
\overrightarrow{OQ} + \overrightarrow{QR} &= \overrightarrow{OR} = D \quad \text{so} \quad (A + B) + C = D
\end{aligned}
$$

Both groupings give the same vector $D$, hence $A + (B + C) = (A + B) + C$. Thus the order of addition of any number of vectors is immaterial.

### 2.5 Components of a Vector

Any vector $A$ in three dimensions can be represented with initial point at the origin $O$ of a rectangular coordinate system. Let $(A_1, A_2, A_3)$ be the rectangular coordinates of the terminal point of $A$. The vectors $A_1\hat{i}$, $A_2\hat{j}$ and $A_3\hat{k}$ are the component vectors of $A$ in the $x$, $y$ and $z$ directions respectively. The resultant of these three is $A$ itself:

$$
A = A_1\hat{i} + A_2\hat{j} + A_3\hat{k}
$$

In particular, the position vector (radius vector) $r$ from $O$ to the point $(x, y, z)$ is

$$
r = x\hat{i} + y\hat{j} + z\hat{k}
$$

### 2.6 Magnitude of a Vector

The magnitude of a vector is shown by two vertical bars on either side of the vector. Given the vector $A = A_1\hat{i} + A_2\hat{j} + A_3\hat{k}$, the magnitude is denoted by $\lvert A \rvert$ and is defined by applying Pythagoras' theorem twice — once in the base plane and once vertically:

$$
\lvert A \rvert = \sqrt{A_1^2 + A_2^2 + A_3^2}
$$

For the position vector $r = x\hat{i} + y\hat{j} + z\hat{k}$ this becomes

$$
\lvert r \rvert = r = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2 + z^2}
$$

### 2.7 Unit Vector

> **Definition (Unit vector).** A unit vector is a vector having unit magnitude. If $A$ is a vector with magnitude $\lvert A \rvert \neq 0$, then

> 

$$
> \hat{a} = \frac{A}{\lvert A \rvert}
>
$$

> is a unit vector having the same direction as $A$.

The construction is simply "divide the vector by its own length." The direction is unchanged because we divided by a positive number; the length becomes $1$ because $\lvert A \rvert / \lvert A \rvert = 1$.

### 2.8 Vector Joining Two Points and Distance Between Them

Let $P$ have coordinates $(x_1, y_1, z_1)$ and $Q$ have coordinates $(x_2, y_2, z_2)$. Their position vectors are

$$
\begin{aligned}
r_1 &= x_1\hat{i} + y_1\hat{j} + z_1\hat{k} \\
r_2 &= x_2\hat{i} + y_2\hat{j} + z_2\hat{k}
\end{aligned}
$$

Since $r_1 + \overrightarrow{PQ} = r_2$, we obtain

$$
\overrightarrow{PQ} = r_2 - r_1 = (x_2 - x_1)\hat{i} + (y_2 - y_1)\hat{j} + (z_2 - z_1)\hat{k}
$$

The magnitude of $\overrightarrow{PQ}$ is the distance between $P$ and $Q$:

$$
\lvert \overrightarrow{PQ} \rvert = \sqrt{(x_2 - x_1)^2 + (y_2 - y_1)^2 + (z_2 - z_1)^2}
$$

### 2.9 Direction Cosines

The direction of a vector in three dimensions is determined by the angles it makes with the three axes of reference. Let

$$
\overrightarrow{OP} = r = a\hat{i} + b\hat{j} + c\hat{k}
$$

and let $\alpha$, $\beta$, $\gamma$ be the angles the vector makes with the $x$, $y$ and $z$ axes respectively. Then

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{a}{r} &= \cos\alpha \quad \text{so} \quad a = r\cos\alpha \\
\frac{b}{r} &= \cos\beta \quad \text{so} \quad b = r\cos\beta \\
\frac{c}{r} &= \cos\gamma \quad \text{so} \quad c = r\cos\gamma
\end{aligned}
$$

> **Definition (Direction cosines).** The numbers $[l, m, n]$ written in square brackets are called the direction cosines of the vector $\overrightarrow{OP}$; they are the cosines of the angles which the vector makes with the three axes of reference. For $r = a\hat{i} + b\hat{j} + c\hat{k}$,

> 

$$
> l = \frac{a}{r}, \qquad m = \frac{b}{r}, \qquad n = \frac{c}{r}
>
$$

> where $r = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2 + c^2}$.

## 3. Key Theorems & Essential Results

### 3.1 The Direction Cosine Identity

> **Theorem.** For any vector with direction cosines $l$, $m$, $n$,

> 

$$
> l^2 + m^2 + n^2 = 1
>
$$

**Proof.** Start from the component relations $a = r\cos\alpha$, $b = r\cos\beta$, $c = r\cos\gamma$ and from the magnitude relation $a^2 + b^2 + c^2 = r^2$. Substituting the component relations into the magnitude relation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
r^2\cos^2\alpha + r^2\cos^2\beta + r^2\cos^2\gamma &= r^2 \\
\cos^2\alpha + \cos^2\beta + \cos^2\gamma &= 1
\end{aligned}
$$

Writing $l = \cos\alpha$, $m = \cos\beta$, $n = \cos\gamma$ yields $l^2 + m^2 + n^2 = 1$. $\blacksquare$

This identity is a powerful check: any triple of numbers offered as direction cosines must satisfy it, and any two of the three determine the third up to sign.

### 3.2 The Unit Vector Result

> **Result.** If $A$ is a non-zero vector, then $\hat{a} = A / \lvert A \rvert$ has magnitude $1$ and the same direction as $A$.

**Proof.** The magnitude of $\hat{a}$ is $\lvert A \rvert / \lvert A \rvert = 1$. Since $\lvert A \rvert > 0$, dividing by it does not reverse the direction. $\blacksquare$

### 3.3 The Resultant of a Chain

> **Result.** For vectors $a, b, c, d$ drawn as a chain, the resultant is the single vector joining the start of the first to the end of the last. If the chain closes, the resultant is the zero vector.

This follows by repeated application of the definition of vector addition, as shown in Section 2.3.

### 3.4 The Distance Formula

> **Result.** The distance between points $P(x_1, y_1, z_1)$ and $Q(x_2, y_2, z_2)$ is

> 

$$
> \lvert \overrightarrow{PQ} \rvert = \sqrt{(x_2 - x_1)^2 + (y_2 - y_1)^2 + (z_2 - z_1)^2}
>
$$

This is the three-dimensional form of Pythagoras' theorem, obtained by taking the magnitude of the difference of the two position vectors.

### 3.5 The Parallelogram Diagonal Result

> **Result.** In a parallelogram with adjacent side vectors $a$ and $b$, the diagonals are $a + b$ and $b - a$, and the diagonals bisect each other.

**Proof.** Let the parallelogram have vertices with $\overrightarrow{AC} = a + b$ and $\overrightarrow{BD} = b - a$. Let $P$ be the point where the diagonals meet. Write $\overrightarrow{AP} = x\,\overrightarrow{AC}$ and $\overrightarrow{BP} = y\,\overrightarrow{BD}$ for scalars $x$ and $y$. Then

$$
\overrightarrow{AB} + \overrightarrow{BP} = \overrightarrow{AP}
$$

so that

$$
a + y(b - a) = x(a + b)
$$

Comparing coefficients of $a$ and of $b$ on the left and right gives $x = y = \tfrac{1}{2}$, so $P$ is the midpoint of both diagonals. $\blacksquare$

### 3.6 The Equation of a Straight Line Through Two Points

> **Result.** The straight line through points with position vectors $a$ and $b$ consists of all points with position vector

> 

$$
> r = a + t(b - a)
>
$$

> where $t$ is a scalar.

**Derivation.** Let $r$ be the position vector of any point $P$ on the line through $A$ and $B$. Then $\overrightarrow{OA} + \overrightarrow{AP} = \overrightarrow{OP}$, and since $\overrightarrow{AP} = t\,\overrightarrow{AB}$ for some scalar $t$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\overrightarrow{OP} &= \overrightarrow{OA} + t\,\overrightarrow{AB} \\
r &= a + t(b - a)
\end{aligned}
$$

If the equation is written as $a - ta - tb - r = 0$, the sum of the coefficients of the vectors is zero, which is the standard test that the four vectors are coplanar in the sense of lying in one line configuration.

## 4. Worked Exemplar Problem with Step-by-Step Solution

### 4.1 The Problem

Find the unit vector parallel to the resultant of the vectors

$$
r_1 = 2\hat{i} + 4\hat{j} - 5\hat{k}, \qquad r_2 = \hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + 3\hat{k}
$$

### 4.2 Step 1 — Form the Resultant

Add the two vectors component by component: add the $\hat{i}$ parts together, the $\hat{j}$ parts together, and the $\hat{k}$ parts together.

$$
\begin{aligned}
R &= r_1 + r_2 \\
&= (2\hat{i} + 4\hat{j} - 5\hat{k}) + (\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + 3\hat{k}) \\
&= 3\hat{i} + 6\hat{j} - 2\hat{k}
\end{aligned}
$$

In words: the $x$-component is $2 + 1 = 3$; the $y$-component is $4 + 2 = 6$; the $z$-component is $-5 + 3 = -2$.

### 4.3 Step 2 — Compute the Magnitude of the Resultant

Square each component, add the squares, and take the square root.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\lvert R \rvert &= \sqrt{3^2 + 6^2 + (-2)^2} \\
&= \sqrt{9 + 36 + 4} \\
&= \sqrt{49} \\
&= 7
\end{aligned}
$$

The resultant has length $7$.

### 4.4 Step 3 — Divide by the Magnitude

A unit vector in the direction of $R$ is obtained by dividing $R$ by its magnitude:

$$
\hat{r} = \frac{R}{\lvert R \rvert} = \frac{1}{7}\left(3\hat{i} + 6\hat{j} - 2\hat{k}\right)
$$

Equivalently, component by component,

$$
\hat{r} = \frac{3}{7}\hat{i} + \frac{6}{7}\hat{j} - \frac{2}{7}\hat{k}
$$

### 4.5 Step 4 — Verify the Answer

Check that the result really has length $1$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\lvert \hat{r} \rvert &= \sqrt{\left(\frac{3}{7}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{6}{7}\right)^2 + \left(-\frac{2}{7}\right)^2} \\
&= \sqrt{\frac{9}{49} + \frac{36}{49} + \frac{4}{49}} \\
&= \sqrt{\frac{49}{49}} \\
&= 1
\end{aligned}
$$

The verification succeeds, so the unit vector is correct.

### 4.6 A Second Worked Example — Direction Cosines

Find the direction cosines $[l, m, n]$ of the vector $r = 3\hat{i} - 2\hat{j} + 6\hat{k}$.

Here $a = 3$, $b = -2$, $c = 6$. First compute the magnitude:

$$
\begin{aligned}
r &= \sqrt{3^2 + (-2)^2 + 6^2} \\
&= \sqrt{9 + 4 + 36} \\
&= \sqrt{49} \\
&= 7
\end{aligned}
$$

Then divide each component by the magnitude:

$$
l = \frac{3}{7}, \qquad m = -\frac{2}{7}, \qquad n = \frac{6}{7}
$$

As a check, $l^2 + m^2 + n^2 = \frac{9}{49} + \frac{4}{49} + \frac{36}{49} = \frac{49}{49} = 1$, as the identity requires.

### 4.7 A Third Worked Example — Vector Between Two Points

Find the vector with initial point $P(x_1, y_1, z_1)$ and terminal point $Q(x_2, y_2, z_2)$, and its magnitude.

The position vectors are $r_1 = x_1\hat{i} + y_1\hat{j} + z_1\hat{k}$ and $r_2 = x_2\hat{i} + y_2\hat{j} + z_2\hat{k}$. Since $r_1 + \overrightarrow{PQ} = r_2$,

$$
\overrightarrow{PQ} = r_2 - r_1 = (x_2 - x_1)\hat{i} + (y_2 - y_1)\hat{j} + (z_2 - z_1)\hat{k}
$$

and its magnitude, which is the distance between $P$ and $Q$, is

$$
\lvert \overrightarrow{PQ} \rvert = \sqrt{(x_2 - x_1)^2 + (y_2 - y_1)^2 + (z_2 - z_1)^2}
$$

### 4.8 A Fourth Worked Example — Resultant of Displacements

Find the resultant of the displacements: $A$ of $10$ m northwest; $B$ of $20$ m at $30^\circ$ north of east; $C$ of $35$ m due south.

Draw the three displacements as a chain, using a stated scale such as $1$ cm representing $5$ m. Start $B$ where $A$ ends, and start $C$ where $B$ ends. The resultant $D$ is the single vector from the start of $A$ to the end of $C$, so $D = A + B + C$. Measuring the resultant against the scale gives a magnitude of about $4.1$ scale units, that is $20.5$ m, and a direction of about $60^\circ$ south of east.

The lesson here is that the chain method works for any number of vectors, and that a careful scale drawing gives both the magnitude and the direction of the resultant.

## 5. High-Yield Exam Takeaways & Common Pitfalls

### 5.1 High-Yield Takeaways

- **Scalar versus vector.** A scalar has magnitude only; a vector has magnitude and direction. Be ready to classify a list of physical quantities.
- **Equality of vectors.** Two vectors are equal when both magnitude and direction agree, regardless of where they are drawn. Sliding a vector does not change it; reversing it multiplies it by $-1$.
- **Chain rule for addition.** Place vectors tip to tail; the resultant runs from the first tail to the last tip. A closed chain gives the zero vector.
- **The two laws.** Addition is commutative, $A + B = B + A$, and associative, $A + (B + C) = (A + B) + C$. These justify adding vectors in any order.
- **Component form.** $A = A_1\hat{i} + A_2\hat{j} + A_3\hat{k}$, and the position vector of $(x, y, z)$ is $r = x\hat{i} + y\hat{j} + z\hat{k}$.
- **Magnitude formula.** $\lvert A \rvert = \sqrt{A_1^2 + A_2^2 + A_3^2}$. This is Pythagoras' theorem applied twice.
- **Unit vector formula.** $\hat{a} = A / \lvert A \rvert$, valid only when $\lvert A \rvert \neq 0$.
- **Distance formula.** $\lvert \overrightarrow{PQ} \rvert = \sqrt{(x_2 - x_1)^)^2 + (y_2 - y_1)^2 + (z_2 - z_1)^2}$.
- **Direction cosines.** $l = a/r$, $m = b/r$, $n = c/r$ with $r = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2 + c^2}$, and always $l^2 + m^2 + n^2 = 1$.
- **Line through two points.** $r = a + t(b - a)$ with $t$ a scalar; the sum of the coefficients of the vectors in the rearranged form is zero.
- **Parallelogram diagonals.** The diagonals are $a + b$ and $b - a$, and they bisect each other at their common midpoint.

### 5.2 Common Pitfalls

- **Forgetting the direction.** Writing only "a force of $5$ N" is incomplete; a vector answer must state magnitude and direction, or be given in component form.
- **Sign errors in components.** A component such as $-5$ must be squared as $(-5)^2 = 25$, not $-25$. The magnitude is never negative.
- **Dropping the square root.** The magnitude is $\sqrt{A_1^2 + A_2^2 + A_3^2}$, not $A_1^2 + A_2^2 + A_3^2$. The squared quantity is the square of the length, not the length.
- **Dividing by zero.** A unit vector exists only for a non-zero vector. If $\lvert A \rvert = 0$, the expression $A/\lvert A \rvert$ is undefined.
- **Reversing the subtraction.** The vector from $P$ to $Q$ is $r_2 - r_1$, not $r_1 - r_2$. Reversing it gives the opposite direction.
- **Mixing up direction cosines with components.** The components are $a$, $b$, $c$; the direction cosines are $a/r$, $b/r$, $c/r$. They are not the same numbers unless $r = 1$.
- **Forgetting the identity check.** After computing direction cosines, always verify $l^2 + m^2 + n^2 = 1$. If it fails, an arithmetic slip has occurred.
- **Assuming a closed chain has a non-zero resultant.** If the end of the last vector meets the start of the first, the resultant is the zero vector, not the perimeter.
- **Adding magnitudes instead of vectors.** Two vectors of magnitudes $5$ and $12$ do not generally have resultant $17$; that happens only when they point the same way. At right angles the resultant is $13$.
- **Losing the scale in graphical work.** When a drawing is used, state the scale and measure both magnitude and direction; a magnitude without a direction is only half the answer.

### 5.3 Recommended Reading

The following standard texts support the material in this unit and are useful for further practice:

- Davis, H. — introductory treatments of vector representation, components and vector algebra.
- Lewis, P. — worked exercises on magnitude, unit vectors and resultants.
- Spiegel, M. — extensive solved problems on vectors and scalars, components and direction cosines.
- Tai, C. — vector methods with applications to geometry and mechanics.

### 5.4 Assessment Guidance

Assessment in this unit typically asks the learner to:

- define scalar and vector quantities and classify given physical quantities;
- draw a chain of vectors to a stated scale and read off the resultant;
- state and illustrate the commutative and associative laws of addition;
- express a vector in component form and compute its magnitude;
- find a unit vector parallel to a given vector or to a resultant;
- find the vector joining two points and the distance between them;
- compute direction cosines and verify the identity $l^2 + m^2 + n^2 = 1$;
- prove elementary geometric results such as the bisection of parallelogram diagonals, and derive the equation of a line through two points.

A sound strategy for any assessment item is to write the vectors in component form first, then apply the magnitude, unit vector or direction cosine formula, and finally verify the answer against the identity or by substitution.

## 1. Core Concept Overview & Intuition

Physical quantities fall into two broad classes. A **scalar** is fully specified by a single real number together with a unit: mass, length, time, temperature, and any real number are scalars. A **vector** requires both a magnitude and a direction: displacement, velocity, force, and acceleration are vectors. The whole of vector algebra is built on the single idea that a vector is an ordered geometric object — an arrow — and that arrows may be added, subtracted, and rescaled by numbers while obeying a small, consistent set of algebraic laws.

Geometrically, a vector is drawn as a directed line segment. The **length** of the segment encodes the magnitude according to a stated scale, the **orientation** of the segment encodes the direction, and the **arrowhead** encodes the sense. The point where the arrow begins is the **initial point**; the point where it ends is the **terminal point**. The vector from $O$ to $P$ is written $\overrightarrow{OP}$ or, analytically, as a single letter with an arrow, $\vec{A}$. Reversing the arrowhead gives $\overrightarrow{PO}$, which has the same magnitude as $\overrightarrow{OP}$ but the opposite sense, and is written $-\vec{A}$. Two vectors are **equal** precisely when they have the same magnitude and the same direction, regardless of where their initial points sit — so a vector may be translated anywhere in space without changing it.

Addition is the central operation. To add $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$, draw them as a chain: start the second where the first ends. The **resultant** is the single vector joining the start of the first to the end of the second. In symbols, if $\overrightarrow{AB}=\vec{a}$ and $\overrightarrow{BC}=\vec{b}$, then $\overrightarrow{AC}=\vec{a}+\vec{b}$. Chaining many vectors $ \vec{a}+\vec{b}+\vec{c}+\vec{d} $ gives a single vector joining the start of the first to the end of the last. If the chain closes on itself — the end of the last vector coincides with the start of the first — the resultant has zero magnitude.

The intuition to carry into every examination is this: **addition of vectors is ordinary bookkeeping of displacements**. Walking $10$ m northwest, then $20$ m at $30^\circ$ north of east, then $35$ m due south leaves you at a single net displacement from your starting point, and that net displacement is the resultant. The magnitude of the resultant is found by the Pythagorean theorem when the components are perpendicular, and by resolving into perpendicular components in general.![the vector ⃗⃗⃗⃗⃗ has an initial point O and final point P and is analytically represented by a letter with an arrow over it, as.](/cdn/cloudflare/prep/visual-crops/2026/10/document-78861d46-43b4-4804-b6c3-11ae1fc63403-page-9-e84fe630.jpg)

## 2. Mathematical Formalization & Core Definitions

> **Definition (Vector and Scalar).** A vector is a quantity having both magnitude and direction, such as displacement, velocity, force, and acceleration. A scalar is a quantity having magnitude but no direction, such as mass, length, time, temperature, and any real number.

> **Definition (Vector Representation).** A vector quantity is represented graphically by a line drawn so that the length of the line denotes the magnitude according to a stated vector scale, the direction of the line denotes the direction in which the quantity acts, and an arrowhead indicates the sense. The vector $\overrightarrow{OP}$ has initial point $O$ and terminal point $P$ and is written analytically as $\vec{A}$; its magnitude is denoted $\lvert\vec{A}\rvert$ or simply $A$. The vector $\overrightarrow{PO}$ has the same magnitude but the opposite sense, so $\overrightarrow{PO}=-\vec{A}$.

> **Definition (Equality of Vectors).** Two vectors $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$ are equal if they have the same magnitude and direction, regardless of the position of their initial points; thus $\vec{A}=\vec{B}$.

> **Definition (Addition of Vectors).** The sum of two vectors $\overrightarrow{AB}$ and $\overrightarrow{BC}$ is the single equivalent resultant vector $\overrightarrow{AC}$, that is $\overrightarrow{AB}+\overrightarrow{BC}=\overrightarrow{AC}$, or $\vec{a}+\vec{b}=\vec{c}$. To add two vectors, draw them as a chain, starting the second where the first ends; the sum is the single vector joining the start of the first to the end of the second.

> **Definition (Components of a Vector).** Any vector $\vec{A}$ in three dimensions may be represented with initial point at the origin $O$ of a rectangular coordinate system. If $(A_1,A_2,A_3)$ are the rectangular coordinates of its terminal point, the vectors $A_1\hat{\imath}$, $A_2\hat{\jmath}$, $A_3\hat{k}$ are the component vectors of $\vec{A}$ in the $x$, $y$, and $z$ directions respectively, and the resultant is



$$
\vec{A}=A_1\hat{\imath}+A_2\hat{\jmath}+A_3\hat{k}.
$$



> **Definition (Magnitude).** The magnitude of $\vec{A}=A_1\hat{\imath}+A_2\hat{\jmath}+A_3\hat{k}$ is



$$
A=\lvert\vec{A}\rvert=\sqrt{A_1^{2}+A_2^{2}+A_3^{2}}.
$$



> In particular the position vector (radius vector) from $O$ to the point $(x,y,z)$ is $\vec{r}=x\hat{\imath}+y\hat{\jmath}+z\hat{k}$ with magnitude $\lvert\vec{r}\rvert=\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}}$.

> **Definition (Unit Vector).** A unit vector is a vector having unit magnitude. If $\vec{A}$ is a vector with magnitude $A\neq 0$, then



$$
\hat{a}=\frac{\vec{A}}{A}
$$



> is a unit vector having the same direction as $\vec{A}$.

> **Definition (Direction Cosines).** The direction of a vector in three dimensions is determined by the angles it makes with the three axes of reference. For $\overrightarrow{OP}=\vec{r}=a\hat{\imath}+b\hat{\jmath}+c\hat{k}$ with $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ the angles made with the $x$, $y$, $z$ axes respectively,



$$
l=\cos\alpha=\frac{a}{r},\qquad m=\cos\beta=\frac{b}{r},\qquad n=\cos\gamma=\frac{c}{r},
$$



> where $r=\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}}$. The triple $[l,m,n]$ is called the direction cosines of $\overrightarrow{OP}$.

**Vector from one point to another.** If $P(x_1,y_1,z_1)$ and $Q(x_2,y_2,z_2)$ have position vectors $\vec{r}_1$ and $\vec{r}_2$, then $\vec{r}_1+\overrightarrow{PQ}=\vec{r}_2$, so



$$
\overrightarrow{PQ}=\vec{r}_2-\vec{r}_1=(x_2-x_1)\hat{\imath}+(y_2-y_1)\hat{\jmath}+(z_2-z_1)\hat{k},
$$



and its magnitude



$$
\lvert\overrightarrow{PQ}\rvert=\sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^{2}+(y_2-y_1)^{2}+(z_2-z_1)^{2}}
$$



is the distance between $P$ and $Q$. The order matters: the initial point's coordinates are subtracted from the terminal point's, so the vector always points from $P$ to $Q$. Reversing the order gives $\overrightarrow{QP}=\vec{r}_1-\vec{r}_2=-\overrightarrow{PQ}$, the same segment traversed in the opposite sense.

**The algebraic laws of addition.** If $\vec{A}$, $\vec{B}$, $\vec{C}$ are vectors and $m$, $n$ are scalars, then:

| Law | Statement | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Commutative | $\vec{A}+\vec{B}=\vec{B}+\vec{A}$ | Order of addition is immaterial |
| Associative | $\vec{A}+(\vec{B}+\vec{C})=(\vec{A}+\vec{B})+\vec{C}$ | Grouping of addition is immaterial |

The commutative law follows from the parallelogram: with $\overrightarrow{OP}=\vec{A}$ and $\overrightarrow{PQ}=\vec{B}$ giving $\overrightarrow{OQ}=\vec{C}$, and with $\overrightarrow{OR}=\vec{B}$ and $\overrightarrow{RQ}=\vec{A}$ also giving $\overrightarrow{OQ}=\vec{C}$, both routes yield the same resultant. The associative law follows from a quadrilateral chain: $\overrightarrow{OP}+\overrightarrow{PQ}=\overrightarrow{OQ}=\vec{A}+\vec{B}$ and $\overrightarrow{PQ}+\overrightarrow{QR}=\overrightarrow{PR}=\vec{B}+\vec{C}$, and both $\overrightarrow{OP}+\overrightarrow{PR}$ and $\overrightarrow{OQ}+\overrightarrow{QR}$ equal $\overrightarrow{OR}=\vec{D}$. Hence the order of addition of any number of vectors is immaterial.

**Resolution into perpendicular components.** The practical engine of the topic is resolution. A displacement of magnitude $F$ at an angle $\theta$ measured from a reference axis contributes $F\cos\theta$ along that axis and $F\sin\theta$ perpendicular to it. Summing the contributions of every vector along each axis gives the components of the resultant, and the magnitude follows from the Pythagorean theorem. The direction is reported as an angle measured from a named axis, with the quadrant stated explicitly (for example, "south of east").

## 3. Key Theorems & Essential Results

> **Result (Magnitude of a Sum of Perpendicular Vectors).** If $\vec{p}$ and $\vec{q}$ are perpendicular, the magnitude of the resultant $\vec{r}=\vec{p}+\vec{q}$ satisfies



$$
r^{2}=p^{2}+q^{2},\qquad r=\sqrt{p^{2}+q^{2}}.
$$



> **Result (Unit Vector Parallel to a Resultant).** If $\vec{R}=\vec{r}_1+\vec{r}_2+\cdots$, then the unit vector parallel to $\vec{R}$ is



$$
\hat{r}=\frac{\vec{R}}{\lvert\vec{R}\rvert},
$$



> and it satisfies $\lvert\hat{r}\rvert=1$.

> **Result (Fundamental Identity for Direction Cosines).** For any vector with direction cosines $[l,m,n]$,



$$
l^{2}+m^{2}+n^{2}=1.
$$



> Indeed $a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}=r^{2}$ gives $r^{2}\cos^{2}\alpha+r^{2}\cos^{2}\beta+r^{2}\cos^{2}\gamma=r^{2}$, hence $\cos^{2}\alpha+\cos^{2}\beta+\cos^{2}\gamma=1$.

> **Result (Zero Resultant of a Closed Chain).** If a chain of vectors forms a closed figure, so that the end of the last vector coincides with the beginning of the first, the resultant sum is a vector with no magnitude, that is $\vec{a}+\vec{b}+\vec{c}+\cdots=\vec{0}$.

**Why the identity holds.** The direction cosines are the ratios of the components to the magnitude. Squaring each ratio and adding recovers the sum of the squared components divided by $r^{2}$, which is exactly $1$ because the squared components add to $r^{2}$. This identity is the standard check on any computed set of direction cosines.

## 4. Worked Exemplar Problem with Step-by-Step Solution

**Problem.** Find the sum or resultant of the following displacements: $A$: $10$ m Northwest; $B$: $20$ m at $30^\circ$ north of east; $C$: $35$ m due south. Report the magnitude and the direction of the resultant.

**Step 1 — Fix a convention.** Take east as the positive $x$-axis and north as the positive $y$-axis. A displacement of magnitude $F$ at angle $\theta$ measured from east contributes $F\cos\theta$ east and $F\sin\theta$ north; a southerly or westerly sense is recorded by the sign of the component. Northwest means $45^\circ$ north of west.

**Step 2 — Resolve each displacement.**

| Vector | Magnitude (m) | Direction | East component (m) | North component (m) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $A$ | $10$ | Northwest | $-10\cos 45^\circ$ | $10\sin 45^\circ$ |
| $B$ | $20$ | $30^\circ$ north of east | $20\cos 30^\circ$ | $20\sin 30^\circ$ |
| $C$ | $35$ | due south | $0$ | $-35$ |

**Step 3 — Evaluate the components numerically.**



$$
A:\quad -10\cos 45^\circ=-7.07,\qquad 10\sin 45^\circ=7.07
$$





$$
B:\quad 20\cos 30^\circ=17.32,\qquad 20\sin 30^\circ=10.00
$$





$$
C:\quad 0.00,\qquad -35.00
$$



**Step 4 — Sum the components.**



$$
R_x=-7.07+17.32+0.00=10.25
$$





$$
R_y=7.07+10.00-35.00=-17.93
$$



**Step 5 — Compute the magnitude.**



$$
\lvert\vec{R}\rvert=\sqrt{(10.25)^{2}+(-17.93)^{2}}=\sqrt{105.06+321.48}=\sqrt{426.54}\approx 20.5\ \text{m}
$$



**Step 6 — Compute the direction.** The east component is positive and the north component is negative, so the resultant points south of east. The angle below the eastward axis is



$$
\theta=\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{17.93}{10.25}\right)\approx 60.2^\circ.
$$



The resultant therefore has magnitude approximately $20.5$ m in a direction approximately $60^\circ$ south of east, which is the standard answer $60^\circ$ south of east.

**Step 7 — Sanity check.** The southward pull of $C$ dominates the northward contributions of $A$ and $B$, while $B$ supplies the largest eastward contribution, so a resultant of about $20$ m pointing south-east is physically reasonable. Always state the quadrant explicitly; a bare angle is incomplete and loses marks.

**A second pattern: unit vector parallel to a resultant.** Given $\vec{r}_1=2\hat{\imath}+4\hat{\jmath}-5\hat{k}$ and $\vec{r}_2=\hat{\imath}+2\hat{\jmath}+3\hat{k}$, first form the resultant



$$
\vec{R}=\vec{r}_1+\vec{r}_2=(2+1)\hat{\imath}+(4+2)\hat{\jmath}+(-5+3)\hat{k}=3\hat{\imath}+6\hat{\jmath}-2\hat{k}.
$$



Its magnitude is



$$
\lvert\vec{R}\rvert=\sqrt{3^{2}+6^{2}+(-2)^{2}}=\sqrt{9+36+4}=\sqrt{49}=7.
$$



The unit vector parallel to $\vec{R}$ is therefore



$$
\hat{r}=\frac{\vec{R}}{\lvert\vec{R}\rvert}=\frac{1}{7}\left(3\hat{\imath}+6\hat{\jmath}-2\hat{k}\right).
$$



Verification that $\lvert\hat{r}\rvert=1$ is expected in a full answer: $\tfrac{1}{49}(9+36+4)=1$.

**A third pattern: direction cosines.** For $\vec{r}=3\hat{\imath}-2\hat{\jmath}+6\hat{k}$ we have $a=3$, $b=-2$, $c=6$ and



$$
r=\sqrt{9+4+36}=\sqrt{49}=7,
$$



so the direction cosines are



$$
l=\frac{3}{7},\qquad m=-\frac{2}{7},\qquad n=\frac{6}{7},
$$



and indeed $l^{2}+m^{2}+n^{2}=\tfrac{9+4+36}{49}=1$. Note the sign of $m$: a component in the negative $y$ direction produces an obtuse angle with the $y$-axis, and dropping that sign is a standard error.

## 5. High-Yield Exam Takeaways & Common Pitfalls

**What examiners repeatedly test.**

- The definitional distinction between scalar and vector, with correctly classified examples.
- The magnitude formula $\lvert\vec{A}\rvert=\sqrt{A_1^{2}+A_2^{2}+A_3^{2}}$ and the unit vector $\hat{a}=\vec{A}/A$.
- The vector between two points, $\overrightarrow{PQ}=\vec{r}_2-\vec{r}_1$, and its magnitude as the distance between them.
- The resultant of a set of displacements given as bearings or as "degrees north/south of east/west", requiring resolution into components.
- Direction cosines and the identity $l^{2}+m^{2}+n^{2}=1$.
- The commutative and associative laws of vector addition, with the parallelogram and quadrilateral chain justifications.

**Answer structure that earns full marks.**

1. State the coordinate convention (which axis is east, which is north) and the sign convention for southerly and westerly components.
2. Resolve every vector into its components, keeping the trigonometric factor explicit before evaluating numerically.
3. Sum the components axis by axis, showing the arithmetic.
4. Compute the magnitude with the Pythagorean formula and the direction with the tangent ratio, naming the quadrant.
5. For unit-vector questions, divide by the magnitude and verify that the result has unit magnitude.
6. For direction-cosine questions, compute $r$ first, then each ratio, and check $l^{2}+m^{2}+n^{2}=1$.

**Common pitfalls.**

- Reporting a bare angle without naming the axis or quadrant; this is incomplete and loses marks.
- Dropping the sign of a component that points south or west, which corrupts both the magnitude and the direction.
- Confusing the order in $\overrightarrow{PQ}=\vec{r}_2-\vec{r}_1$; reversing it gives $-\overrightarrow{PQ}$, the opposite vector.
- Forgetting to divide by the magnitude when forming a unit vector, or dividing by the wrong quantity such as the sum of the components.
- Writing a direction cosine without its sign, which misplaces the vector in the wrong octant.
- Treating the magnitude of a sum as the sum of the magnitudes; $\lvert\vec{A}+\vec{B}\rvert=\lvert\vec{A}\rvert+\lvert\vec{B}\rvert$ holds only when the vectors are parallel and in the same sense.

## 1. Core Concept Overview & Intuition

Physical quantities fall into two broad classes. A **scalar** is a quantity possessing magnitude only, such as mass, length, time, temperature, or any real number. A **vector** is a quantity possessing both magnitude and direction, such as displacement, velocity, force, and acceleration. The distinction is not cosmetic: scalars combine by ordinary arithmetic, whereas vectors combine by a geometric law of addition that respects direction.

A vector is represented graphically by a directed line segment. The length of the segment encodes the magnitude according to a stated vector scale, the orientation of the segment encodes the direction of action, and an arrowhead encodes the sense. The vector from initial point $O$ to terminal point $P$ is written $\overrightarrow{OP}$ or $\vec{A}$, and its magnitude is written $\lvert\overrightarrow{OP}\rvert$ or $\lvert\vec{A}\rvert$. The reversed segment $\overrightarrow{PO}$ represents a vector of equal magnitude but opposite sense, denoted $-\vec{A}$. Two vectors $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$ are **equal**, written $\vec{A}=\vec{B}$, precisely when they have the same magnitude and the same direction, regardless of where their initial points are placed.

The central intuition of vector algebra is the **chain rule of addition**: to add vectors, place them head to tail, and the resultant is the single vector joining the start of the first to the end of the last. This construction is the engine behind every calculation in this unit — magnitudes via Pythagoras, unit vectors via normalization, and resultants of many displacements via successive chaining.

## 2. Mathematical Formalization & Core Definitions

> **Definition (Vector and Scalar).** A vector is a quantity having both magnitude and direction. A scalar is a quantity having magnitude but no direction.

> **Definition (Equality of Vectors).** Two vectors $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$ are equal if they have the same magnitude and direction, regardless of the position of their initial points.

> **Definition (Addition of Vectors).** The sum of two vectors $\overrightarrow{AB}$ and $\overrightarrow{BC}$ is the single equivalent vector $\overrightarrow{AC}$, that is $\overrightarrow{AB}+\overrightarrow{BC}=\overrightarrow{AC}$, or in letter notation $\vec{a}+\vec{b}=\vec{c}$.

The chain construction extends to any finite number of vectors. Drawing $\vec{a},\vec{b},\vec{c},\vec{d}$ head to tail gives



$$
\begin{aligned}
\vec{a}+\vec{b} &= \overrightarrow{AC}, \\
\overrightarrow{AC}+\vec{c} &= \overrightarrow{AD}, \\
\overrightarrow{AD}+\vec{d} &= \overrightarrow{AE}.
\end{aligned}
$$



Hence $\vec{a}+\vec{b}+\vec{c}+\vec{d}=\overrightarrow{AE}$, the single vector joining the start of the first to the end of the last. If the chain closes on itself — the end of the last vector coinciding with the beginning of the first — the resultant has no magnitude.

### Components of a Vector

Any vector $\vec{A}$ in three dimensions may be placed with initial point at the origin $O$ of a rectangular coordinate system. If $(A_1,A_2,A_3)$ are the rectangular coordinates of the terminal point, the vectors $A_1\hat{\imath}$, $A_2\hat{\jmath}$, $A_3\hat{k}$ are the **component vectors** of $\vec{A}$ in the $x$, $y$, and $z$ directions respectively, and their resultant is $\vec{A}$:



$$
\vec{A}=A_1\hat{\imath}+A_2\hat{\jmath}+A_3\hat{k}.
$$



The **magnitude** of $\vec{A}$ is obtained by applying Pythagoras' theorem twice (once in the base plane, once vertically):



$$
\lvert\vec{A}\rvert=\sqrt{A_1^{2}+A_2^{2}+A_3^{2}}.
$$



In particular, the **position vector** (radius vector) from $O$ to the point $(x,y,z)$ is



$$
\vec{r}=x\hat{\imath}+y\hat{\jmath}+z\hat{k},
\qquad
\lvert\vec{r}\rvert=\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}}.
$$



> **Definition (Unit Vector).** A unit vector is a vector having unit magnitude. If $\vec{A}$ is a vector with magnitude $\lvert\vec{A}\rvert\neq 0$, then $\hat{a}=\dfrac{\vec{A}}{\lvert\vec{A}\rvert}$ is a unit vector having the same direction as $\vec{A}$.

The operation $\vec{A}\mapsto\vec{A}/\lvert\vec{A}\rvert$ is called **normalization**. It rescales the vector to length one while preserving direction, and it is the standard device for extracting a pure direction from a computed resultant.

### Vector from One Point to Another

Let $P(x_1,y_1,z_1)$ and $Q(x_2,y_2,z_2)$ have position vectors



$$
\vec{r}_1=x_1\hat{\imath}+y_1\hat{\jmath}+z_1\hat{k},
\qquad
\vec{r}_2=x_2\hat{\imath}+y_2\hat{\jmath}+z_2\hat{k}.
$$



Since $\vec{r}_1+\overrightarrow{PQ}=\vec{r}_2$, the displacement from $P$ to $Q$ is



$$
\overrightarrow{PQ}=\vec{r}_2-\vec{r}_1=(x_2-x_1)\hat{\imath}+(y_2-y_1)\hat{\jmath}+(z_2-z_1)\hat{k},
$$



with magnitude



$$
\lvert\overrightarrow{PQ}\rvert=\sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^{2}+(y_2-y_1)^{2}+(z_2-z_1)^{2}},
$$



which is exactly the distance between $P$ and $Q$.

### Direction Cosines

The direction of a vector in three dimensions is fixed by the angles it makes with the three coordinate axes. Let $\vec{r}=a\hat{\imath}+b\hat{\jmath}+c\hat{k}$ with magnitude $r=\lvert\vec{r}\rvert$, and let $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ be the angles made with the $x$, $y$, and $z$ axes respectively. Then



$$
\frac{a}{r}=\cos\alpha,\qquad \frac{b}{r}=\cos\beta,\qquad \frac{c}{r}=\cos\gamma.
$$



Squaring and adding, and using $a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}=r^{2}$,



$$
\begin{aligned}
r^{2}\cos^{2}\alpha+r^{2}\cos^{2}\beta+r^{2}\cos^{2}\gamma &= r^{2}, \\
\cos^{2}\alpha+\cos^{2}\beta+\cos^{2}\gamma &= 1.
\end{aligned}
$$



Writing $l=\cos\alpha$, $m=\cos\beta$, $n=\cos\gamma$, the triple $[l,m,n]$ is called the set of **direction cosines** of $\vec{r}$, and



$$
l^{2}+m^{2}+n^{2}=1,
\qquad
l=\frac{a}{r},\quad m=\frac{b}{r},\quad n=\frac{c}{r}.
$$



## 3. Key Theorems & Essential Results

> **Theorem (Commutative Law of Addition).** For any vectors $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$, $\vec{A}+\vec{B}=\vec{B}+\vec{A}$.

*Proof.* Construct the parallelogram with adjacent sides $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$. Along one route $\overrightarrow{OP}+\overrightarrow{PQ}=\overrightarrow{OQ}$, i.e. $\vec{A}+\vec{B}=\vec{C}$. Along the other route $\overrightarrow{OR}+\overrightarrow{RQ}=\overrightarrow{OQ}$, i.e. $\vec{B}+\vec{A}=\vec{C}$. Both routes terminate at the same point, hence $\vec{A}+\vec{B}=\vec{B}+\vec{A}$. $\square$

> **Theorem (Associative Law of Addition).** For any vectors $\vec{A},\vec{B},\vec{C}$, $\vec{A}+(\vec{B}+\vec{C})=(\vec{A}+\vec{B})+\vec{C}$.

*Proof.* Take points $O,P,Q,R$ with $\overrightarrow{OP}=\vec{A}$, $\overrightarrow{PQ}=\vec{B}$, $\overrightarrow{QR}=\vec{C}$, and let $\overrightarrow{OR}=\vec{D}$. Then $\overrightarrow{OP}+\overrightarrow{PQ}=\overrightarrow{OQ}=\vec{A}+\vec{B}$ and $\overrightarrow{PQ}+\overrightarrow{QR}=\overrightarrow{PR}=\vec{B}+\vec{C}$. Grouping the first way, $\overrightarrow{OP}+\overrightarrow{PR}=\overrightarrow{OR}=\vec{D}$, i.e. $\vec{A}+(\vec{B}+\vec{C})=\vec{D}$. Grouping the second way, $\overrightarrow{OQ}+\overrightarrow{QR}=\overrightarrow{OR}=\vec{D}$, i.e. $(\vec{A}+\vec{B})+\vec{C}=\vec{D}$. Hence the two groupings agree. $\square$

Consequently the order of addition of any number of vectors is immaterial, and a sum may be regrouped or reordered at will.

> **Result (Magnitude of a Resultant).** If $\vec{R}=\vec{r}_1+\vec{r}_2+\cdots+\vec{r}_n$ with $\vec{R}=R_1\hat{\imath}+R_2\hat{\jmath}+R_3\hat{k}$, then $\lvert\vec{R}\rvert=\sqrt{R_1^{2}+R_2^{2}+R_3^{2}}$, and a unit vector parallel to $\vec{R}$ is $\hat{r}=\vec{R}/\lvert\vec{R}\rvert$.

> **Result (Right-Angled Resultant).** If two vectors of magnitudes $p$ and $q$ act at right angles, the magnitude of their resultant satisfies $p^{2}+q^{2}=r^{2}$, so $r=\sqrt{p^{2}+q^{2}}$.

> **Result (Direction Cosine Identity).** For any nonzero vector, $l^{2}+m^{2}+n^{2}=1$.

> **Result (Collinearity and Coplanarity of Position Vectors).** Any vector $\vec{r}$ lying in the plane of two non-collinear vectors $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ can be written $\vec{r}=x\vec{a}+y\vec{b}$ for scalars $x,y$; in three-dimensional space, any vector can be written $\vec{r}=x\vec{a}+y\vec{b}+z\vec{c}$ for scalars $x,y,z$. Comparing coefficients of independent vectors on the two sides of an identity is a valid method of solution.

> **Result (Closed Vector Chain).** If a chain of vectors returns to its starting point, so that the terminal point of the last vector coincides with the initial point of the first, the resultant sum is a vector of zero magnitude.

## 4. Worked Exemplar Problem with Step-by-Step Solution

**Problem.** Find the unit vector parallel to the resultant of $\vec{r}_1=2\hat{\imath}+4\hat{\jmath}-5\hat{k}$ and $\vec{r}_2=\hat{\imath}+2\hat{\jmath}+3\hat{k}$, and verify that the resulting vector has unit magnitude.

**Step 1 — Form the resultant by componentwise addition.**



$$
\begin{aligned}
\vec{R} &= \vec{r}_1+\vec{r}_2 \\
&= (2\hat{\imath}+4\hat{\jmath}-5\hat{k})+(\hat{\imath}+2\hat{\jmath}+3\hat{k}) \\
&= 3\hat{\imath}+6\hat{\jmath}-2\hat{k}.
\end{aligned}
$$



**Step 2 — Compute the magnitude of the resultant.**



$$
\begin{aligned}
\lvert\vec{R}\rvert &= \sqrt{3^{2}+6^{2}+(-2)^{2}} \\
&= \sqrt{9+36+4} \\
&= \sqrt{49} \\
&= 7.
\end{aligned}
$$



**Step 3 — Normalize to obtain the unit vector.**



$$
\hat{r}=\frac{\vec{R}}{\lvert\vec{R}\rvert}=\frac{1}{7}\left(3\hat{\imath}+6\hat{\jmath}-2\hat{k}\right).
$$



**Step 4 — Verify unit magnitude.**



$$
\begin{aligned}
\lvert\hat{r}\rvert &= \sqrt{\left(\tfrac{3}{7}\right)^{2}+\left(\tfrac{6}{7}\right)^{2}+\left(-\tfrac{2}{7}\right)^{2}} \\
&= \frac{1}{7}\sqrt{9+36+4} \\
&= \frac{7}{7} \\
&= 1.
\end{aligned}
$$



The verification confirms the normalization is correct.

**Companion calculation (direction cosines).** For $\vec{r}=3\hat{\imath}-2\hat{\jmath}+6\hat{k}$ we have $a=3$, $b=-2$, $c=6$ and



$$
r=\sqrt{9+4+36}=\sqrt{49}=7,
$$



so the direction cosines are



$$
l=\frac{3}{7},\qquad m=-\frac{2}{7},\qquad n=\frac{6}{7},
$$



and indeed $l^{2}+m^{2}+n^{2}=\tfrac{9}{49}+\tfrac{4}{49}+\tfrac{36}{49}=1$.

**Companion calculation (right-angled resultant).** A force of $5\,\text{N}$ due East and a force of $12\,\text{N}$ due North act at right angles. By Pythagoras' theorem,



$$
\begin{aligned}
p^{2}+q^{2} &= r^{2}, \\
25+144 &= 169, \\
r &= \sqrt{169}=13\,\text{N}.
\end{aligned}
$$



**Companion calculation (resultant of several displacements).** For displacements $A$ of $10\,\text{m}$ Northwest, $B$ of $20\,\text{m}$ at $30^{\circ}$ north of east, and $C$ of $35\,\text{m}$ due south, the resultant is $\vec{D}=\vec{A}+\vec{B}+\vec{C}$, formed by joining the initial point of $A$ to the terminal point of $C$. Measured graphically on a scale of $5\,\text{m}$ per unit, the resultant has magnitude $4.1$ units, i.e. $20.5\,\text{m}$, and direction $60^{\circ}$ south of east.

**Companion calculation (displacement between two points).** For $P(x_1,y_1,z_1)$ and $Q(x_2,y_2,z_2)$,



$$
\overrightarrow{PQ}=(x_2-x_1)\hat{\imath}+(y_2-y_1)\hat{\jmath}+(z_2-z_1)\hat{k},
$$



whose magnitude is the distance between the points.

## 5. High-Yield Exam Takeaways & Common Pitfalls

### Lesson Learning Outcomes

By the end of this unit the student should be able to: distinguish scalar from vector quantities and classify physical examples of each; represent a vector graphically with a stated scale and analytically in component form; add any number of vectors by the chain construction and state the commutative and associative laws; compute the magnitude of a vector and of a resultant; normalize a vector to obtain a unit vector in a prescribed direction; compute the displacement vector between two points and its magnitude; and determine the direction cosines of a vector and verify the identity $l^{2}+m^{2}+n^{2}=1$.

### Magnitude, Unit Vector and Resultant — Calculation Checklist

| Task | Formula | Guard condition |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Magnitude in 3D | $\lvert\vec{A}\rvert=\sqrt{A_1^{2}+A_2^{2}+A_3^{2}}$ | none |
| Magnitude in 2D | $\lvert\vec{A}\rvert=\sqrt{A_1^{2}+A_2^{2}}$ | none |
| Unit vector | $\hat{a}=\vec{A}/\lvert\vec{A}\rvert$ | requires $\lvert\vec{A}\rvert\neq 0$ |
| Resultant | $\vec{R}=\sum_i\vec{r}_i$ componentwise | add like components only |
| Distance $PQ$ | $\lvert\overrightarrow{PQ}\rvert=\sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^{2}+(y_2-y_1)^{2}+(z_2-z_1)^{2}}$ | subtract in consistent order |
| Direction cosines | $l=a/r,\ m=b/r,\ n=c/r$ | check $l^{2}+m^{2}+n^{2}=1$ |
| Right-angled resultant | $r=\sqrt{p^{2}+q^{2}}$ | only for perpendicular components |

### Assessment

Assessment in this unit targets the following recurring question types: computing the resultant of a set of displacements given as bearings and distances, and reporting both magnitude and direction; finding a unit vector parallel to a computed resultant and verifying unit magnitude; finding the vector joining two given points together with its magnitude; extracting direction cosines from a component form; and proving elementary geometric facts by expressing position vectors in terms of two or three independent vectors and comparing coefficients. Marks are awarded for correct componentwise addition, correct magnitude evaluation, correct normalization, and explicit verification steps.

### Common Pitfalls

- **Adding magnitudes instead of vectors.** The magnitude of a sum is not the sum of magnitudes; $\lvert\vec{A}+\vec{B}\rvert\neq\lvert\vec{A}\rvert+\lvert\vec{B}\rvert$ in general. Always add componentwise first, then take the magnitude.
- **Sign errors in components.** A component directed along the negative axis carries a minus sign; squaring removes it in the magnitude but not in the direction cosines, where $m=-\tfrac{2}{7}$ must retain its sign.
- **Forgetting the guard condition.** Normalization is undefined for the zero vector; a closed vector chain has zero resultant and admits no unit vector.
- **Mixing up initial and terminal points.** The displacement is $\vec{r}_2-\vec{r}_1$, not $\vec{r}_1-\vec{r}_2$; the reversed order gives the opposite sense.
- **Omitting the verification.** When asked for a unit vector, always square and add the components to confirm the result equals one.
- **Treating direction cosines as angles.** The direction cosines are the cosines of the angles, not the angles themselves, and they satisfy $l^{2}+m^{2}+n^{2}=1$.
- **Assuming a graphical scale is exact.** Graphical construction gives an approximate magnitude and bearing; state the scale and round consistently with it.

### Prescribed Reading

The prescribed reading for this unit is the course material itself, whose opening chapter develops vector representation, addition of vectors, vector algebra, components of a vector, unit vectors and direction cosines, together with the worked examples on resultants of forces and displacements and on the displacement between two points. Students should work through that chapter's definitions and examples in full, since the definitions of scalar and vector quantities, the chain and parallelogram constructions, the component formalism and the direction-cosine identity used throughout this unit are all developed there.
