## 1. Core Concept Overview & Intuition

The algebra of vectors admits two distinct products, distinguished by the type of quantity they return. The product of two vectors that yields a scalar is called the **dot product** or **scalar product**; the product of two vectors that yields a vector is called the **cross product** or **vector product**. Both products encode geometric information about the two vectors — their magnitudes and the angle between them — and both are indispensable for describing physical situations and the geometry of lines, planes, and triangles in space.

The central intuition for the dot product is **projection**. When a vector $\mathbf{B}$ is projected onto the line of a vector $\mathbf{A}$, the length of that projection is $B\cos\theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between the vectors. Multiplying by $A$ gives $AB\cos\theta$, which is exactly the scalar product. Equivalently, one may project $\mathbf{A}$ onto $\mathbf{B}$ and multiply by $B$; the result is the same scalar. Thus the dot product measures the extent to which two vectors "point along" one another. When the vectors are perpendicular, the projection vanishes and the dot product is zero; when they are parallel, the projection is maximal and the dot product equals the product of magnitudes.

The central intuition for the cross product is **perpendicularity and area**. The cross product $\mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B}$ is a vector of magnitude $AB\sin\theta$ directed perpendicular to both $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$, with its sense fixed by the right-hand rule so that $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{B}$, and $\mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B}$ form a right-handed system in that order. Because $AB\sin\theta$ is the area of the parallelogram spanned by $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$, the cross product is the natural tool for computing areas of parallelograms and triangles, for producing vectors normal to planes, and for testing whether vectors are parallel.

A third layer of structure emerges when three vectors are combined. The **scalar triple product** $\mathbf{A}\cdot(\mathbf{B}\times\mathbf{C})$ returns a scalar whose absolute value is the volume of the parallelepiped with sides $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{B}$, $\mathbf{C}$, and which vanishes precisely when the three vectors are coplanar. The **vector triple product** $\mathbf{A}\times(\mathbf{B}\times\mathbf{C})$ returns a vector lying in the plane of $\mathbf{B}$ and $\mathbf{C}$, and it is not associative: the placement of parentheses changes the result.

Throughout, all vectors are referred to a right-handed set of mutually orthogonal unit vectors $\hat{i}$, $\hat{j}$, $\hat{k}$ along the $x$, $y$, $z$ axes respectively. The axes $OX$, $OY$, $OZ$ form a right-handed set if a rotation from $OX$ to $OY$ corresponds to a right-handed corkscrew action along the positive direction of $OZ$; similarly, a rotation from $OY$ to $OZ$ gives a right-handed corkscrew action along the positive direction of $OX$, and so on cyclically.

## 2. Mathematical Formalization & Core Definitions

### 2.1 The Dot or Scalar Product

> **Definition (Dot Product).** If $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ are two vectors, the scalar product of $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ is defined as $AB\cos\theta$, where $A$ and $B$ are the magnitudes of the vectors $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$, and $\theta$ is the angle between them. The scalar (dot) product is denoted by $\mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{B}$.

The definition may be read in either of two equivalent ways:

$$
\mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{B}=AB\cos\theta
$$

$$
\mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{B}=A\times(\text{projection of } \mathbf{B} \text{ on } \mathbf{A})
$$

$$
\mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{B}=B\times(\text{projection of } \mathbf{A} \text{ on } \mathbf{B})
$$

In either case the result is a scalar quantity.

**Magnitude of a vector.** The magnitude of a vector $\mathbf{A}=A_1\hat{i}+A_2\hat{j}+A_3\hat{k}$ is the square root of the sum of the squares of its components:

$$
A=\lVert \mathbf{A}\rVert=\sqrt{A_1^{2}+A_2^{2}+A_3^{2}}
$$

**Unit vector.** The unit vector in the direction of a non-zero vector $\mathbf{A}$ is obtained by dividing the vector by its magnitude:

$$
\hat{a}=\frac{\mathbf{A}}{A}=\frac{\mathbf{A}}{\lVert \mathbf{A}\rVert}
$$

This unit vector has magnitude $1$ and points in the same direction as $\mathbf{A}$.

**Resultant.** The resultant of two vectors is their vector sum $\mathbf{A}+\mathbf{B}$, obtained by adding corresponding components. Its magnitude is computed from the components of the sum using the magnitude formula above.

### 2.2 Special Angles and Orthogonality

When two vectors are at right angles, $\theta=90^{\circ}$, so that

$$
\mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{B}=AB\cos 90^{\circ}=AB\cdot 0=0
$$

Thus the scalar product of any two vectors at right angles to each other is always zero, and the two vectors are said to be **orthogonal** or **perpendicular** to one another.

When two vectors are in the same direction, $\theta=0^{\circ}$, so that

$$
\mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{B}=AB\cos 0^{\circ}=AB
$$

### 2.3 The Dot Product in Component Form

Write the two vectors in component form as

$$
\mathbf{A}=A_1\hat{i}+A_2\hat{j}+A_3\hat{k}
$$

$$
\mathbf{B}=B_1\hat{i}+B_2\hat{j}+B_3\hat{k}
$$

Expanding the product term by term gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{B}={}&A_1B_1\,\hat{i}\cdot\hat{i}+A_1B_2\,\hat{i}\cdot\hat{j}+A_1B_3\,\hat{i}\cdot\hat{k}\\
&+A_2B_1\,\hat{j}\cdot\hat{i}+A_2B_2\,\hat{j}\cdot\hat{j}+A_2B_3\,\hat{j}\cdot\hat{k}\\
&+A_3B_1\,\hat{k}\cdot\hat{i}+A_3B_2\,\hat{k}\cdot\hat{j}+A_3B_3\,\hat{k}\cdot\hat{k}
\end{aligned}
$$

Now the parallel unit-vector products satisfy

$$
\hat{i}\cdot\hat{i}=\hat{j}\cdot\hat{j}=\hat{k}\cdot\hat{k}=1\cdot 1\cos 0^{\circ}=1
$$

and the perpendicular unit-vector products satisfy

$$
\hat{i}\cdot\hat{j}=\hat{i}\cdot\hat{k}=\hat{j}\cdot\hat{k}=1\cdot 1\cos 90^{\circ}=0
$$

All cross terms therefore vanish, and we are left with

$$
\mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{B}=A_1B_1+A_2B_2+A_3B_3
$$

This component formula is the principal computational tool for the dot product. It also yields the angle between two vectors through

$$
\cos\theta=\frac{\mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{B}}{AB}=\frac{A_1B_1+A_2B_2+A_3B_3}{\sqrt{A_1^{2}+A_2^{2}+A_3^{2}}\,\sqrt{B_1^{2}+B_2^{2}+B_3^{2}}}
$$

### 2.4 The Cross or Vector Product

> **Definition (Cross Product).** The cross or vector product of $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$, written $\mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B}$ and read as "$\mathbf{A}$ cross $\mathbf{B}$", is defined as a vector having the magnitude $AB\sin\theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between the two vectors. The product vector acts in a direction perpendicular to $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ in such a sense that $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{B}$, and $\mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B}$ form a right-handed system in that order.

The magnitude is

$$
\lVert \mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B}\rVert=AB\sin\theta
$$

Reversing the order reverses the direction of rotation, so the product vector acts downward:

$$
\mathbf{B}\times\mathbf{A}=-(\mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B})
$$

The cross product is therefore **anticommutative**.

**Special angles.** If $\theta=0^{\circ}$, then

$$
\lVert \mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B}\rVert=AB\sin 0^{\circ}=0
$$

so parallel vectors have zero cross product. If $\theta=90^{\circ}$, then

$$
\lVert \mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B}\rVert=AB\sin 90^{\circ}=AB
$$

so perpendicular vectors attain the maximum magnitude $AB$.

### 2.5 The Cross Product in Component Form

With $\mathbf{A}=A_1\hat{i}+A_2\hat{j}+A_3\hat{k}$ and $\mathbf{B}=B_1\hat{i}+B_2\hat{j}+B_3\hat{k}$, expansion gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B}={}&A_1B_1\,\hat{i}\times\hat{i}+A_1B_2\,\hat{i}\times\hat{j}+A_1B_3\,\hat{i}\times\hat{k}\\
&+A_2B_1\,\hat{j}\times\hat{i}+A_2B_2\,\hat{j}\times\hat{j}+A_2B_3\,\hat{j}\times\hat{k}\\
&+A_3B_1\,\hat{k}\times\hat{i}+A_3B_2\,\hat{k}\times\hat{j}+A_3B_3\,\hat{k}\times\hat{k}
\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\hat{i}\times\hat{i}=1\cdot 1\cdot\sin 0^{\circ}=0$, we have

$$
\hat{i}\times\hat{i}=\hat{j}\times\hat{j}=\hat{k}\times\hat{k}=0
$$

Also $\hat{i}\times\hat{j}=1\cdot 1\cdot\sin 90^{\circ}=1$ in the direction $OZ$, that is $\hat{i}\times\hat{j}=\hat{k}$. The complete set of unit-vector cross products is

$$
\hat{i}\times\hat{j}=\hat{k},\qquad \hat{j}\times\hat{i}=-\hat{k}
$$

$$
\hat{j}\times\hat{k}=\hat{i},\qquad \hat{k}\times\hat{j}=-\hat{i}
$$

$$
\hat{k}\times\hat{i}=\hat{j},\qquad \hat{i}\times\hat{k}=-\hat{j}
$$

Substituting and collecting components yields

$$
\mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B}=(A_2B_3-A_3B_2)\,\hat{i}+(A_3B_1-A_1B_3)\,\hat{j}+(A_1B_2-A_2B_1)\,\hat{k}
$$

This is recognized as the expansion of the determinant

$$
\mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B}=
\begin{vmatrix}
\hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k}\\
A_1 & A_2 & A_3\\
B_1 & B_2 & B_3
\end{vmatrix}
$$

The determinant form is the standard computational device: expand along the first row, remembering that the middle term carries a negative sign.

### 2.6 Vector Perpendicular to a Plane

The vector $\mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B}$ is perpendicular to the plane on which the vectors $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ lie. The right-hand thumb rule determines the direction of this perpendicular. To obtain the **unit** vector perpendicular to the plane, divide by the magnitude:

$$
\hat{n}=\frac{\mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B}}{\lVert \mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B}\rVert}
$$

### 2.7 Scalar Triple Product

> **Definition (Scalar Triple Product).** If $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{B}$, $\mathbf{C}$ are three vectors, the scalar formed by the product $\mathbf{A}\cdot(\mathbf{B}\times\mathbf{C})$ is called the scalar triple product.

For $\mathbf{A}=A_1\hat{i}+A_2\hat{j}+A_3\hat{k}$, $\mathbf{B}=B_1\hat{i}+B_2\hat{j}+B_3\hat{k}$, $\mathbf{C}=C_1\hat{i}+C_2\hat{j}+C_3\hat{k}$, the scalar triple product is the determinant

$$
\mathbf{A}\cdot(\mathbf{B}\times\mathbf{C})=
\begin{vmatrix}
A_1 & A_2 & A_3\\
B_1 & B_2 & B_3\\
C_1 & C_2 & C_3
\end{vmatrix}
$$

### 2.8 Vector Triple Product

> **Definition (Vector Triple Product).** If $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{B}$ and $\mathbf{C}$ are three vectors, then $\mathbf{A}\times(\mathbf{B}\times\mathbf{C})$ and $(\mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B})\times\mathbf{C}$ are called vector triple products.

The expansion identity is

$$
\mathbf{A}\times(\mathbf{B}\times\mathbf{C})=(\mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{C})\,\mathbf{B}-(\mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{B})\,\mathbf{C}
$$

The result lies in the plane of $\mathbf{B}$ and $\mathbf{C}$, and the two bracketings generally differ, so parentheses are essential.

## 3. Key Theorems & Essential Results

> **Result (Perpendicularity Test).** Two non-zero vectors $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ are perpendicular if and only if $\mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{B}=0$.

> **Result (Parallelism Test).** Two non-zero vectors $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ are parallel if and only if $\mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B}=\mathbf{0}$.

> **Result (Projection Formula).** The projection of $\mathbf{A}$ on $\mathbf{B}$ equals $\mathbf{A}\cdot\hat{b}$, where $\hat{b}=\mathbf{B}/\lVert \mathbf{B}\rVert$ is the unit vector in the direction of $\mathbf{B}$.

> **Result (Cosine Rule).** If $A$, $B$, $C$ are the three sides of a triangle and $\theta$ is the angle between the vectors $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$, then

> 

$$
C^{2}=A^{2}+B^{2}-2AB\cos\theta
$$

*Derivation.* From the triangle relation $\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{B}+\mathbf{C}$, equivalently $\mathbf{C}=\mathbf{A}-\mathbf{B}$. Then

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{C}\cdot\mathbf{C}&=(\mathbf{A}-\mathbf{B})\cdot(\mathbf{A}-\mathbf{B})\\
&=\mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{A}-2\,\mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{B}+\mathbf{B}\cdot\mathbf{B}
\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\mathbf{C}\cdot\mathbf{C}=C^{2}$, $\mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{A}=A^{2}$, $\mathbf{B}\cdot\mathbf{B}=B^{2}$ and $\mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{B}=AB\cos\theta$, the stated identity follows.

> **Result (Equation of a Plane).** The plane perpendicular to a vector $\mathbf{A}$ and passing through the terminal point of a position vector $\mathbf{B}$ has equation $\mathbf{r}\cdot\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{B}\cdot\mathbf{A}$, where $\mathbf{r}$ is the position vector of a general point on the plane.

*Derivation.* Let $Q$ be the terminal point of $\mathbf{B}$ and $P$ a general point of the plane with position vector $\mathbf{r}$. The vector $\overrightarrow{PQ}=\mathbf{B}-\mathbf{r}$ lies in the plane and is therefore perpendicular to the normal $\mathbf{A}$, so $(\mathbf{B}-\mathbf{r})\cdot\mathbf{A}=0$, which rearranges to $\mathbf{r}\cdot\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{B}\cdot\mathbf{A}$.

> **Result (Distance from a Point to a Plane).** The distance from the point $(x_1,y_1,z_1)$ to the plane $ax+by+cz=d$ is

> 

$$
\text{distance}=\frac{\lvert ax_1+by_1+cz_1-d\rvert}{\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}}}
$$

> **Result (Area of a Parallelogram and Triangle).** The area of the parallelogram with adjacent sides $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ is $\lVert \mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B}\rVert$. The area of a triangle is half the area of a parallelogram, hence

> 

$$
\text{area of triangle}=\tfrac{1}{2}\lVert \mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B}\rVert
$$

> **Result (Properties of the Scalar Triple Product).** The scalar triple product satisfies

> 

$$
\mathbf{A}\cdot(\mathbf{B}\times\mathbf{C})=\mathbf{B}\cdot(\mathbf{C}\times\mathbf{A})=\mathbf{C}\cdot(\mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B})
$$

> and

> 

$$
\mathbf{A}\cdot(\mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B})=0
$$

> the latter because two rows of the determinant are identical. Interchanging two rows of a determinant reverses its sign, which accounts for the cyclic symmetry.

> **Result (Volume and Coplanarity).** The scalar triple product in absolute value represents the volume of a parallelepiped with sides $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{B}$ and $\mathbf{C}$. The scalar triple product provides a test to show whether three given vectors lie in the same plane: the vectors are coplanar if and only if $\mathbf{A}\cdot(\mathbf{B}\times\mathbf{C})=0$.

> **Result (Non-Associativity of the Cross Product).** In general

> 

$$
\mathbf{A}\times(\mathbf{B}\times\mathbf{C})\neq(\mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B})\times\mathbf{C}
$$

> so parentheses are required in $\mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B}\times\mathbf{C}$ to avoid ambiguity.

## 4. Worked Exemplar Problem with Step-by-Step Solution

**Problem.** Given the position vectors $\mathbf{A}=3\hat{i}+\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$ and $\mathbf{B}=\hat{i}-2\hat{j}-4\hat{k}$ of points $P$ and $Q$ respectively:

(a) find an equation for the plane passing through $Q$ and perpendicular to the line $PQ$;

(b) find the distance from the point $(-1,1,1)$ to that plane.

**Solution.**

*Part (a).* Let the position vector of a general point $R$ on the plane be $\mathbf{r}=x\hat{i}+y\hat{j}+z\hat{k}$. The direction vector of the line $PQ$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\overrightarrow{PQ}&=\overrightarrow{OQ}-\overrightarrow{OP}\\
&=\mathbf{B}-\mathbf{A}\\
&=(\hat{i}-2\hat{j}-4\hat{k})-(3\hat{i}+\hat{j}+2\hat{k})\\
&=-2\hat{i}-3\hat{j}-6\hat{k}
\end{aligned}
$$

Since the plane is perpendicular to $PQ$, the vector $\overrightarrow{PQ}$ serves as a normal to the plane, and every vector lying in the plane is orthogonal to it. In particular,

$$
\overrightarrow{PQ}\cdot\overrightarrow{QR}=0
$$

Now

$$
\begin{aligned}
\overrightarrow{QR}&=\overrightarrow{OR}-\overrightarrow{OQ}\\
&=(x-1)\hat{i}+(y+2)\hat{j}+(z+4)\hat{k}
\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting,

$$
(-2\hat{i}-3\hat{j}-6\hat{k})\cdot\big[(x-1)\hat{i}+(y+2)\hat{j}+(z+4)\hat{k}\big]=0
$$

Evaluating the dot product componentwise,

$$
-2(x-1)-3(y+2)-6(z+4)=0
$$

Expanding,

$$
-2x+2-3y-6-6z-24=0
$$

which simplifies to

$$
2x+3y+6z+28=0
$$

This is the required equation of the plane.

*Part (b).* Write the plane in the form $ax+by+cz=d$ with $a=2$, $b=3$, $c=6$ and $d=-28$. The distance from $(x_1,y_1,z_1)$ to the plane is

$$
\text{distance}=\frac{\lvert ax_1+by_1+cz_1-d\rvert}{\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}}}
$$

For the point $(-1,1,1)$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{distance}&=\frac{\lvert 2(-1)+3(1)+6(1)+28\rvert}{\sqrt{2^{2}+3^{2}+6^{2}}}\\
&=\frac{\lvert -2+3+6+28\rvert}{7}\\
&=\frac{35}{7}\\
&=5
\end{aligned}
$$

The distance from $(-1,1,1)$ to the plane is $5$ units.

**Supplementary exemplar (angle between two vectors).** If $\mathbf{A}=2\hat{i}+2\hat{j}-\hat{k}$ and $\mathbf{B}=6\hat{i}-3\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$, then

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{B}&=A_1B_1+A_2B_2+A_3B_3\\
&=(2)(6)+(2)(-3)+(-1)(2)\\
&=12-6-2\\
&=4
\end{aligned}
$$

The magnitudes are $A=\sqrt{4+4+1}=3$ and $B=\sqrt{36+9+4}=7$, so $AB=21$ and

$$
\cos\theta=\frac{4}{21}
$$

giving $\theta\approx 79^{\circ}$.

**Supplementary exemplar (perpendicularity condition).** Determine the values of $a$ such that $\mathbf{A}=a\hat{i}-2\hat{j}+\hat{k}$ and $\mathbf{B}=2a\hat{i}+a\hat{j}-4\hat{k}$ are perpendicular. Perpendicularity requires $\mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{B}=0$:

$$
(a)(2a)+(-2)(a)+(1)(-4)=0
$$

so that

$$
2a^{2}-2a-4=0
$$

or

$$
a^{2}-a-2=0
$$

Factoring, $(a-2)(a+1)=0$, from which $a=2$ or $a=-1$.

**Supplementary exemplar (projection).** The projection of $\mathbf{A}=\hat{i}-2\hat{j}+\hat{k}$ on $\mathbf{B}=4\hat{i}-4\hat{j}+7\hat{k}$ is $\mathbf{A}\cdot\hat{b}$. First,

$$
\hat{b}=\frac{4\hat{i}-4\hat{j}+7\hat{k}}{\sqrt{4^{2}+(-4)^{2}+7^{2}}}=\frac{4}{9}\hat{i}-\frac{4}{9}\hat{j}+\frac{7}{9}\hat{k}
$$

Then

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{A}\cdot\hat{b}&=(\hat{i}-2\hat{j}+\hat{k})\cdot\left(\frac{4}{9}\hat{i}-\frac{4}{9}\hat{j}+\frac{7}{9}\hat{k}\right)\\
&=\frac{4}{9}+\frac{8}{9}+\frac{7}{9}\\
&=\frac{19}{9}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Supplementary exemplar (direction cosines).** For $\mathbf{A}=3\hat{i}-6\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$ with magnitude $7$, the angles $\alpha$, $\beta$, $\gamma$ with the positive $x$, $y$, $z$ axes satisfy

$$
\cos\alpha=\frac{3}{7},\qquad \cos\beta=-\frac{6}{7},\qquad \cos\gamma=\frac{2}{7}
$$

so that $\alpha=\cos^{-1}(3/7)\approx 64.6^{\circ}$, $\beta=\cos^{-1}(-6/7)\approx 149^{\circ}$ and $\gamma=\cos^{-1}(2/7)\approx 73.4^{\circ}$.

**Supplementary exemplar (right-angled triangle).** The vectors $\mathbf{A}=3\hat{i}-2\hat{j}+\hat{k}$, $\mathbf{B}=\hat{i}-3\hat{j}+5\hat{k}$, $\mathbf{C}=2\hat{i}+\hat{j}-4\hat{k}$ form a triangle because $\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{B}+\mathbf{C}$, so the sum of two of them equals the third. Computing $\mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{C}$ gives zero, so $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{C}$ are perpendicular and the triangle is right-angled.

**Supplementary exemplar (area of a triangle).** For the triangle with vertices $P(1,3,2)$, $Q(2,-1,1)$, $R(-1,2,3)$, the side vectors are $\overrightarrow{PQ}=\hat{i}-4\hat{j}-\hat{k}$ and $\overrightarrow{PR}=-2\hat{i}-\hat{j}+\hat{k}$. The area is

$$
\text{area}=\tfrac{1}{2}\lVert \overrightarrow{PQ}\times\overrightarrow{PR}\rVert=\tfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{107}
$$

**Supplementary exemplar (scalar triple product).** For $\mathbf{A}=2\hat{i}-3\hat{j}+4\hat{k}$, $\mathbf{B}=\hat{i}+2\hat{j}-\hat{k}$ and $\mathbf{C}=3\hat{i}-\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$, first compute

$$
\mathbf{B}\times\mathbf{C}=-\hat{i}-8\hat{j}+5\hat{k}
$$

Then

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{A}\cdot(\mathbf{B}\times\mathbf{C})&=(2\hat{i}-3\hat{j}+4\hat{k})\cdot(-\hat{i}-8\hat{j}+5\hat{k})\\
&=-2+24+20\\
&=42
\end{aligned}
$$

**Supplementary exemplar (non-associativity).** For $\mathbf{A}=3\hat{i}-\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$, $\mathbf{B}=2\hat{i}+\hat{j}-\hat{k}$ and $\mathbf{C}=\hat{i}-2\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$, one finds $\mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B}=-\hat{i}+7\hat{j}+5\hat{k}$, and hence

$$
(\mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B})\times\mathbf{C}=15\hat{i}+15\hat{j}-15\hat{k}
$$

whereas

$$
\mathbf{A}\times(\mathbf{B}\times\mathbf{C})=15\hat{i}+15\hat{j}-15\hat{k}
$$

is obtained by a separate expansion, confirming that the two bracketings must be distinguished and that parentheses are required in $\mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B}\times\mathbf{C}$.

## 5. High-Yield Exam Takeaways & Common Pitfalls

### Lesson Learning Outcomes

By the end of this unit the learner should be able to:

1. Determine the dot and cross product of two vectors.
2. Determine a vector perpendicular to a plane.
3. Evaluate scalar triple and vector triple products.

### Magnitude, Unit Vector and Resultant — Checklist

- Compute magnitude as $A=\sqrt{A_1^{2}+A_2^{2}+A_3^{2}}$; never omit the square root.
- Compute the unit vector as $\hat{a}=\mathbf{A}/A$; verify that its magnitude is $1$.
- Compute the resultant by adding components first, then taking the magnitude of the sum. Do not add magnitudes.
- The projection of $\mathbf{A}$ on $\mathbf{B}$ is $\mathbf{A}\cdot\hat{b}$, a scalar; the vector projection is $(\mathbf{A}\cdot\hat{b})\,\hat{b}$.

### High-Yield Results to Memorize

| Result | Formula |
| --- | --- |
| Dot product, geometric | $\mathbf{A}\cdot$\mathbf{B}=AB\cos\theta$ |
| Dot product, component | $\mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{B}=A_1B_1+A_2B_2+A_3B_3$ |
| Angle between vectors | $\cos\theta=\dfrac{\mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{B}}{AB}$ |
| Cross product, magnitude | $\lVert \mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B}\rVert=AB\sin\theta$ |
| Cross product, determinant | $\mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B}=

$$
\begin{vmatrix}
\hat{i}&\hat{j}&\hat{k}\A_1&A_2&A_3\B_1&B_2&B_3
\end{vmatrix}
$$

$ |
| Unit normal to a plane | $\hat{n}=\dfrac{\mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B}}{\lVert \mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B}\rVert}$ |
| Scalar triple product | $\mathbf{A}\cdot(\mathbf{B}\times\mathbf{C})=

$$
\begin{vmatrix}
A_1&A_2&A_3\B_1&B_2&B_3\C_1&C_2&C_3
\end{vmatrix}
$$

$ |
| Vector triple product | $\mathbf{A}\times(\mathbf{B}\times\mathbf{C})=(\mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{C})\,\mathbf{B}-(\mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{B})\,\mathbf{C}$ |
| Area of triangle | $\tfrac{1}{2}\lVert \mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B}\rVert$ |
| Volume of parallelepiped | $\lvert \mathbf{A}\cdot(\mathbf{B}\times\mathbf{C})\rvert$ |
| Distance point to plane | $\dfrac{\lvert ax_1+by_1+cz_1-d\rvert}{\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}}}$ |

### Common Pitfalls

- **Confusing the two products.** The dot product returns a scalar; the cross product returns a vector. A question asking for an angle or a projection requires the dot product; a question asking for a normal, an area, or a perpendicular direction requires the cross product.
- **Sign errors in the determinant expansion.** The middle term of the cross-product determinant carries a negative sign. Writing $(A_1B_3-A_3B_1)\hat{j}$ instead of $(A_3B_1-A_1B_3)\hat{j}$ is the most frequent computational error.
- **Forgetting anticommutativity.** Always use $\mathbf{B}\times\mathbf{A}=-(\mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B})$. Reversing the order reverses the normal direction.
- **Dropping parentheses in triple products.** The vector triple product is not associative; $\mathbf{A}\times(\mathbf{B}\times\mathbf{C})$ and $(\mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B})\times\mathbf{C}$ are generally different vectors. Never write $\mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B}\times\mathbf{C}$ without brackets.
- **Misapplying the perpendicularity test.** $\mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{B}=0$ tests perpendicularity; $\mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B}=\mathbf{0}$ tests parallelism. Do not interchange them.
- **Omitting the absolute value in distance and volume.** Distance and volume are non-negative; the scalar triple product itself may be negative, so take $\lvert \mathbf{A}\cdot(\mathbf{B}\times\mathbf{C})\rvert$ for volume.
- **Normalizing incorrectly.** When forming a unit normal, divide the whole vector $\mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B}$ by its magnitude, not by the magnitudes of $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ separately.
- **Sign slips in the plane equation.** When the normal is $\overrightarrow{PQ}=\mathbf{B}-\mathbf{A}$, the plane equation is $\mathbf{r}\cdot(\mathbf{B}-\mathbf{A})=\mathbf{B}\cdot(\mathbf{B}-\mathbf{A})$. Substituting a general point and expanding carefully avoids arithmetic errors of the kind that produce $+28$ instead of $-28$.
- **Angle range.** The inverse cosine returns a value in $[0^{\circ},180^{\circ}]$; a negative cosine correctly signals an obtuse angle, as in $\beta\approx 149^{\circ}$ above.

### Assessment

1. Find the angle between $\mathbf{A}=2\hat{i}+2\hat{j}-\hat{k}$ and $\mathbf{B}=6\hat{i}-3\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$.
2. Find the projection of the vector $\mathbf{A}=\hat{i}-2\hat{j}+\hat{k}$ on the vector $\mathbf{B}=4\hat{i}-4\hat{j}+7\hat{k}$.
3. Find the area of the triangle with vertices $P(1,3,2)$, $Q(2,-1,1)$ and $R(-1,2,3)$.
4. Determine a unit vector perpendicular to the plane containing $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$.
5. Evaluate the scalar triple product $\mathbf{A}\cdot(\mathbf{B}\times\mathbf{C})$ and hence state whether the three vectors are coplanar.
6. Show that $\mathbf{A}\times(\mathbf{B}\times\mathbf{C})\neq(\mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B})\times\mathbf{C}$ for suitable vectors, and explain why parentheses are required.

- Tai, C. — geometric interpretation of the cross product and right-handed systems.

## 1. Core Concept Overview & Intuition

The algebra of vectors admits two distinct multiplicative operations. The first combines two vectors to produce a single real number, and is therefore called the **dot product** or **scalar product**. The second combines two vectors to produce a new vector, and is therefore called the **cross product** or **vector product**. Both operations encode geometric information about the pair of vectors: the dot product measures the extent to which two vectors point along one another, while the cross product measures the extent to which they fail to be parallel and records the orientation of the plane they span.

The central intuition for the dot product is **projection**. If $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ are vectors with magnitudes $A$ and $B$ and $\theta$ is the angle between them, then $B\cos\theta$ is the signed length of the shadow that $\mathbf{B}$ casts on the line of $\mathbf{A}$. Multiplying this shadow length by $A$ gives the scalar $AB\cos\theta$. Equivalently, one may project $\mathbf{A}$ onto $\mathbf{B}$ and multiply by $B$. The result is the same scalar either way, and this symmetry is the defining feature of the operation.

The central intuition for the cross product is **perpendicularity and orientation**. The magnitude $AB\sin\theta$ is the area of the parallelogram whose adjacent sides are $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$. The direction of $\mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B}$ is perpendicular to both factors, and the sense of that direction is fixed by the right-hand rule: if the fingers of the right hand curl from $\mathbf{A}$ toward $\mathbf{B}$, the thumb points along $\mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B}$. Reversing the order of the factors reverses the sense of rotation, so the product vector points the opposite way. This is the geometric origin of the anti-commutative law $\mathbf{B}\times\mathbf{A}=-(\mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B})$.

A coordinate frame $\mathrm{OX}$, $\mathrm{OY}$, $\mathrm{OZ}$ is called a **right-handed set** when a rotation from $\mathrm{OX}$ to $\mathrm{OY}$ corresponds to the advance of a right-handed corkscrew along the positive direction of $\mathrm{OZ}$; similarly, a rotation from $\mathrm{OY}$ to $\mathrm{OZ}$ corresponds to a right-handed corkscrew advance along the positive direction of $\mathrm{OX}$, and so on cyclically. All component formulas below presuppose such a frame.

The two products interact with the angle between vectors in complementary ways. When two vectors are parallel, the dot product is maximal and the cross product vanishes. When two vectors are perpendicular, the dot product vanishes and the cross product is maximal. These two extreme cases are the most frequently tested facts in the entire topic, and they supply the standard tests for orthogonality and parallelism.![action along the positive direction of OZ.](/cdn/cloudflare/prep/visual-crops/2026/10/document-d0c6c84b-5e48-4773-a688-196f76ad7045-page-27-fdf224e7.jpg)

## 2. Mathematical Formalization & Core Definitions

### 2.1 The Dot or Scalar Product

> **Definition (Dot Product).** If $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ are two vectors, the scalar product of $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ is defined as $AB\cos\theta$, where $A$ and $B$ are the magnitudes of $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ respectively, and $\theta$ is the angle between them. The scalar product is denoted $\mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{B}$.

Thus



$$
\mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{B}=AB\cos\theta
$$



with the equivalent projection interpretation



$$
\mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{B}=A\times(\text{projection of } \mathbf{B} \text{ on } \mathbf{A})=B\times(\text{projection of } \mathbf{A} \text{ on } \mathbf{B})
$$



and in either case the result is a scalar quantity.

The magnitude of a vector $\mathbf{A}=A_1\hat{\imath}+A_2\hat{\jmath}+A_3\hat{k}$ is obtained from the dot product of the vector with itself, since the angle between a vector and itself is zero:



$$
A=\lVert\mathbf{A}\rVert=\sqrt{A_1^2+A_2^2+A_3^2}
$$



The **unit vector** in the direction of $\mathbf{A}$ is the vector of unit magnitude parallel to $\mathbf{A}$, namely



$$
\hat{a}=\frac{\mathbf{A}}{A}=\frac{\mathbf{A}}{\sqrt{A_1^2+A_2^2+A_3^2}}
$$



The **resultant** of two vectors is their vector sum, and its magnitude is recovered from the dot product of the resultant with itself, which produces the cosine rule derived in Section 3.

### 2.2 Special Angles

When the two vectors are at right angles, $\theta=90^{\circ}$ and



$$
\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}=ab\cos 90^{\circ}=ab\cdot 0=0
$$



so the scalar product of any two vectors at right angles to each other is always zero, and the two vectors are said to be **orthogonal** or **perpendicular**.

When the two vectors point in the same direction, $\theta=0^{\circ}$ and



$$
\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}=ab\cos 0^{\circ}=ab
$$



so the dot product equals the product of the magnitudes.

### 2.3 Component Form of the Dot Product

Write the two vectors in component form as



$$
\mathbf{A}=A_1\hat{\imath}+A_2\hat{\jmath}+A_3\hat{k}
$$





$$
\mathbf{B}=B_1\hat{\imath}+B_2\hat{\jmath}+B_3\hat{k}
$$



Expanding the product term by term gives



$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{B}={}&A_1B_1\,\hat{\imath}\cdot\hat{\imath}+A_1B_2\,\hat{\imath}\cdot\hat{\jmath}+A_1B_3\,\hat{\imath}\cdot\hat{k}\\
&+A_2B_1\,\hat{\jmath}\cdot\hat{\imath}+A_2B_2\,\hat{\jmath}\cdot\hat{\jmath}+A_2B_3\,\hat{\jmath}\cdot\hat{k}\\
&+A_3B_1\,\hat{k}\cdot\hat{\imath}+A_3B_2\,\hat{k}\cdot\hat{\jmath}+A_3B_3\,\hat{k}\cdot\hat{k}
\end{aligned}
$$



Now the parallel basis products satisfy



$$
\hat{\imath}\cdot\hat{\imath}=\hat{\jmath}\cdot\hat{\jmath}=\hat{k}\cdot\hat{k}=1\cdot 1\cos 0^{\circ}=1
$$



and the mixed basis products satisfy



$$
\hat{\imath}\cdot\hat{\jmath}=\hat{\imath}\cdot\hat{k}=\hat{\jmath}\cdot\hat{k}=1\cdot 1\cos 90^{\circ}=0
$$



so all cross terms vanish and one is left with



$$
\mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{B}=A_1B_1+A_2B_2+A_3B_3
$$



This is the computational workhorse of the topic: the scalar product is the sum of the products of corresponding components.

### 2.4 The Cross or Vector Product

> **Definition (Cross Product).** The cross or vector product of $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$, written $\mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B}$ and read "$\mathbf{A}$ cross $\mathbf{B}$", is defined as a vector having magnitude $AB\sin\theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between the two vectors. The product vector acts in a direction perpendicular to $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ in such a sense that $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{B}$ and $(\mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B})$ form a right-handed system in that order.

Thus



$$
\lVert\mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B}\rVert=AB\sin\theta
$$



Reversing the order reverses the direction of rotation, and the product vector acts downward, so that



$$
\mathbf{B}\times\mathbf{A}=-(\mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B})
$$



If $\theta=0^{\circ}$, then $\mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B}=AB\sin 0^{\circ}=0$, and if $\theta=90^{\circ}$, then $\mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B}=AB\sin 90^{\circ}=AB$.

### 2.5 Component Form of the Cross Product

With $\mathbf{A}=A_1\hat{\imath}+A_2\hat{\jmath}+A_3\hat{k}$ and $\mathbf{B}=B_1\hat{\imath}+B_2\hat{\jmath}+B_3\hat{k}$, expanding term by term gives



$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B}={}&A_1B_1\,\hat{\imath}\times\hat{\imath}+A_1B_2\,\hat{\imath}\times\hat{\jmath}+A_1B_3\,\hat{\imath}\times\hat{k}\\
&+A_2B_1\,\hat{\jmath}\times\hat{\imath}+A_2B_2\,\hat{\jmath}\times\hat{\jmath}+A_2B_3\,\hat{\jmath}\times\hat{k}\\
&+A_3B_1\,\hat{k}\times\hat{\imath}+A_3B_2\,\hat{k}\times\hat{\jmath}+A_3B_3\,\hat{k}\times\hat{k}
\end{aligned}
$$



Since $\hat{\imath}\times\hat{\imath}=1\cdot 1\cdot\sin 0^{\circ}=0$, the parallel products vanish:



$$
\hat{\imath}\times\hat{\imath}=\hat{\jmath}\times\hat{\jmath}=\hat{k}\times\hat{k}=0
$$



Also $\hat{\imath}\times\hat{\jmath}=1\cdot 1\cdot\sin 90^{\circ}=1$ in the direction $\mathrm{OZ}$, that is $\hat{\imath}\times\hat{\jmath}=\hat{k}$. The complete cyclic table of basis products is



$$
\hat{\imath}\times\hat{\jmath}=\hat{k},\qquad \hat{\jmath}\times\hat{k}=\hat{\imath},\qquad \hat{k}\times\hat{\imath}=\hat{\jmath}
$$





$$
\hat{\jmath}\times\hat{\imath}=-\hat{k},\qquad \hat{k}\times\hat{\jmath}=-\hat{\imath},\qquad \hat{\imath}\times\hat{k}=-\hat{\jmath}
$$



Collecting terms yields



$$
\mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B}=(A_2B_3-A_3B_2)\hat{\imath}+(A_3B_1-A_1B_3)\hat{\jmath}+(A_1B_2-A_2B_1)\hat{k}
$$



which is recognized as the expansion of the determinant



$$
\mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B}=
\begin{vmatrix}
\hat{\imath} & \hat{\jmath} & \hat{k}\\
A_1 & A_2 & A_3\\
B_1 & B_2 & B_3
\end{vmatrix}
$$



The determinant form is the standard computational device: expand along the first row, remembering that the middle term carries a negative sign.

### 2.6 Vector Perpendicular to a Plane

The vector $\mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B}$ is perpendicular to the plane on which the vectors $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ lie, and the three vectors form a right-handed system. The right-hand thumb rule determines the direction of the perpendicular. To obtain the **unit vector perpendicular to the plane**, one normalizes:



$$
\hat{n}=\frac{\mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B}}{\lVert\mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B}\rVert}
$$



### 2.7 Triple Products

> **Definition (Scalar Triple Product).** If $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{B}$, $\mathbf{C}$ are three vectors, the scalar formed by the product $\mathbf{A}\cdot(\mathbf{B}\times\mathbf{C})$ is called the scalar triple product.

For $\mathbf{A}=A_1\hat{\imath}+A_2\hat{\jmath}+A_3\hat{k}$, $\mathbf{B}=B_1\hat{\imath}+B_2\hat{\jmath}+B_3\hat{k}$ and $\mathbf{C}=C_1\hat{\imath}+C_2\hat{\jmath}+C_3\hat{k}$,



$$
\mathbf{A}\cdot(\mathbf{B}\times\mathbf{C})=
\begin{vmatrix}
A_1 & A_2 & A_3\\
B_1 & B_2 & B_3\\
C_1 & C_2 & C_3
\end{vmatrix}
$$



> **Definition (Vector Triple Product).** If $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{B}$ and $\mathbf{C}$ are three vectors, then $\mathbf{A}\times(\mathbf{B}\times\mathbf{C})$ and $(\mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B})\times\mathbf{C}$ are called vector triple products.

## 3. Key Theorems & Essential Results

> **Theorem (Orthogonality Test).** Two non-null vectors $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ are perpendicular if and only if $\mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{B}=0$.

This follows directly from $\mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{B}=AB\cos\theta$: for non-null vectors $A\neq 0$ and $B\neq 0$, the product vanishes exactly when $\cos\theta=0$, that is $\theta=90^{\circ}$.

> **Theorem (Parallelism Test).** Two non-null vectors are parallel if and only if $\mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B}=\mathbf{0}$.

This follows from $\lVert\mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B}\rVert=AB\sin\theta$: the magnitude vanishes exactly when $\sin\theta=0$, that is $\theta=0^{\circ}$ or $\theta=180^{\circ}$.

> **Theorem (Cosine Rule).** If $A$, $B$, $C$ are the three sides of a triangle and $\theta$ is the angle between the vectors $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$, then



$$
C^2=A^2+B^2-2AB\cos\theta
$$



**Proof.** From the triangle relation $\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{B}+\mathbf{C}$, equivalently $\mathbf{C}=\mathbf{A}-\mathbf{B}$. Forming the dot product of $\mathbf{C}$ with itself,



$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{C}\cdot\mathbf{C}&=(\mathbf{A}-\mathbf{B})\cdot(\mathbf{A}-\mathbf{B})\\
&=\mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{A}-2\,\mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{B}+\mathbf{B}\cdot\mathbf{B}
\end{aligned}
$$



Since $\mathbf{C}\cdot\mathbf{C}=C^2$, $\mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{A}=A^2$, $\mathbf{B}\cdot\mathbf{B}=B^2$ and $\mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{B}=AB\cos\theta$, the result follows. $\blacksquare$

> **Theorem (Properties of the Scalar Triple Product).** The scalar triple product satisfies



$$
\mathbf{A}\cdot(\mathbf{B}\times\mathbf{C})=\mathbf{B}\cdot(\mathbf{C}\times\mathbf{A})=\mathbf{C}\cdot(\mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B})
$$



> and



$$
\mathbf{A}\cdot(\mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B})=0
$$



**Proof.** The first identity holds because interchanging two rows of a determinant reverses its sign, and a cyclic permutation of three rows amounts to two interchanges, so the determinant is unchanged. The second holds because two rows of the determinant are identical, and a determinant with two identical rows is zero. $\blacksquare$

> **Theorem (Geometric Meaning of the Scalar Triple Product).** The scalar triple product in absolute value represents the volume of a parallelepiped with sides $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{B}$ and $\mathbf{C}$.

> **Theorem (Coplanarity Test).** Three vectors lie in the same plane if and only if their scalar triple product is zero.

The scalar triple product therefore provides a test to show whether three given vectors are coplanar.

> **Theorem (Vector Triple Product Expansion).** For any three vectors,



$$
\mathbf{A}\times(\mathbf{B}\times\mathbf{C})=\mathbf{B}(\mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{C})-\mathbf{C}(\mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{B})
$$



This is the standard expansion, often remembered as "middle vector times dot of the outer pair, minus outer vector times dot of the other pair". The expansion is verified by writing out components and collecting terms.

> **Theorem (Non-Associativity of the Cross Product).** In general,



$$
(\mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B})\times\mathbf{C}\neq\mathbf{A}\times(\mathbf{B}\times\mathbf{C})
$$



Parentheses are therefore mandatory in any expression involving a vector triple product, since omitting them renders the expression ambiguous.

> **Theorem (Area Interpretations).** The magnitude $\lVert\mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B}\rVert$ is the area of the parallelogram with adjacent sides $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$. The area of a triangle with two of its sides given by $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ is half the area of that parallelogram, namely



$$
\text{Area of triangle}=\tfrac{1}{2}\lVert\mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B}\rVert
$$



> **Theorem (Equation of a Plane).** The equation of the plane perpendicular to a vector $\mathbf{A}$ and passing through the terminal point of a position vector $\mathbf{B}$ is



$$
\mathbf{r}\cdot\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{B}\cdot\mathbf{A}
$$



> where $\mathbf{r}$ is the position vector of a general point on the plane.

**Proof.** Let $\mathbf{r}$ be the position vector of a general point $P$ on the plane and let $Q$ be the terminal point of $\mathbf{B}$. The vector $\overrightarrow{QP}=\mathbf{B}-\mathbf{r}$ lies in the plane and is therefore perpendicular to the normal $\mathbf{A}$, so $(\mathbf{B}-\mathbf{r})\cdot\mathbf{A}=0$, which rearranges to $\mathbf{r}\cdot\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{B}\cdot\mathbf{A}$. $\blacksquare$

> **Theorem (Distance from a Point to a Plane).** The perpendicular distance from the point $(x_1,y_1,z_1)$ to the plane $ax+by+cz=d$ is



$$
\text{distance}=\frac{\lvert ax_1+by_1+cz_1-d\rvert}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2+c^2}}
$$



The distance from the origin to the plane is the projection of the position vector of any point on the plane onto the unit normal, which is the special case $x_1=y_1=z_1=0$.

> **Theorem (Direction Cosines).** If $\alpha$, $\beta$, $\gamma$ are the angles that a vector $\mathbf{A}$ makes with the positive $x$, $y$, $z$ axes respectively, then



$$
\cos\alpha=\frac{A_1}{A},\qquad \cos\beta=\frac{A_2}{A},\qquad \cos\gamma=\frac{A_3}{A}
$$



**Proof.** Since $\mathbf{A}\cdot\hat{\imath}=A\cos\alpha$ and also $\mathbf{A}\cdot\hat{\imath}=A_1$, division by $A$ gives the first relation; the others follow identically. $\blacksquare$

## 4. Worked Exemplar Problem with Step-by-Step Solution

**Problem.** Given $\mathbf{A}=3\hat{\imath}+\hat{\jmath}+2\hat{k}$ and $\mathbf{B}=\hat{\imath}-2\hat{\jmath}-4\hat{k}$ as position vectors of points $P$ and $Q$ respectively:

(a) find an equation for the plane passing through $Q$ and perpendicular to the line $PQ$;

(b) find the distance from the point $(-1,1,1)$ to that plane.

**Solution.**

**Step 1 — Identify the normal to the plane.** The plane passes through $Q$ and is perpendicular to the line $PQ$, so the direction vector $\overrightarrow{PQ}$ serves as the normal. Compute



$$
\overrightarrow{PQ}=\overrightarrow{OQ}-\overrightarrow{OP}=\mathbf{B}-\mathbf{A}
$$





$$
\begin{aligned}
\overrightarrow{PQ}&=(\hat{\imath}-2\hat{\jmath}-4\hat{k})-(3\hat{\imath}+\hat{\jmath}+2\hat{k})\\
&=-2\hat{\imath}-3\hat{\jmath}-6\hat{k}
\end{aligned}
$$



**Step 2 — Set up the perpendicularity condition.** Let $R(x,y,z)$ be a general point on the plane with position vector $\mathbf{r}=x\hat{\imath}+y\hat{\jmath}+z\hat{k}$. Since the plane is perpendicular to $PQ$, the vector $\overrightarrow{QR}$ lies in the plane and must satisfy



$$
\overrightarrow{PQ}\cdot\overrightarrow{QR}=0
$$



Now



$$
\overrightarrow{QR}=\overrightarrow{OR}-\overrightarrow{OQ}=(x-1)\hat{\imath}+(y+2)\hat{\jmath}+(z+4)\hat{k}
$$



**Step 3 — Evaluate the dot product.** Substituting,



$$
(-2\hat{\imath}-3\hat{\jmath}-6\hat{k})\cdot\big[(x-1)\hat{\imath}+(y+2)\hat{\jmath}+(z+4)\hat{k}\big]=0
$$



Using the component formula for the dot product,



$$
-2(x-1)-3(y+2)-6(z+4)=0
$$



**Step 4 — Simplify to standard form.** Expanding,



$$
-2x+2-3y-6-6z-24=0
$$





$$
-2x-3y-6z-28=0
$$



Multiplying through by $-1$,



$$
2x+3y+6z+28=0
$$



This is the required equation of the plane. Written in the form $ax+by+cz=d$ with $a=2$, $b=3$, $c=6$, it reads $2x+3y+6z=-28$.

**Step 5 — Compute the distance from the given point.** For the point $(x_1,y_1,z_1)=(-1,1,1)$ and the plane $ax+by+cz=d$,



$$
\text{distance}=\frac{\lvert ax_1+by_1+cz_1-d\rvert}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2+c^2}}
$$



Here $d=-28$, so



$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{distance}&=\frac{\lvert 2(-1)+3(1)+6(1)+28\rvert}{\sqrt{2^2+3^2+6^2}}\\
&=\frac{\lvert -2+3+6+28\rvert}{\sqrt{4+9+36}}\\
&=\frac{35}{7}\\
&=5
\end{aligned}
$$



The distance from $(-1,1,1)$ to the plane is $5$ units.

**Supplementary exemplar — angle between two vectors.** For $\mathbf{A}=2\hat{\imath}+2\hat{\jmath}-\hat{k}$ and $\mathbf{B}=6\hat{\imath}-3\hat{\jmath}+2\hat{k}$, the component formula gives



$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{B}&=A_1B_1+A_2B_2+A_3B_3\\
&=(2)(6)+(2)(-3)+(-1)(2)\\
&=12-6-2\\
&=4
\end{aligned}
$$



The magnitudes are $A=\sqrt{4+4+1}=3$ and $B=\sqrt{36+9+4}=7$, so $AB=21$ and



$$
\cos\theta=\frac{4}{21}
$$



giving $\theta\approx 79^{\circ}$. This illustrates the standard two-step procedure: compute the dot product by components, then divide by the product of the magnitudes.

**Supplementary exemplar — perpendicularity with an unknown parameter.** Determine the values of $a$ for which $\mathbf{A}=a\hat{\imath}-2\hat{\jmath}+\hat{k}$ and $\mathbf{B}=2a\hat{\imath}+a\hat{\jmath}-4\hat{k}$ are perpendicular. The vectors are perpendicular exactly when their dot product is zero:



$$
(a\hat{\imath}-2\hat{\jmath}+\hat{k})\cdot(2a\hat{\imath}+a\hat{\jmath}-4\hat{k})=0
$$





$$
2a^2-2a-4=0
$$





$$
a^2-a-2=0
$$



Factoring gives $(a-2)(a+1)=0$, hence $a=2$ or $a=-1$.

**Supplementary exemplar — projection onto a direction.** To find the projection of $\mathbf{A}=\hat{\imath}-2\hat{\jmath}+\hat{k}$ on $\mathbf{B}=4\hat{\imath}-4\hat{\jmath}+7\hat{k}$, first normalize $\mathbf{B}$:



$$
\hat{b}=\frac{\mathbf{B}}{\lVert\mathbf{B}\rVert}=\frac{4\hat{\imath}-4\hat{\jmath}+7\hat{k}}{\sqrt{16+16+49}}=\frac{4}{9}\hat{\imath}-\frac{4}{9}\hat{\jmath}+\frac{7}{9}\hat{k}
$$



Then the projection is the scalar $\mathbf{A}\cdot\hat{b}$:



$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{A}\cdot\hat{b}&=(\hat{\imath}-2\hat{\jmath}+\hat{k})\cdot\left(\frac{4}{9}\hat{\imath}-\frac{4}{9}\hat{\jmath}+\frac{7}{9}\hat{k}\right)\\
&=\frac{4}{9}+\frac{8}{9}+\frac{7}{9}\\
&=\frac{19}{9}
\end{aligned}
$$



**Supplementary exemplar — area of a triangle.** For the triangle with vertices $P(1,3,2)$, $Q(2,-1,1)$ and $R(-1,2,3)$, form two side vectors:



$$
\overrightarrow{PQ}=\hat{\imath}-4\hat{\jmath}-\hat{k},\qquad \overrightarrow{PR}=-2\hat{\imath}-\hat{\jmath}+\hat{k}
$$



The area of the triangle is half the magnitude of the cross product of these sides:



$$
\text{Area}=\tfrac{1}{2}\lVert\overrightarrow{PQ}\times\overrightarrow{PR}\rVert=\tfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{107}
$$



**Supplementary exemplar — non-associativity.** For $\mathbf{A}=3\hat{\imath}-\hat{\jmath}+2\hat{k}$, $\mathbf{B}=2\hat{\imath}+\hat{\jmath}-\hat{k}$ and $\mathbf{C}=\hat{\imath}-2\hat{\jmath}+2\hat{k}$, one computes $\mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B}=-\hat{\imath}+7\hat{\jmath}+5\hat{k}$ and then



$$
(\mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B})\times\mathbf{C}=15\hat{\imath}+15\hat{\jmath}-15\hat{k}
$$



while the alternative bracketing gives a different vector. Hence $(\mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B})\times\mathbf{C}\neq\mathbf{A}\times(\mathbf{B}\times\mathbf{C})$, which demonstrates the need for parentheses in any vector triple product.

## 5. High-Yield Exam Takeaways & Common Pitfalls

### 5.1 Lesson Learning Outcomes

By the end of this unit the learner should be able to:

1. Determine the dot and cross product of two vectors.
2. Determine a vector perpendicular to a plane.
3. Evaluate scalar triple and vector triple products.

Every examination question in this topic maps onto one of these three outcomes, and the worked exemplars are organized to match them.

### 5.2 Magnitude, Unit Vector and Resultant — the Computational Core

The magnitude, unit vector and resultant subtopic supplies the numerical machinery on which every other calculation depends. The essential chain is:

- Magnitude: $A=\sqrt{A_1^2+A_2^2+A_3^2}$, obtained as $\sqrt{\mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{A}}$.
- Unit vector: $\hat{a}=\mathbf{A}/A$, which always has magnitude $1$ and points in the direction of $\mathbf{A}$.
- Resultant: $\mathbf{R}=\mathbf{A}+\mathbf{B}$, with magnitude $R=\sqrt{\mathbf{R}\cdot\mathbf{R}}$ and direction $\hat{r}=\mathbf{R}/R$.

The resultant's magnitude satisfies $\mathbf{R}\cdot\mathbf{R}=A^2+B^2+2AB\cos\theta$. This is the same identity as the cosine rule with the sign of the cross term reversed, and it is the standard route to the magnitude of a sum of two vectors given their magnitudes and the angle between them.

### 5.3 Assessment Checklist

The assessment items for this unit are of three standard types, and each has a fixed procedure:

- **Angle between two vectors.** Compute $\mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{B}$ by components, compute $A$ and $B$, then use $\cos\theta=\dfrac{\mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{B}}{AB}$ and take the inverse cosine. Always report the angle in the range $0^{\circ}$ to $180^{\circ}$.
- **Projection of one vector on another.** Normalize the target vector to obtain $\hat{b}$, then evaluate the scalar $\mathbf{A}\cdot\hat{b}$. Do not confuse the scalar projection with the vector projection; the scalar projection is a number, the vector projection is $(\mathbf{A}\cdot\hat{b})\hat{b}$.
- **Area of a triangle from three vertices.** Form two side vectors from a common vertex, take their cross product, and halve the magnitude. For vertices $P,Q,R$, one convenient choice is



$$
\text{Area}=\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert(Q-P)\times(R-P)\right\rVert.
$$



Choosing a different common vertex gives the same area. A quoted numerical area must equal this value; if the cross product of the chosen side vectors does not have the required magnitude, the quoted value is wrong and must be recomputed.

### 5.4 Pitfalls to Avoid

- **Sign errors in the determinant expansion.** The middle component of $\mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B}$ carries a negative sign. Writing the determinant and expanding carefully along the first row prevents the most common arithmetic error in the entire topic.
- **Confusing the two products.** The dot product returns a scalar; the cross product returns a vector. A question asking for "the product" without qualification is ambiguous, and the expected answer is determined by whether the requested quantity is a number or a vector.
- **Forgetting anti-commutativity.** $\mathbf{B}\times\mathbf{A}=-(\mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B})$, not $\mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B}$. The magnitude is unchanged but the direction reverses.
- **Omitting parentheses in triple products.** Since $(\mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B})\times\mathbf{C}\neq\mathbf{A}\times(\mathbf{B}\times\mathbf{C})$, an unparenthesized triple product is meaningless. State the bracketing explicitly.
- **Using the wrong distance formula sign.** The distance formula uses $\lvert ax_1+by_1+cz_1-d\rvert$ with the plane written as $ax+by+cz=d$. If the plane is written as $ax+by+cz+d=0$, the constant must be moved to the right-hand side before substitution, or the sign convention must be adjusted consistently.
- **Treating a zero dot product as "no answer".** A zero dot product is a definite conclusion: the vectors are perpendicular. Similarly, a zero cross product means the vectors are parallel, not that the calculation has failed.
- **Normalizing before projecting.** The projection onto $\mathbf{B}$ uses the unit vector $\hat{b}$, not $\mathbf{B}$ itself. Projecting onto $\mathbf{B}$ without normalizing gives a result scaled by $\lVert\mathbf{B}\rVert$.
- **Stating an area without verifying it.** For a triangle with vertices $P,Q,R$, the area must be $\frac{1}{2}\lVert(Q-P)\times(R-P)\rVert$. Any quoted value, such as a value involving $\sqrt{107}$, is correct only if that cross product magnitude is exactly the value used.

### 5.5 Reference Sources

The standard references supporting this unit are the texts by H. Davis, P. Lewis, M. Spiegel and C. Tai. These are cited as the approved reading for the topic; the definitions, component formulas, triple-product identities and geometric interpretations developed above are consistent with the treatment in those sources. Students should consult them for additional exercises on the dot product, cross product, scalar triple product, vector triple product, and the geometric applications to planes, distances and areas.

### 5.6 Summary of Essential Formulas

| Quantity | Formula |
| --- | --- |
| Dot product (geometric) | $\mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{B}=AB\cos\theta$ |
| Dot product (components) | $\mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{B}=A_1B_1+A_2B_2+A_3B_3$ |
| Magnitude | $A=\sqrt{A_1^2+A_2^2+A_3^2}$ |
| Unit vector | $\hat{a}=\mathbf{A}/A$ |
| Angle between vectors | $\cos\theta=\dfrac{\mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{B}}{AB}$ |
| Cross product (geometric) | $\lVert\mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B}\rVert=AB\sin\theta$ |
| Cross product (components) | $\mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B}=(A_2B_3-A_3B_2)\hat{\imath}-(A_1B_3-A_3B_1)\hat{\jmath}+(A_1B_2-A_2B_1)\hat{k}$ |
| Unit normal to plane spanned by two vectors | $\hat{n}=\dfrac{\mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B}}{\lVert\mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B}\rVert}$ |
| Scalar triple product (components) | $\mathbf{A}\cdot(\mathbf{B}\times\mathbf{C})=A_1(B_2C_3-B_3C_2)-A_2(B_1C_3-B_3C_1)+A_3(B_1C_2-B_2C_1)$ |
| Vector triple product | $\mathbf{A}\times(\mathbf{B}\times\mathbf{C})=\mathbf{B}(\mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{C})-\mathbf{C}(\mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{B})$ |
| Area of parallelogram | $\lVert\mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B}\rVert$ |
| Area of triangle | $\tfrac{1}{2}\lVert\mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B}\rVert$ |
| Volume of parallelepiped | $\lvert\mathbf{A}\cdot(\mathbf{B}\times\mathbf{C})\rvert$ |
| Plane through terminal point of $\mathbf{B}$ perpendicular to $\mathbf{A}$ | $\mathbf{r}\cdot\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{B}\cdot\mathbf{A}$ |
| Distance from point to plane | $\dfrac{\lvert ax_1+by_1+cz_1-d\rvert}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2+c^2}}$ |
| Cosine rule | $C^2=A^2+B^2-2AB\cos\theta$ |

Equivalently, the cross product and scalar triple product can be written as determinants:



$$
\mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B}=
\begin{vmatrix}
\hat{\imath} & \hat{\jmath} & \hat{k} \\
A_1 & A_2 & A_3 \\
B_1 & B_2 & B_3
\end{vmatrix}
$$





$$
\mathbf{A}\cdot(\mathbf{B}\times\mathbf{C})=
\begin{vmatrix}
A_1 & A_2 & A_3 \\
B_1 & B_2 & B_3 \\
C_1 & C_2 & C_3
\end{vmatrix}
$$



These formulas, together with the orthogonality test $\mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{B}=0$, the parallelism test $\mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B}=\mathbf{0}$, and the coplanarity test $\mathbf{A}\cdot(\mathbf{B}\times\mathbf{C})=0$, constitute the complete toolkit required for the assessment items of this unit.

## 1. Core Concept Overview & Intuition

Imagine you are pulling a heavy box along the floor with a rope. You pull with a certain force, and the rope makes some angle with the floor. Only the part of your pull that points along the floor actually helps move the box forward. The part of the pull pointing upward does nothing to slide the box. This everyday situation captures the central idea of this topic: when two vectors meet at an angle, we often care about how much of one vector "acts along" the other.

A vector is a quantity with both size (called magnitude) and direction. Force, displacement, and velocity are vectors. Two different products let us combine two vectors, and they answer two different questions.

The first product answers: "How much of one vector lies along the other?" The answer is a single number, a scalar, so this product is called the **dot product** or **scalar product**. In the rope example, the dot product of the force vector with the direction of the floor gives the useful forward pull.

The second product answers: "What single vector is perpendicular to both of these vectors?" The answer is a new vector, so this product is called the **cross product** or **vector product**. If you hold a screwdriver and turn it from one direction toward another, the screw advances along a line perpendicular to both turning directions. That advancing direction is exactly what the cross product produces.

Where the analogy stops being exact: a real rope has thickness and the box has friction, but vectors are pure arrows with no thickness. We treat them as ideal arrows starting from a common point.

The two products are useful because they let us measure angles between arrows, test whether arrows are at right angles, find projections, build equations of planes, and compute areas and volumes. All of these ideas are built from the same two definitions, so once the definitions are clear, the rest follows step by step.

## 2. Mathematical Formalization & Core Definitions

### 2.1 Magnitude of a Vector

The **magnitude** of a vector is its length. It is written with vertical bars, for example $\lvert A \rvert$, and is a non-negative number. If a vector is written in component form as

$$
A=A_{1}\hat{i}+A_{2}\hat{j}+A_{3}\hat{k}
$$

then its magnitude is found by the distance formula:

$$
\lvert A \rvert=\sqrt{A_{1}^{2}+A_{2}^{2}+A_{3}^{2}}
$$

Here $\hat{i}$, $\hat{j}$, $\hat{k}$ are the unit vectors pointing along the positive $x$, $y$, and $z$ axes. A **unit vector** is a vector of length one. The unit vector in the direction of $A$ is obtained by dividing $A$ by its own length:

$$
\hat{a}=\frac{A}{\lvert A \rvert}
$$

This process is called normalising the vector. It keeps the direction but rescales the length to one.

The **resultant** of two vectors is the single vector obtained by adding them. In component form, addition is done component by component:

$$
A+B=(A_{1}+B_{1})\hat{i}+(A_{2}+B_{2})\hat{j}+(A_{3}+B_{3})\hat{k}
$$

The magnitude of the resultant is then found using the magnitude formula above.

### 2.2 The Dot or Scalar Product

> If $A$ and $B$ are two vectors, the scalar product of $A$ and $B$ is defined as $AB\cos\theta$, where $A$ and $B$ are the magnitudes of the vectors $A$ and $B$, and $\theta$ is the angle between them.

The dot product is written $A\cdot B$. So

$$
A\cdot B=AB\cos\theta
$$

This can be read in two equivalent ways: it equals the magnitude of $A$ multiplied by the projection of $B$ on $A$, or the magnitude of $B$ multiplied by the projection of $A$ on $B$. In either case the result is a scalar quantity, that is, a plain number with no direction.

A **projection** is the "shadow" length of one vector cast along the direction of another. If $\hat{b}$ is the unit vector in the direction of $B$, then the projection of $A$ on $B$ is $A\cdot\hat{b}$.

Two special angles follow immediately from the definition. If the vectors are at right angles, $\theta=90^{\circ}$, then $\cos 90^{\circ}=0$, so $A\cdot B=0$. Such vectors are called **orthogonal** or **perpendicular**. If the vectors point in the same direction, $\theta=0^{\circ}$, then $\cos 0^{\circ}=1$, so $A\cdot B=AB$.

When both vectors are written in component form, expanding the product term by term and using the facts that $\hat{i}\cdot\hat{i}=\hat{j}\cdot\hat{j}=\hat{k}\cdot\hat{k}=1$ and that $\hat{i}\cdot\hat{j}=\hat{i}\cdot\hat{k}=\hat{j}\cdot\hat{k}=0$ leaves only three terms:

$$
A\cdot B=A_{1}B_{1}+A_{2}B_{2}+A_{3}B_{3}
$$

This component formula is the workhorse for all dot product calculations.

### 2.3 The Cross or Vector Product

> The cross or vector product of $A$ and $B$, written $A\times B$ and read as "$A$ cross $B$", is defined as a vector having the magnitude $AB\sin\theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between the two vectors. The product vector acts in a direction perpendicular to $A$ and $B$ in such a sense that $A$, $B$, and $A\times B$ form a right-handed system in that order.

The magnitude is therefore

$$
\lvert A\times B \rvert=AB\sin\theta
$$

The direction is fixed by the **right-hand rule**. The axes $OX$, $OY$, $OZ$ form a right-handed set if a rotation from $OX$ to $OY$ drives a right-handed corkscrew along the positive $OZ$ direction. Reversing the order of the vectors reverses the direction of rotation, so

$$
B\times A=-(A\times B)
$$

This means the cross product is not commutative.

Two special angles again follow. If $\theta=0^{\circ}$, then $\sin 0^{\circ}=0$, so $A\times B=0$. If $\theta=90^{\circ}$, then $\sin 90^{\circ}=1$, so $\lvert A\times B \rvert=AB$.

For component form, the basis products are $\hat{i}\times\hat{i}=\hat{j}\times\hat{j}=\hat{k}\times\hat{k}=0$ and

$$
\hat{i}\times\hat{j}=\hat{k},\qquad \hat{j}\times\hat{k}=\hat{i},\qquad \hat{k}\times\hat{i}=\hat{j}
$$

with the reverse orders giving the negatives. Expanding term by term gives

$$
A\times B=(A_{2}B_{3}-A_{3}B_{2})\hat{i}+(A_{3}B_{1}-A_{1}B_{3})\hat{j}+(A_{1}B_{2}-A_{2}B_{1})\hat{k}
$$

This is exactly the expansion of the determinant

$$
A\times B=\begin{vmatrix}\hat{i}&\hat{j}&\hat{k}\A_{1}&A_{2}&A_{3}\B_{1}&B_{2}&B_{3}\end{vmatrix}
$$

The determinant form is the standard shortcut for computing a cross product.

### 2.4 Vector Perpendicular to a Plane

The vector $A\times B$ is perpendicular to the plane in which $A$ and $B$ lie. The right-hand thumb rule gives its direction. To obtain the unit vector perpendicular to that plane, divide by the magnitude:

$$
\hat{n}=\frac{A\times B}{\lvert A\times B \rvert}
$$

### 2.5 Triple Products

> If $A$, $B$, $C$ are three vectors, the scalar formed by the product $A\cdot(B\times C)$ is called the scalar triple product.

In determinant form,

$$
A\cdot(B\times C)=\begin{vmatrix}A_{1}&A_{2}&A_{3}\B_{1}&B_{2}&B_{3}\C_{1}&C_{2}&C_{3}\end{vmatrix}
$$

> If $A$, $B$, and $C$ are three vectors, then $A\times(B\times C)$ and $(A\times B)\times C$ are called vector triple products.

The vector triple product satisfies the expansion

$$
A\times(B\times C)=(A\cdot C)B-(A\cdot B)C
$$

## 3. Key Theorems & Essential Results

> **Theorem (Cosine Rule).** For a triangle with sides $A$, $B$, $C$ and angle $\theta$ between the vectors $A$ and $B$, one has $C^{2}=A^{2}+B^{2}-2AB\cos\theta$.

The proof uses the dot product. From the triangle relation $C=A-B$, taking the dot product of $C$ with itself gives

$$
\begin{aligned}C\cdot C&=(A-B)\cdot(A-B)\\&=A\cdot A-2A\cdot B+B\cdot B\end{aligned}
$$

and since $A\cdot A=A^{2}$, $B\cdot B=B^{2}$, and $A\cdot B=AB\cos\theta$, the result follows.

> **Theorem (Properties of the Scalar Triple Product).** The scalar triple product satisfies $A\cdot(B\times C)=B\cdot(C\times A)=C\cdot(A\times B)$, and $A\cdot(A\times B)=0$.

The first property holds because interchanging two rows of a determinant reverses its sign, and a cyclic rearrangement of three rows amounts to two such interchanges. The second holds because two rows of the determinant become identical.

> **Theorem (Geometric Meaning).** The absolute value of the scalar triple product represents the volume of a parallelepiped with sides $A$, $B$, and $C$.

> **Theorem (Coplanarity Test).** Three vectors lie in the same plane if and only if their scalar triple product is zero.

> **Theorem (Area of a Parallelogram and Triangle).** The area of the parallelogram with sides $A$ and $B$ is $\lvert A\times B \rvert$. The area of the triangle with the same two sides is $\tfrac{1}{2}\lvert A\times B \rvert$.

> **Theorem (Distance from a Point to a Plane).** If a plane has equation $ax+by+cz=d$, then the distance from the point $(x_{1},y_{1},z_{1})$ to the plane is

> 

$$
\frac{\lvert ax_{1}+by_{1}+cz_{1}-d \rvert}{\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}}}
$$

> **Theorem (Non-Associativity of the Cross Product).** In general $(A\times B)\times C\neq A\times(B\times C)$, so parentheses are essential in a triple cross product.

## 4. Worked Exemplar Problem with Step-by-Step Solution

**Problem.** Given $A=3\hat{i}+\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$ and $B=\hat{i}-2\hat{j}-4\hat{k}$ as position vectors of points $P$ and $Q$ respectively:

(a) find an equation for the plane passing through $Q$ and perpendicular to the line $PQ$;

(b) find the distance from the point $(-1,1,1)$ to that plane.

**Step 1. Find the direction vector of the line $PQ$.**

The vector from $P$ to $Q$ is $Q$ minus $P$:

$$
\begin{aligned}PQ&=B-A\\&=(1-3)\hat{i}+(-2-1)\hat{j}+(-4-2)\hat{k}\\&=-2\hat{i}-3\hat{j}-6\hat{k}\end{aligned}
$$

This vector is normal (perpendicular) to the required plane.

**Step 2. Set up the perpendicularity condition.**

Let $R(x,y,z)$ be any point on the plane, with position vector $r$. Then

$$
QR=r-B=(x-1)\hat{i}+(y+2)\hat{j}+(z+4)\hat{k}
$$

Because the plane is perpendicular to $PQ$, the vector $QR$ lies in the plane and must be perpendicular to $PQ$. Hence their dot product is zero:

$$
PQ\cdot QR=0
$$

**Step 3. Expand the dot product.**

$$
\begin{aligned}(-2)(x-1)+(-3)(y+2)+(-6)(z+4)&=0\\-2x+2-3y-6-6z-24&=0\\-2x-3y-6z-28&=0\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying through by $-1$ gives the plane equation

$$
2x+3y+6z+28=0
$$

**Step 4. Apply the distance formula.**

Rewrite the plane as $2x+3y+6z=-28$, so $a=2$, $b=3$, $c=6$, $d=-28$. The distance from $(-1,1,1)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{distance}&=\frac{\lvert 2(-1)+3(1)+6(1)+28 \rvert}{\sqrt{2^{2}+3^{2}+6^{2}}}\\&=\frac{\lvert -2+3+6+28 \rvert}{7}\\&=\frac{35}{7}\\&=5\end{aligned}
$$

So the distance from the point to the plane is $5$ units.

**Step 5. Interpret the answer.** The plane is a flat sheet through $Q$ standing at right angles to the line $PQ$. The number $5$ is the shortest straight-line gap from the given point to that sheet.

## 5. High-Yield Exam Takeaways & Common Pitfalls

**Takeaways.**

- The dot product gives a scalar; the cross product gives a vector. Always check which type of answer the question expects.
- Use $A\cdot B=A_{1}B_{1}+A_{2}B_{2}+A_{3}B_{3}$ for the dot product and the determinant for the cross product. Both are fast and reliable.
- To find an angle between two vectors, use $\cos\theta=\dfrac{A\cdot B}{AB}$.
- To test perpendicularity, check whether the dot product is zero.
- To test parallelism, check whether the cross product is zero.
- To find a unit vector, divide the vector by its magnitude.
- To find a projection of $A$ on $B$, compute $A\cdot\hat{b}$ where $\hat{b}=B/\lvert B \rvert$.
- To find a plane perpendicular to a given vector, use $(r-r_{0})\cdot n=0$ where $n$ is the normal vector and $r_{0}$ is a point on the plane.
- To find the area of a triangle from three vertices, form two side vectors from one vertex and take half the magnitude of their cross product.
- To test coplanarity of three vectors, check whether the scalar triple product is zero.
- To find the volume of a parallelepiped, take the absolute value of the scalar triple product.

**Common pitfalls.**

- Forgetting that $B\times A=-(A\times B)$. Reversing the order flips the sign.
- Writing $A\times B$ as a scalar. It is a vector with three components.
- Dropping the absolute value in the distance formula. Distance is never negative.
- Mixing up the plane equation signs. Always re-derive from $(r-r_{0})\cdot n=0$ rather than memorising.
- Assuming $(A\times B)\times C=A\times(B\times C)$. The cross product is not associative, so parentheses matter.
- Using degrees and radians interchangeably in $\cos\theta$ and $\sin\theta$. Match the mode of your calculator to the units in the question.
- Forgetting to normalise before projecting. The projection formula uses the unit vector $\hat{b}$, not $B$ itself.
- Confusing the scalar triple product with the vector triple product. The first is a number; the second is a vector.
- Omitting the check that three vectors actually form a triangle before applying the cosine rule. Verify $A=B+C$ or that the sum is zero first.
- Rounding too early in multi-step problems. Keep full precision until the final answer.
