## 1. Core Concept Overview & Intuition

The dot and cross products are the two fundamental ways of multiplying vectors. They answer two different geometric questions, and the entire topic is built on keeping them apart.

The **dot (scalar) product** measures how much one vector points along another. Its output is a single number (a scalar). It is the tool for angles between vectors, projections, perpendicularity tests, and equations of planes.

The **cross (vector) product** measures the "turning" or "spread" between two vectors. Its output is a new vector, perpendicular to both inputs. It is the tool for perpendicular directions, areas of parallelograms and triangles, and the triple products.

The unifying geometric idea is the angle $\theta$ between the two vectors. Both products are built from the same three ingredients: the magnitudes $A$ and $B$, and the angle $\theta$. The dot product uses $\cos\theta$; the cross product uses $\sin\theta$. This single observation explains almost every result in the chapter:

- When $\theta=0^{\circ}$ (parallel vectors), $\cos\theta=1$ and $\sin\theta=0$, so the dot product is maximal and the cross product vanishes.
- When $\theta=90^{\circ}$ (perpendicular vectors), $\cos\theta=0$ and $\sin\theta=1$, so the dot product vanishes and the cross product is maximal.

A second unifying idea is **projection**. The dot product $A\cdot B$ equals $A$ times the projection of $B$ on $A$, and equally equals $B$ times the projection of $A$ on $B$. This is why the dot product produces distances from points to planes and equations of planes.

A third idea is **orientation**. The cross product is not symmetric: reversing the order reverses the direction of the product vector, so $B\times A=-(A\times B)$. The direction is fixed by the right-hand rule, which makes $A$, $B$, and $A\times B$ a right-handed system in that order.

## 2. Mathematical Formalization & Core Definitions

### 2.1 The Dot or Scalar Product

> **Definition (Dot Product).** If $A$ and $B$ are two vectors, the scalar product of $A$ and $B$ is defined as $AB\cos\theta$, where $A$ and $B$ are the magnitudes of the vectors $A$ and $B$, and $\theta$ is the angle between them. The scalar (dot) product is denoted by $A\cdot B$.

The definition carries two equivalent projection readings:

$$
A\cdot B=AB\cos\theta
$$

$$
A\cdot B=A\times(\text{projection of }B\text{ on }A)
$$

$$
A\cdot B=B\times(\text{projection of }A\text{ on }B)
$$

In every case the result is a scalar quantity.

**Special angles.** If the two vectors are at right angles, $\theta=90^{\circ}$, so

$$
A\cdot B=AB\cos 90^{\circ}=AB(0)=0
$$

and the vectors are called orthogonal or perpendicular. If the two vectors are in the same direction, $\theta=0^{\circ}$, so

$$
A\cdot B=AB\cos 0^{\circ}=AB
$$

**Component form.** Write

$$
A=A_1\hat{i}+A_2\hat{j}+A_3\hat{k}
$$

$$
B=B_1\hat{i}+B_2\hat{j}+B_3\hat{k}
$$

Expanding the product term by term gives nine terms:

$$
A\cdot B=(A_1\hat{i}+A_2\hat{j}+A_3\hat{k})\cdot(B_1\hat{i}+B_2\hat{j}+B_3\hat{k})
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
A\cdot B={}&A_1B_1\,\hat{i}\cdot\hat{i}+A_1B_2\,\hat{i}\cdot\hat{j}+A_1B_3\,\hat{i}\cdot\hat{k}\\
&+A_2B_1\,\hat{j}\cdot\hat{i}+A_2B_2\,\hat{j}\cdot\hat{j}+A_2B_3\,\hat{j}\cdot\hat{k}\\
&+A_3B_1\,\hat{k}\cdot\hat{i}+A_3B_2\,\hat{k}\cdot\hat{j}+A_3B_3\,\hat{k}\cdot\hat{k}
\end{aligned}
$$

Now the basis products are fixed by the definition:

$$
\hat{i}\cdot\hat{i}=\hat{j}\cdot\hat{j}=\hat{k}\cdot\hat{k}=(1)(1)\cos 0^{\circ}=1
$$

$$
\hat{i}\cdot\hat{j}=\hat{i}\cdot\hat{k}=\hat{j}\cdot\hat{k}=(1)(1)\cos 90^{\circ}=0
$$

Only the three "matching" terms survive, so

$$
A\cdot B=A_1B_1+A_2B_2+A_3B_3
$$

This is the master computational formula for the dot product and the starting point of most exam proofs.

### 2.2 The Cross or Vector Product

> **Definition (Cross Product).** The cross or vector product of $A$ and $B$, written $A\times B$ and read "A cross B", is defined as a vector having magnitude $AB\sin\theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between the two vectors. The product vector acts in a direction perpendicular to $A$ and $B$ in such a sense that $A$, $B$, and $A\times B$ form a right-handed system in that order.

The magnitude is

$$
\lVert A\times B\rVert=AB\sin\theta
$$

**Right-hand rule.** The axes $OX$, $OY$, $OZ$ form a right-handed set if rotation from $OX$ to $OY$ corresponds to a right-handed corkscrew action along the positive direction of $OZ$; similarly, rotation from $OY$ to $OZ$ gives right-hand corkscrew action along the positive direction of $OX$.

**Reversal of order.** The product $B\times A$ reverses the direction of rotation, so the product vector acts in the opposite direction:

$$
B\times A=-(A\times B)
$$

**Special angles.** If $\theta=0^{\circ}$, then $A\times B=AB\sin 0^{\circ}=0$. If $\theta=90^{\circ}$, then $A\times B=AB\sin 90^{\circ}=AB$.

**Component form.** Expanding as for the dot product:

$$
\begin{aligned}
A\times B={}&A_1B_1\,\hat{i}\times\hat{i}+A_1B_2\,\hat{i}\times\hat{j}+A_1B_3\,\hat{i}\times\hat{k}\\
&+A_2B_1\,\hat{j}\times\hat{i}+A_2B_2\,\hat{j}\times\hat{j}+A_2B_3\,\hat{j}\times\hat{k}\\
&+A_3B_1\,\hat{k}\times\hat{i}+A_3B_2\,\hat{k}\times\hat{j}+A_3B_3\,\hat{k}\times\hat{k}
\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\hat{i}\times\hat{i}=(1)(1)\sin 0^{\circ}=0$, we have

$$
\hat{i}\times\hat{i}=\hat{j}\times\hat{j}=\hat{k}\times\hat{k}=0
$$

Since $\hat{i}\times\hat{j}=(1)(1)\sin 90^{\circ}=1$ in the direction $OZ$, we have $\hat{i}\times\hat{j}=\hat{k}$. The complete cyclic table is

$$
\hat{i}\times\hat{j}=\hat{k},\qquad \hat{j}\times\hat{k}=\hat{i},\qquad \hat{k}\times\hat{i}=\hat{j}
$$

$$
\hat{j}\times\hat{i}=-\hat{k},\qquad \hat{k}\times\hat{j}=-\hat{i},\qquad \hat{i}\times\hat{k}=-\hat{j}
$$

Collecting terms gives

$$
A\times B=(A_2B_3-A_3B_2)\hat{i}+(A_3B_1-A_1B_3)\hat{j}+(A_1B_2-A_2B_1)\hat{k}
$$

which is recognised as the expansion of the determinant

$$
A\times B=
\begin{vmatrix}
\hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k}\\
A_1 & A_2 & A_3\\
B_1 & B_2 & B_3
\end{vmatrix}
$$

### 2.3 Unit Vector and Perpendicular Direction

The unit vector in the direction of a vector $B$ is

$$
\hat{b}=\frac{B}{\lVert B\rVert}
$$

The vector $A\times B$ is perpendicular to the plane containing $A$ and $B$, and the unit vector perpendicular to that plane is

$$
\frac{A\times B}{\lVert A\times B\rVert}
$$

### 2.4 Triple Products

> **Definition (Scalar Triple Product).** If $A$, $B$, $C$ are three vectors, the scalar formed by the product $A\cdot(B\times C)$ is called the scalar triple product.

With $A=A_1\hat{i}+A_2\hat{j}+A_3\hat{k}$, $B=B_1\hat{i}+B_2\hat{j}+B_3\hat{k}$, $C=C_1\hat{i}+C_2\hat{j}+C_3\hat{k}$, the scalar triple product is the determinant

$$
A\cdot(B\times C)=
\begin{vmatrix}
A_1 & A_2 & A_3\\
B_1 & B_2 & B_3\\
C_1 & C_2 & C_3
\end{vmatrix}
$$

> **Definition (Vector Triple Product).** If $A$, $B$ and $C$ are three vectors, then $A\times(B\times C)$ and $(A\times B)\times C$ are called vector triple products.

The expansion identity is

$$
A\times(B\times C)=(A\cdot C)B-(A\cdot B)C
$$

## 3. Key Theorems & Essential Results

> **Theorem (Commutativity of the Dot Product).** For any two vectors $A=A_1\hat{i}+A_2\hat{j}+A_3\hat{k}$ and $B=B_1\hat{i}+B_2\hat{j}+B_3\hat{k}$, we have $A\cdot B=B\cdot A$.

**Proof.** By the component definition,

$$
A\cdot B=A_1B_1+A_2B_2+A_3B_3
$$

Similarly,

$$
B\cdot A=B_1A_1+B_2A_2+B_3A_3
$$

Since multiplication of real numbers is commutative, $A_1B_1=B_1A_1$, $A_2B_2=B_2A_2$ and $A_3B_3=B_3A_3$. Hence the two sums are identical and $A\cdot B=B\cdot A$. $\blacksquare$

> **Theorem (Distributive Laws).** For vectors $A$, $B$, $C$ and scalar $m$, the following laws are valid: $A\cdot(B+C)=A\cdot B+A\cdot C$; $A\times(B+C)=A\times B+A\times C$; and $m(A\cdot B)=(mA)\cdot B=A\cdot(mB)$.

> **Theorem (Anti-commutativity of the Cross Product).** For any two vectors $A$ and $B$, we have $A\times B=-(B\times A)$.

**Proof.** Reversing the order reverses the direction of rotation, so the product vector acts in the opposite direction while retaining the same magnitude $AB\sin\theta$. Hence $B\times A=-(A\times B)$. $\blacksquare$

> **Theorem (Cosine Rule).** If $A$, $B$, $C$ are the three sides of a triangle with $\theta$ the angle between the vectors $A$ and $B$, then $C^2=A^2+B^2-2AB\cos\theta$.

**Proof.** From the triangle relation $A=B+C$, equivalently $C=A-B$. Then

$$
\begin{aligned}
C\cdot C&=(A-B)\cdot(A-B)\\
&=A\cdot A-2A\cdot B+B\cdot B
\end{aligned}
$$

Since $C\cdot C=C^2$, $A\cdot A=A^2$, $B\cdot B=B^2$ and $A\cdot B=AB\cos\theta$, we obtain

$$
C^2=A^2+B^2-2AB\cos\theta
$$

$\blacksquare$

> **Theorem (Properties of the Scalar Triple Product).** The scalar triple product satisfies: (i) $A\cdot(B\times C)=B\cdot(C\times A)=C\cdot(A\times B)$; and (ii) $A\cdot(A\times B)=0$.

**Proof of (i).** Interchanging two rows of a determinant reverses its sign, so

$$
A\cdot(B\times C)=
\begin{vmatrix}
A_1 & A_2 & A_3\\
B_1 & B_2 & B_3\\
C_1 & C_2 & C_3
\end{vmatrix}
=-\begin{vmatrix}
B_1 & B_2 & B_3\\
A_1 & A_2 & A_3\\
C_1 & C_2 & C_3
\end{vmatrix}
=B\cdot(C\times A)
$$

and the same cyclic argument gives $B\cdot(C\times A)=C\cdot(A\times B)$.

**Proof of (ii).** In the determinant

$$
A\cdot(A\times B)=
\begin{vmatrix}
A_1 & A_2 & A_3\\
A_1 & A_2 & A_3\\
B_1 & B_2 & B_3
\end{vmatrix}
$$

two rows are identical, so the determinant is zero. $\blacksquare$

> **Theorem (Volume and Coplanarity).** The scalar triple product in absolute value represents the volume of a parallelepiped with sides $A$, $B$ and $C$. The scalar triple product provides a test to show whether three given vectors lie in the same plane: the vectors are coplanar if and only if $A\cdot(B\times C)=0$.

> **Theorem (Area of a Parallelogram and Triangle).** The magnitude $\lVert A\times B\rVert$ is the area of the parallelogram with adjacent sides $A$ and $B$. The area of a triangle is half the area of a parallelogram, hence the area of a triangle is $\tfrac{1}{2}\lVert A\times B\rVert$.

> **Theorem (Non-associativity of the Cross Product).** In general $A\times(B\times C)\neq(A\times B)\times C$, so parentheses are required in $A\times B\times C$ to avoid ambiguity.

> **Theorem (Equation and Distance for a Plane).** If $A$ is a vector perpendicular to a plane and $B$ is the position vector of a point $Q$ on the plane, then for the position vector $r$ of any point $P$ on the plane, $(B-r)\cdot A=0$, equivalently $r\cdot A=B\cdot A$. The distance from the origin to the plane is the projection of $B$ on $A$, namely $B\cdot\hat{a}$ where $\hat{a}=A/\lVert A\rVert$. The distance from the point $(x_1,y_1,z_1)$ to the plane $ax+by+cz=d$ is

$$
\text{distance}=\frac{\lvert ax_1+by_1+cz_1-d\rvert}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2+c^2}}
$$

> **Theorem (Angles with the Coordinate Axes).** If $\alpha$, $\beta$, $\gamma$ are the angles that $A=A_1\hat{i}+A_2\hat{j}+A_3\hat{k}$ makes with the positive $x$, $y$, $z$ axes respectively, then

$$
\cos\alpha=\frac{A_1}{\lVert A\rVert},\qquad \cos\beta=\frac{A_2}{\lVert A\rVert},\qquad \cos\gamma=\frac{A_3}{\lVert A\rVert}
$$

## 4. Worked Exemplar Problem with Step-by-Step Solution

### 4.1 Dot Product, Angle, and Perpendicularity

**Example (Dot product and angle).** If $A=2\hat{i}+2\hat{j}-\hat{k}$ and $B=6\hat{i}-3\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$, find $A\cdot B$ and the angle between $A$ and $B$.

**Step 1 — Compute the dot product by components.**

$$
A\cdot B=(2)(6)+(2)(-3)+(-1)(2)
$$

$$
A\cdot B=12-6-2=4
$$

**Step 2 — Compute the magnitudes.**

$$
\lVert A\rVert=\sqrt{2^2+2^2+(-1)^2}=\sqrt{9}=3
$$

$$
\lVert B\rVert=\sqrt{6^2+(-3)^2+2^2}=\sqrt{49}=7
$$

**Step 3 — Use $A\cdot B=AB\cos\theta$.** Here $AB=(3)(7)=21$, so

$$
\cos\theta=\frac{4}{21}
$$

$$
\theta=\cos^{-1}\!\left(\frac{4}{21}\right)\approx 79^{\circ}
$$

**Example (Perpendicularity condition).** Determine the values of $a$ so that $A=a\hat{i}-2\hat{j}+\hat{k}$ and $B=2a\hat{i}+a\hat{j}-4\hat{k}$ are perpendicular.

**Step 1 — Set the dot product to zero.**

$$
(a)(2a)+(-2)(a)+(1)(-4)=0
$$

**Step 2 — Simplify to a quadratic.**

$$
2a^2-2a-4=0
$$

$$
a^2-a-2=0
$$

**Step 3 — Factor and solve.**

$$
(a-2)(a+1)=0
$$

$$
a=2\quad\text{or}\quad a=-1
$$

**Example (Right-angled triangle).** Show that $A=3\hat{i}-2\hat{j}+\hat{k}$, $B=\hat{i}-3\hat{j}+5\hat{k}$, $C=2\hat{i}+\hat{j}-4\hat{k}$ form a right-angled triangle.

**Step 1 — Show the vectors close into a triangle.** By trial, $A=B+C$, so the three vectors do form a triangle.

**Step 2 — Test for a right angle.** Compute

$$
A\cdot C=(3)(2)+(-2)(1)+(1)(-4)=6-2-4=0
$$

Since $A\cdot C=0$, the vectors $A$ and $C$ are perpendicular, so the triangle is right-angled.

**Example (Angles with the axes).** Find the angles that $A=3\hat{i}-6\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$ makes with the coordinate axes.

**Step 1 — Compute the magnitude.**

$$
\lVert A\rVert=\sqrt{3^2+(-6)^2+2^2}=\sqrt{49}=7
$$

**Step 2 — Apply the direction cosine formulas.**

$$
\cos\alpha=\frac{3}{7}\quad\Rightarrow\quad \alpha=\cos^{-1}\!\left(\frac{3}{7}\right)\approx 64.6^{\circ}
$$

$$
\cos\beta=\frac{-6}{7}\quad\Rightarrow\quad \beta=\cos^{-1}\!\left(-\frac{6}{7}\right)\approx 149^{\circ}
$$

$$
\cos\gamma=\frac{2}{7}\quad\Rightarrow\quad \gamma=\cos^{-1}\!\left(\frac{2}{7}\right)\approx 73.4^{\circ}
$$

**Example (Projection).** Find the projection of $A=\hat{i}-2\hat{j}+\hat{k}$ on $B=4\hat{i}-4\hat{j}+7\hat{k}$.

**Step 1 — Compute the magnitude of $B$.**

$$
\lVert B\rVert=\sqrt{4^2+(-4)^2+7^2}=\sqrt{81}=9
$$

**Step 2 — Form the unit vector.**

$$
\hat{b}=\frac{4}{9}\hat{i}-\frac{4}{9}\hat{j}+\frac{7}{9}\hat{k}
$$

**Step 3 — Project using $A\cdot\hat{b}$.**

$$
A\cdot\hat{b}=(1)\frac{4}{9}+(-2)\left(-\frac{4}{9}\right)+(1)\frac{7}{9}
$$

$$
A\cdot\hat{b}=\frac{4+8+7}{9}=\frac{19}{9}
$$

**Example (Equation of a plane and distance).** Find an equation for the plane perpendicular to $A=2\hat{i}+3\hat{j}+6\hat{k}$ and passing through the terminal point of $B=\hat{i}+5\hat{j}+3\hat{k}$, and find the distance from the origin to the plane.

**Step 1 — Use the perpendicularity condition.** Let $r$ be the position vector of a general point $P$ on the plane and $Q$ the terminal point of $B$. Since $B-r$ is perpendicular to $A$,

$$
(B-r)\cdot A=0
$$

$$
r\cdot A=B\cdot A
$$

**Step 2 — Expand in rectangular coordinates.**

$$
(x\hat{i}+y\hat{j}+z\hat{k})\cdot(2\hat{i}+3\hat{j}+6\hat{k})=(\hat{i}+5\hat{j}+3\hat{k})\cdot(2\hat{i}+3\hat{j}+6\hat{k})
$$

$$
2x+3y+6z=2+15+18
$$

$$
2x+3y+6z=35
$$

**Step 3 — Compute the distance as a projection.** The unit vector in the direction of $A$ is

$$
\hat{a}=\frac{2}{7}\hat{i}+\frac{3}{7}\hat{j}+\frac{6}{7}\hat{k}
$$

since $\lVert A\rVert=\sqrt{4+9+36}=7$. Then

$$
B\cdot\hat{a}=(1)\frac{2}{7}+(5)\frac{3}{7}+(3)\frac{6}{7}=\frac{2+15+18}{7}=5
$$

The distance from the origin to the plane is $5$.

**Example (Plane through a point perpendicular to a line).** Given $A=3\hat{i}+\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$ and $B=\hat{i}-2\hat{j}-4\hat{k}$ as position vectors of points $P$ and $Q$, find an equation for the plane passing through $Q$ and perpendicular to line $PQ$, and the distance from $(-1,1,1)$ to that plane.

**Step 1 — Find the direction vector of the line.**

$$
PQ=OQ-OP=-2\hat{i}-3\hat{j}-6\hat{k}
$$

**Step 2 — Impose perpendicularity.** For a point $R$ with position vector $r$ on the plane,

$$
QR=OR-OQ=(x-1)\hat{i}+(y+2)\hat{j}+(z+4)\hat{k}
$$

Since the plane is perpendicular to $PQ$, $PQ\cdot QR=0$:

$$
(-2\hat{i}-3\hat{j}-6\hat{k})\cdot\big[(x-1)\hat{i}+(y+2)\hat{j}+(z+4)\hat{k}\big]=0
$$

**Step 3 — Expand.**

$$
-2(x-1)-3(y+2)-6(z+4)=0
$$

$$
-2x+2-3y-6-6z-24=0
$$

$$
2x+3y+6z+28=0
$$

**Step 4 — Apply the distance formula.** With $a=2$, $b=3$, $c=6$, $d=-28$ and $(x_1,y_1,z_1)=(-1,1,1)$,

$$
\text{distance}=\frac{\lvert 2(-1)+3(1)+6(1)+28\rvert}{\sqrt{2^2+3^2+6^2}}
$$

$$
\text{distance}=\frac{\lvert -2+3+6+28\rvert}{7}=\frac{35}{7}=5
$$

### 4.2 Cross Product, Areas, and Triple Products

**Example (Area of a triangle).** Find the area of the triangle with vertices $P(1,3,2)$, $Q(2,-1,1)$, $R(-1,2,3)$.

**Step 1 — Form two side vectors.**

$$
PQ=\hat{i}-4\hat{j}-\hat{k}
$$

$$
PR=-2\hat{i}-\hat{j}+\hat{k}
$$

**Step 2 — Take the cross product.**

$$
PQ\times PR=
\begin{vmatrix}
\hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k}\\
1 & -4 & -1\\
-2 & -1 & 1
\end{vmatrix}
$$

$$
PQ\times PR=\big[(-4)(1)-(-1)(-1)\big]\hat{i}-\big[(1)(1)-(-1)(-2)\big]\hat{j}+\big[(1)(-1)-(-4)(-2)\big]\hat{k}
$$

$$
PQ\times PR=(-4-1)\hat{i}-(1-2)\hat{j}+(-1-8)\hat{k}
$$

$$
PQ\times PR=-5\hat{i}+\hat{j}-9\hat{k}
$$

**Step 3 — Take the magnitude and halve it.**

$$
\lVert PQ\times PR\rVert=\sqrt{(-5)^2+1^2+(-9)^2}=\sqrt{107}
$$

$$
\text{Area}=\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{107}
$$

**Example (Scalar triple product).** Evaluate $A\cdot(B\times C)$ for $A=2\hat{i}-3\hat{j}+4\hat{k}$, $B=\hat{i}-2\hat{j}-3\hat{k}$, $C=2\hat{i}+\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$.

**Step 1 — Compute $B\times C$.**

$$
B\times C=
\begin{vmatrix}
\hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k}\\
1 & -2 & -3\\
2 & 1 & 2
\end{vmatrix}
$$

$$
B\times C=\big[(-2)(2)-(-3)(1)\big]\hat{i}-\big[(1)(2)-(-3)(2)\big]\hat{j}+\big[(1)(1)-(-2)(2)\big]\hat{k}
$$

$$
B\times C=-\hat{i}-8\hat{j}+5\hat{k}
$$

**Step 2 — Dot with $A$.**

$$
A\cdot(B\times C)=(2)(-1)+(-3)(-8)+(4)(5)
$$

$$
A\cdot(B\times C)=-2+24+20=42
$$

Since the result is nonzero, the three vectors are not coplanar, and the parallelepiped with sides $A$, $B$, $C$ has volume $42$.

**Example (Non-associativity).** For $A=3\hat{i}-\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$, $B=2\hat{i}+\hat{j}-\hat{k}$, $C=\hat{i}-2\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$, compare $A\times(B\times C)$ with $(A\times B)\times C$.

**Step 1 — Compute $B\times C$.**

$$
B\times C=
\begin{vmatrix}
\hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k}\\
2 & 1 & -1\\
1 & -2 & 2
\end{vmatrix}
=0\hat{i}-5\hat{j}-5\hat{k}
$$

**Step 2 — Compute $A\times(B\times C)$.**

$$
A\times(B\times C)=
\begin{vmatrix}
\hat{i} & \hat{j} &
$$

A\times(B\times C)=

$$
\begin{vmatrix}
\hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k}
3 & -1 & 2
0 & -5 & -5
\end{vmatrix}
$$

A\times(B\times C)=\big[(-1)(-5)-(2)(-5)\big]\hat{i}-\big[(3)(-5)-(2)(0)\big]\hat{j}+\big[(3)(-5)-(-1)(0)\big]\hat{k}

A\times(B\times C)=15\hat{i}+15\hat{j}-15\hat{k}

$$
**Step 3 — Compute $A\times B$.**
$$

A\times B=

$$
\begin{vmatrix}
\hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k}
3 & -1 & 2
2 & 1 & -1
\end{vmatrix}
$$

A\times B=\big[(-1)(-1)-(2)(1)\big]\hat{i}-\big[(3)(-1)-(2)(2)\big]\hat{j}+\big[(3)(1)-(-1)(2)\big]\hat{k}

A\times B=-\hat{i}+7\hat{j}+5\hat{k}

$$
**Step 4 — Compute $(A\times B)\times C$.**
$$

(A\times B)\times C=

$$
\begin{vmatrix}
\hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k}
-1 & 7 & 5
1 & -2 & 2
\end{vmatrix}
$$

(A\times B)\times C=\big[(7)(2)-(5)(-2)\big]\hat{i}-\big[(-1)(2)-(5)(1)\big]\hat{j}+\big[(-1)(-2)-(7)(1)\big]\hat{k}

(A\times B)\times C=24\hat{i}+7\hat{j}-5\hat{k}

$$
**Step 5 — Compare.** The two results differ, so
$$

A\times(B\times C)\neq(A\times B)\times C

$$
which shows the need for parentheses in $A\times B\times C$ to avoid ambiguity.
**Example (Unit vector perpendicular to a plane).** Find a unit vector perpendicular to the plane containing $A$ and $B$.
**Step 1 — Compute the cross product $A\times B$.** This vector is perpendicular to the plane on which $A$ and $B$ lie.
**Step 2 — Normalise it.**
$$

\hat{n}=\frac{A\times B}{\lVert A\times B\rVert}

$$
The direction of $A\times B$ is fixed by the right-hand thumb rule, and the three vectors $A$, $B$, $A\times B$ form a right-handed system.
### 4.3 Examination-Style Multi-Part Question
**Question.** (a) State the distributive and commutative laws for dot and vector products. (b) Define the scalar triple product $A\cdot(B\times C)$ and the vector triple product $A\times(B\times C)$. (c) Find the area of the triangle with vertices $P(2,3,5)$, $Q(4,2,-1)$, $R(3,6,4)$.
**Part (a) — Laws.**
Dot product: $A\cdot B=B\cdot A$ (commutative) and $A\cdot(B+C)=A\cdot B+A\cdot C$ (distributive).
Vector product: $A\times B=-(B\times A)$ (anti-commutative) and $A\times(B+C)=A\times B+A\times C$ (distributive).
**Part (b) — Definitions.** The scalar triple product $A\cdot(B\times C)$ is the scalar obtained by crossing $B$ with $C$ and then dotting the result with $A$; in determinant form it equals the determinant whose rows are the components of $A$, $B$, $C$. The vector triple product $A\times(B\times C)$ is the vector obtained by crossing $B$ with $C$ and then crossing $A$ with that result; it expands as $(A\cdot C)B-(A\cdot B)C$.
**Part (c) — Area of the triangle.**
**Step 1 — Form two side vectors from $P$.**
$$

PQ=(4-2)\hat{i}+(2-3)\hat{j}+(-1-5)\hat{k}=2\hat{i}-\hat{j}-6\hat{k}

PR=(3-2)\hat{i}+(6-3)\hat{j}+(4-5)\hat{k}=\hat{i}+3\hat{j}-\hat{k}

$$
**Step 2 — Take the cross product.**
$$

PQ\times PR=

$$
\begin{vmatrix}
\hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k}
2 & -1 & -6
1 & 3 & -1
\end{vmatrix}
$$

PQ\times PR=\big[(-1)(-1)-(-6)(3)\big]\hat{i}-\big[(2)(-1)-(-6)(1)\big]\hat{j}+\big[(2)(3)-(-1)(1)\big]\hat{k}

PQ\times PR=(1+18)\hat{i}-(-2+6)\hat{j}+(6+1)\hat{k}

PQ\times PR=19\hat{i}-4\hat{j}+7\hat{k}

$$
**Step 3 — Take the magnitude and halve it.**
$$

\lVert PQ\times PR\rVert=\sqrt{19^2+(-4)^2+7^2}=\sqrt{361+16+49}=\sqrt{426}

Area=\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{426}

$$
## 5. High-Yield Exam Takeaways & Common Pitfalls
### 5.1 Lesson Learning Outcomes as Exam Targets
The stated outcomes of this unit are: determine the dot and cross product; determine a vector perpendicular to a plane; and evaluate scalar triple and vector triple products. Every examination question in this topic maps onto one of these three verbs, so treat them as a checklist.
- **"Determine the dot and cross product"** signals a computation question: component expansion, angle between vectors, perpendicularity condition, projection, or area.
- **"Determine a vector perpendicular to a plane"** signals a normalisation question: compute $A\times B$, then divide by its magnitude.
- **"Evaluate scalar triple and vector triple products"** signals a determinant question, often combined with a coplanarity or volume interpretation.
### 5.2 Magnitude, Unit Vector and Resultant — The Recurring Toolkit
Almost every multi-mark question in this topic is assembled from four primitive operations. Master them as reflexes.
| Operation | Formula | Typical use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Magnitude | $\lVert A\rVert=\sqrt{A_1^2+A_2^2+A_3^2}$ | denominator in every angle or projection |
| Unit vector | $\hat{a}=A/\lVert A\rVert$ | projection, perpendicular direction, distance to plane |
| Resultant | $R=A+B$ componentwise | forming side vectors $PQ=OQ-OP$ |
| Angle | $\cos\theta=\dfrac{A\cdot B}{\lVert A\rVert\lVert B\rVert}$ | angle between vectors, direction cosines |
The single most common source of lost marks is a wrong magnitude. Compute $\lVert A\rVert$ and $\lVert B\rVert$ explicitly and write them down before substituting into the cosine formula.
### 5.3 High-Frequency Question Patterns
- **Commutativity proof (short-mark question).** Write both vectors in component form, expand both dot products, invoke commutativity of real multiplication, conclude. Do not attempt a geometric argument when the question supplies components; the marking scheme expects the component proof.
- **Perpendicularity with an unknown parameter.** Set the dot product to zero, simplify to a quadratic, factor, and state both roots. Omitting one root is a standard error.
- **Right-angled triangle verification.** Two separate marks are usually available: one for showing the vectors close into a triangle (sum of two equals the third, or total sum zero), one for showing a dot product vanishes.
- **Direction cosines.** Always divide each component by the full magnitude, and keep the sign of the component. A negative cosine correctly yields an obtuse angle.
- **Projection.** Project onto the unit vector, not onto the raw vector. The answer is a scalar, not a vector.
- **Plane equation.** Use $r\cdot A=B\cdot A$ when a normal and a point are given; use $PQ\cdot QR=0$ when the plane is perpendicular to a line through two given points.
- **Distance to a plane.** Substitute into $\lvert ax_1+by_1+cz_1-d\rvert/\sqrt{a^2+b^2+c^2}$ with the plane first written in the form $ax+by+cz=d$. Sign errors inside the absolute value are the usual failure point.
- **Area of a triangle.** Form two side vectors from a common vertex, cross them, take the magnitude, then halve. Forgetting the factor $\tfrac{1}{2}$ is the most frequent single-mark loss in the whole topic.
- **Scalar triple product.** Evaluate as a $3\times3$ determinant; interpret a zero result as coplanarity and a nonzero result as the parallelepiped volume.
- **Vector triple product.** Expand with $(A\cdot C)B-(A\cdot B)C$ rather than computing two cross products in sequence, and always retain parentheses.
### 5.4 Common Pitfalls and Traps
- **Confusing the two products.** The dot product returns a scalar; the cross product returns a vector. A scalar answer to an area question, or a vector answer to an angle question, is automatically wrong.
- **Dropping the minus signs in the cross product.** The middle component of the determinant carries a minus sign: $-(A_1B_3-A_3B_1)$. Recompute the middle term separately.
- **Assuming commutativity for the cross product.** $A\times B=-(B\times A)$; reversing order flips the direction.
- **Assuming associativity.** $A\times(B\times C)\neq(A\times B)\times C$ in general; the worked comparison above shows the two results differ.
- **Using $\cos$ where $\sin$ belongs.** The dot product uses $\cos\theta$; the cross product magnitude uses $\sin\theta$. Mixing them inverts every parallel/perpendicular conclusion.
- **Forgetting that parallel vectors give a zero cross product.** A zero cross product is a valid and often expected answer; do not treat it as an error.
- **Sign slips in the distance formula.** Write the plane as $ax+by+cz-d=0$ consistently before substituting the point.
- **Leaving the angle in the wrong form.** State both the exact value, such as $\cos^{-1}(4/21)$, and the approximate degree value when the question asks for an angle.
### 5.5 Answer Structure and Marking Rubric Tips
- **Show the component setup.** Examiners award method marks for writing $A=A_1\hat{i}+A_2\hat{j}+A_3\hat{k}$ and $B=B_1\hat{i}+B_2\hat{j}+B_3\hat{k}$ before any computation.
- **One line per logical step.** Compute the dot product, then the magnitudes, then the cosine, then the angle. Each line is a potential mark.
- **State the geometric conclusion in words.** After obtaining $A\cdot C=0$, write explicitly that $A$ and $C$ are perpendicular and hence the triangle is right-angled. The conclusion carries marks independently of the arithmetic.
- **Label determinant expansions.** Write the determinant, then the cofactor expansion, then the simplified vector. Do not collapse these into one line.
- **Carry exact surds to the end.** Keep $\sqrt{107}$ or $\sqrt{426}$ in the final area answer; premature decimal rounding loses accuracy marks.
- **Verify with a second method where cheap.** For a triangle, confirm closure by checking that the three vectors sum to zero; for a triple product, confirm the cyclic permutation gives the same value.
### 5.6 Time-Management Strategy
- **Short-mark proofs first.** The commutativity proof and the statement of distributive and commutative laws are fast, high-certainty marks. Secure them before attempting long computations.
- **Budget the determinant questions.** A cross product determinant takes roughly two minutes; a triple product roughly three. If a multi-part question carries seven marks for an area, allocate proportionally more time there.
- **Park the distance-to-plane part.** It is a single substitution once the plane equation is correct, so complete the plane equation first and return to the distance.
- **Check units of the answer type before moving on.** Scalar for dot product, vector for cross product, scalar for area and volume, angle in degrees or radians as requested.

payload.content:
## 1. Core Concept Overview & Intuition

The algebra of vectors admits two distinct multiplicative operations. The first, the **dot (scalar) product**, consumes two vectors and returns a single real number. The second, the **cross (vector) product**, consumes two vectors and returns a third vector. These two products are the analytical engine for measuring lengths, angles, projections, areas, volumes, perpendicularity, coplanarity, and the geometry of planes and triangles in three-dimensional space.

The intuition behind the dot product is **projection**. When two vectors are placed tail-to-tail, the component of one vector lying along the direction of the other is obtained by multiplying its length by the cosine of the included angle. The dot product is precisely the product of one vector's magnitude with the signed projection of the other onto it. Consequently, the dot product is largest (equal to the product of magnitudes) when the vectors are parallel, and it vanishes when they are perpendicular, because a perpendicular vector casts no shadow along the other's direction.

The intuition behind the cross product is **area and orientation**. Two non-parallel vectors span a parallelogram; the cross product has magnitude equal to the area of that parallelogram and direction normal (perpendicular) to the plane containing the two vectors. The sense of that normal is fixed by the right-hand rule: if the fingers of the right hand curl from the first vector toward the second, the thumb points along the product vector. This orientation dependence is why the cross product is **anti-commutative**: reversing the order of the factors reverses the normal.

Both products are built from the same geometric data — the magnitudes of the two vectors and the angle between them — but they respond to that angle in complementary ways: the dot product tracks $\cos\theta$ and the cross product tracks $\sin\theta$. Because $\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta=1$, the two products together encode the full geometry of a pair of vectors.![the two vectors are orthogonal or perpendicular to one another.](/cdn/cloudflare/prep/visual-crops/2026/10/document-d0c6c84b-5e48-4773-a688-196f76ad7045-page-22-830af1aa.jpg)

## 2. Mathematical Formalization & Core Definitions

### 2.1 The Dot (Scalar) Product

> **Definition (Dot Product).** If $A$ and $B$ are two vectors, the scalar product of $A$ and $B$ is defined as $AB\cos\theta$, where $A$ and $B$ are the magnitudes of the vectors $A$ and $B$, and $\theta$ is the angle between them. The scalar (dot) product is denoted $A\cdot B$.

Thus



$$
A\cdot B=AB\cos\theta
$$



and this quantity equals either $A$ times the projection of $B$ on $A$, or $B$ times the projection of $A$ on $B$. In either case the result is a scalar quantity.

**Geometric reading of the definition.** Consider two position vectors drawn from a common origin $O$, with $OA=7$ units and $OB=5$ units and an included angle of $45^{\circ}$. Then



$$
OA\cdot OB=OA\cdot OB\cos\theta=7\cdot 5\cos 45^{\circ}=35.2
$$



to three significant figures. The product is a pure number carrying the units of the product of the two lengths.

**Special angles.** The definition immediately yields three structural facts.

- If $\theta=90^{\circ}$, then $a\cdot b=ab\cos 90^{\circ}=ab\cdot 0=0$. The scalar product of any two vectors at right angles is always zero, and the vectors are said to be **orthogonal** or **perpendicular**.

- If the two vectors point in the same direction, then $\theta=0^{\circ}$ and $a\cdot b=ab\cos 0^{\circ}=ab$.
- If the two vectors point in opposite directions, then $\theta=180^{\circ}$ and $a\cdot b=-ab$.

### 2.2 The Dot Product in Component Form

Write the two vectors in component form as



$$
A=A_1\hat{i}+A_2\hat{j}+A_3\hat{k}
$$





$$
B=B_1\hat{i}+B_2\hat{j}+B_3\hat{k}
$$



Expanding the product bilinearly gives nine elementary products:



$$
\begin{aligned}
A\cdot B={}&A_1B_1\,\hat{i}\cdot\hat{i}+A_1B_2\,\hat{i}\cdot\hat{j}+A_1B_3\,\hat{i}\cdot\hat{k}\\
&+A_2B_1\,\hat{j}\cdot\hat{i}+A_2B_2\,\hat{j}\cdot\hat{j}+A_2B_3\,\hat{j}\cdot\hat{k}\\
&+A_3B_1\,\hat{k}\cdot\hat{i}+A_3B_2\,\hat{k}\cdot\hat{j}+A_3B_3\,\hat{k}\cdot\hat{k}
\end{aligned}
$$



Now $\hat{i}\cdot\hat{i}=\hat{j}\cdot\hat{j}=\hat{k}\cdot\hat{k}=1\cdot 1\cos 0^{\circ}=1$, while $\hat{i}\cdot\hat{j}=\hat{i}\cdot\hat{k}=\hat{j}\cdot\hat{k}=1\cdot 1\cos 90^{\circ}=0$. The six cross terms vanish and we are left with



$$
A\cdot B=A_1B_1+A_2B_2+A_3B_3
$$



This is the working formula for every dot-product computation.

### 2.3 The Cross (Vector) Product

> **Definition (Cross Product).** The cross or vector product of $A$ and $B$, written $A\times B$ and read " $A$ cross $B$ ", is defined as a vector having magnitude $AB\sin\theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between the two vectors. The product vector acts in a direction perpendicular to $A$ and $B$ in such a sense that $A$, $B$, and $(A\times B)$ form a right-handed system in that order.

Thus



$$
\lvert A\times B\rvert=AB\sin\theta
$$



**Right-handed axes.** For vectors in space, axes of reference are normally defined by the right-hand rule. The axes $OX$, $OY$, $OZ$ form a right-handed set if rotation from $OX$ to $OY$ takes a right-handed corkscrew action along the positive direction of $OZ$; similarly, rotation from $OY$ to $OZ$ gives right-hand corkscrew action along the positive direction of $OX$, and so on cyclically.

**Anti-commutativity.** The product $B\times A$ reverses the direction of rotation, so the product vector acts downward; hence



$$
B\times A=-(A\times B)
$$



**Special angles.** If $\theta=0^{\circ}$, then $A\times B=AB\sin 0^{\circ}=0$, so parallel vectors have zero cross product. If $\theta=90^{\circ}$, then $A\times B=AB\sin 90^{\circ}=AB$, so the magnitude is maximal for perpendicular vectors.

### 2.4 The Cross Product in Component Form

Expanding bilinearly as before,



$$
\begin{aligned}
A\times B={}&A_1B_1\,\hat{i}\times\hat{i}+A_1B_2\,\hat{i}\times\hat{j}+A_1B_3\,\hat{i}\times\hat{k}\\
&+A_2B_1\,\hat{j}\times\hat{i}+A_2B_2\,\hat{j}\times\hat{j}+A_2B_3\,\hat{j}\times\hat{k}\\
&+A_3B_1\,\hat{k}\times\hat{i}+A_3B_2\,\hat{k}\times\hat{j}+A_3B_3\,\hat{k}\times\hat{k}
\end{aligned}
$$



Since $\hat{i}\times\hat{i}=1\cdot 1\sin 0^{\circ}=0$, we have $\hat{i}\times\hat{i}=\hat{j}\times\hat{j}=\hat{k}\times\hat{k}=0$. Also $\hat{i}\times\hat{j}=1\cdot 1\sin 90^{\circ}=1$ in the direction $OZ$, that is $\hat{i}\times\hat{j}=\hat{k}$. The complete multiplication table of the basis vectors is



$$
\hat{i}\times\hat{j}=\hat{k},\qquad \hat{j}\times\hat{k}=\hat{i},\qquad \hat{k}\times\hat{i}=\hat{j}
$$





$$
\hat{j}\times\hat{i}=-\hat{k},\qquad \hat{k}\times\hat{j}=-\hat{i},\qquad \hat{i}\times\hat{k}=-\hat{j}
$$



Collecting terms gives



$$
A\times B=(A_2B_3-A_3B_2)\hat{i}+(A_3B_1-A_1B_3)\hat{j}+(A_1B_2-A_2B_1)\hat{k}
$$



which is recognized as the expansion of the determinant



$$
A\times B=
\begin{vmatrix}
\hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k}\\
A_1 & A_2 & A_3\\
B_1 & B_2 & B_3
\end{vmatrix}
$$



The determinant form is the standard computational device: expand along the first row, remembering the alternating signs $+,-,+$.

## 3. Key Theorems & Essential Results

> **Theorem (Commutativity of the Dot Product).** For any two vectors $A=A_1\hat{i}+A_2\hat{j}+A_3\hat{k}$ and $B=B_1\hat{i}+B_2\hat{j}+B_3\hat{k}$, we have $A\cdot B=B\cdot A$.

*Proof.* By the component definition,



$$
A\cdot B=A_1B_1+A_2B_2+A_3B_3
$$



and similarly



$$
B\cdot A=B_1A_1+B_2A_2+B_3A_3
$$



Since multiplication of real numbers is commutative, $A_iB_i=B_iA_i$ for each $i=1,2,3$, hence the two sums are identical and $A\cdot B=B\cdot A$. $\blacksquare$

> **Theorem (Distributive Laws).** For vectors $A$, $B$, $C$ and scalar $\lambda$: $A\cdot(B+C)=A\cdot B+A\cdot C$; $A\times(B+C)=A\times B+A\times C$; and $\lambda(A\cdot B)=(\lambda A)\cdot B=A\cdot(\lambda B)$.

These follow by expanding both sides in components and regrouping terms.

> **Theorem (Cosine Rule).** If $A$, $B$, $C$ are the three sides of a triangle and $\theta$ is the angle between the vectors $A$ and $B$, then $C^2=A^2+B^2-2AB\cos\theta$.

*Proof.* From the vector triangle, $A=B+C$, equivalently $C=A-B$. Then



$$
\begin{aligned}
C\cdot C&=(A-B)\cdot(A-B)\\
&=A\cdot A-2A\cdot B+B\cdot B
\end{aligned}
$$



Since $C\cdot C=C^2$, $A\cdot A=A^2$, $B\cdot B=B^2$ and $A\cdot B=AB\cos\theta$, we obtain



$$
C^2=A^2+B^2-2AB\cos\theta
$$



which is the cosine rule for plane triangles. $\blacksquare$

> **Theorem (Equation of a Plane).** The plane perpendicular to a vector $A$ and passing through the terminal point of a position vector $B$ consists of all points with position vector $r$ satisfying $(B-r)\cdot A=0$, equivalently $r\cdot A=B\cdot A$.

> **Theorem (Distance from a Point to a Plane).** The distance from the point $(x_1,y_1,z_1)$ to the plane $ax+by+cz=d$ is



$$
\text{distance}=\frac{ax_1+by_1+cz_1-d}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2+c^2}}
$$



## 4. Worked Exemplar Problem with Step-by-Step Solution

**Problem.** For the vectors $A=2\hat{i}+2\hat{j}-\hat{k}$ and $B=6\hat{i}-3\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$:

(a) compute $A\cdot B$ and hence the angle between them;

(b) find a unit vector perpendicular to the plane containing $A$ and $B$;

(c) find the area of the parallelogram with adjacent sides $A$ and $B$.

**Solution.**

**(a) Dot product and angle.** By the component formula,



$$
A\cdot B=(2)(6)+(2)(-3)+(-1)(2)=12-6-2=4
$$



The magnitudes are



$$
\lvert A\rvert=\sqrt{2^2+2^2+(-1)^2}=\sqrt{9}=3
$$





$$
\lvert B\rvert=\sqrt{6^2+(-3)^2+2^2}=\sqrt{49}=7
$$



Hence



$$
\cos\theta=\frac{A\cdot B}{\lvert A\rvert\lvert B\rvert}=\frac{4}{21}
$$



so



$$
\theta=\cos^{-1}\!\left(\frac{4}{21}\right)\approx 79^{\circ}
$$



**(b) Unit normal to the plane.** The vector $A\times B$ is perpendicular to both $A$ and $B$, hence normal to the plane they span. Expanding the determinant,



$$
A\times B=
\begin{vmatrix}
\hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k}\\
2 & 2 & -1\\
6 & -3 & 2
\end{vmatrix}
$$





$$
=\big((2)(2)-(-1)(-3)\big)\hat{i}-\big((2)(2)-(-1)(6)\big)\hat{j}+\big((2)(-3)-(2)(6)\big)\hat{k}
$$





$$
A\times B=\hat{i}-10\hat{j}-18\hat{k}
$$



Its magnitude is



$$
\lvert A\times B\rvert=\sqrt{1^2+(-10)^2+(-18)^2}=\sqrt{1+100+324}=\sqrt{425}=5\sqrt{17}
$$



so the required unit vector is



$$
\hat{n}=\frac{1}{5\sqrt{17}}\big(\hat{i}-10\hat{j}-18\hat{k}\big)
$$



and its negative is the equally valid unit normal in the opposite sense.

**(c) Area of the parallelogram.** The area of the parallelogram with adjacent sides $A$ and $B$ is the magnitude of their cross product, already computed in part (b):



$$
\text{Area}=\lvert A\times B\rvert=5\sqrt{17}\approx 20.6
$$



## 5. Common Pitfalls & Exam Strategy

**Dot versus cross: which product answers which question.** The dot product returns a scalar and is the tool for angles, projections, orthogonality tests and plane equations. The cross product returns a vector and is the tool for perpendicular directions, areas and the orientation of a plane. A frequent error is to reach for the cross product when only an angle is wanted, or to reach for the dot product when a normal direction is required. Decide first whether the answer must be a number or a vector.

**Sign discipline in the determinant expansion.** The middle term of the determinant expansion carries a minus sign:



$$
A\times B=(A_2B_3-A_3B_2)\hat{i}-(A_1B_3-A_3B_1)\hat{j}+(A_1B_2-A_2B_1)\hat{k}
$$



Dropping this minus sign is the single most common computational slip. A reliable safeguard is to check the result against the basis table: for $A=\hat{i}$ and $B=\hat{j}$ the formula must return $\hat{k}$, and for $A=\hat{j}$ and $B=\hat{i}$ it must return $-\hat{k}$.

**Order matters in the cross product.** Because $B\times A=-(A\times B)$, the order of the factors fixes the sense of the normal. When a problem asks for "the" unit normal, state that either sign is acceptable, or choose the sign dictated by the geometry of the question.

**Zero products carry information.** A vanishing dot product certifies perpendicularity; a vanishing cross product certifies parallelism, since $\lvert A\times B\rvert=AB\sin\theta$ vanishes exactly when $\theta=0^{\circ}$ or $\theta=180^{\circ}$. In a right-angled-triangle problem, computing the three pairwise dot products and finding one of them zero is a complete and rigorous proof of the right angle.

**Angles with the coordinate axes.** The angle $\alpha$ that $A$ makes with the positive $x$-axis is obtained from $A\cdot\hat{i}=A\cos\alpha$, so $\cos\alpha=A_1/\lvert A\rvert$; the other two angles follow by cyclic replacement of the component. Always divide by the full magnitude $\lvert A\rvert$, not by a single component, and expect an obtuse angle whenever the corresponding component is negative.

**Projections.** The projection of $A$ on $B$ is $A\cdot\hat{b}$, where $\hat{b}=B/\lvert B\rvert$ is the unit vector along $B$. Forgetting to normalize $B$ produces $A\cdot B$, which is the projection scaled by $\lvert B\rvert$ and is dimensionally wrong for a length.

**Planes and distances.** For a plane through the terminal point of $B$ with normal $A$, the equation is $r\cdot A=B\cdot A$; in coordinates this reads $A_1x+A_2y+A_3z=A_1B_1+A_2B_2+A_3B_3$. The distance from the origin to that plane is the projection of $B$ on the unit normal, namely $B\cdot A/\lvert A\rvert$. When applying the point-to-plane distance formula, substitute the coordinates with their signs intact and divide by $\sqrt{a^2+b^2+c^2}$, the magnitude of the normal vector.

**Checking magnitudes.** A quick sanity check on any cross product is the identity $\lvert A\times B\rvert^2=\lvert A\rvert^2\lvert B\rvert^2-(A\cdot B)^2$, which follows from $\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta=1$. If the computed cross product and the computed dot product fail this relation, an arithmetic error has occurred.

blocks.text: 1. Core Concept Overview & Intuition

The reciprocal set of vectors is a construction that, given a set of three non-coplanar vectors, produces a second set of three vectors with a very specific mutual relationship. The guiding geometric idea is stated plainly in the course material: reciprocal vectors are formed by choosing a vector perpendicular to two lattice vectors and of length reciprocal to the third lattice vector. In other words, each member of the reciprocal set is built so that it is orthogonal to the two vectors it is *not* paired with, while its length is controlled by the vector it *is* paired with.

The single-vector version of the idea is the simplest entry point. The vector which has the same direction as a given vector but has magnitude reciprocal to that of the given vector is called the reciprocal of that vector. So if a vector has length $5$, its reciprocal points the same way but has length $1/5$. This is a pure rescaling along a fixed direction, and it already contains the essential feature of the full construction: direction is preserved, magnitude is inverted.

The full reciprocal set extends this to three vectors simultaneously. Given a set of three vectors, the reciprocal set consists of three vectors chosen so that each one is perpendicular to the other two members of the original set and has magnitude equal to the reciprocal of the remaining member. The defining property that makes the construction useful is the pattern of dot products between the original set and the reciprocal set: each vector of the original set has a dot product of unity with its own reciprocal partner and a dot product of zero with the other two reciprocal vectors. This is the vector-algebra analogue of an orthonormal basis, except that the original vectors need not be orthogonal or of unit length.

Intuition for why such a set must exist: three non-coplanar vectors span all of three-dimensional space, so any vector can be written as a combination of them. The reciprocal set is precisely the set of vectors that "reads off" the coefficients in such a combination. If a vector is expressed as a sum of scalar multiples of the original three vectors, then dotting with the corresponding reciprocal vector isolates the matching coefficient, because all the other dot products vanish. This is the mechanism that makes reciprocal sets valuable in later applications, and it is the reason the course asks you to evaluate dot products between a vector and its reciprocal.

The construction is closely tied to the cross product and the scalar triple product, both of which are prior knowledge for this unit. The cross product of two vectors is perpendicular to both, which supplies the required perpendicularity; the scalar triple product of the three original vectors measures the volume they span and supplies the normalising factor that produces the reciprocal magnitudes. The whole evaluation therefore reduces to computing three cross products and dividing by one scalar triple product.
2. Mathematical Formalization & Core Definitions

blocks.title: Definition (Reciprocal of a single vector)
blocks.content: Let $\vec{a}$ be a non-zero vector. The vector which has the same direction as $\vec{a}$ but magnitude reciprocal to that of $\vec{a}$ is called the reciprocal of $\vec{a}$.

blocks.text: Writing $\lVert \vec{a} \rVert$ for the magnitude of $\vec{a}$, the reciprocal of $\vec{a}$ is the vector
because this vector is a positive scalar multiple of $\vec{a}$ (hence has the same direction) and its magnitude is

which is the reciprocal of the magnitude of $\vec{a}$. The unit vector in the direction of $\vec{a}$ is $\hat{a}=\vec{a}/\lVert \vec{a} \rVert$, and the reciprocal of $\vec{a}$ can equally be written as $\hat{a}/\lVert \vec{a} \rVert$, confirming that direction is preserved and only the length is inverted.

blocks.title: Definition (Reciprocal set of vectors)
blocks.content: Let $\vec{a}$, $\vec{b}$, $\vec{c}$ be three non-coplanar vectors, so that their scalar triple product $\vec{a}\cdot(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})$ is non-zero. The reciprocal set is the triple $\vec{a}'$, $\vec{b}'$, $\vec{c}'$ defined by

blocks.text: Each definition is read directly off the geometric description. The vector $\vec{a}'$ is proportional to $\vec{b}\times\vec{c}$, so it is perpendicular to both $\vec{b}$ and $\vec{c}$; its length is reciprocal to the length of $\vec{a}$ in the sense that the normalising denominator is the volume spanned by the three original vectors. The cyclic order of the cross products is what pairs each reciprocal vector with the correct original vector.

The symbols used throughout are as follows. The arrows denote vectors in three-dimensional space; $\times$ denotes the cross product; $\cdot$ denotes the dot product; $\lVert \vec{a} \rVert$ denotes magnitude; and $\vec{a}\cdot(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})$ denotes the scalar triple product, a real number equal to the signed volume of the parallelepiped spanned by the three vectors. The hats $\hat{i}$, $\hat{j}$, $\hat{k}$ denote the standard mutually perpendicular unit vectors along the coordinate axes.

blocks.title: Definition (Dot-product pairing property)
blocks.content: The reciprocal set satisfies
and

blocks.text: This is the property the course discussion asks you to investigate: the dot product between a vector and its own reciprocal is unity, and the dot product between a vector and any other member of the reciprocal set is zero. It is the exact analogue of the Kronecker delta relation for an orthonormal basis, generalised to a non-orthogonal set.
3. Key Theorems & Essential Results

blocks.title: Theorem (Existence and uniqueness of the reciprocal set)
blocks.content: Let $\vec{a}$, $\vec{b}$, $\vec{c}$ be non-coplanar vectors. Then the reciprocal set exists, is unique, and is given by the cross-product formulas of the previous section.

Uniqueness follows because the perpendicularity and magnitude conditions pin down each reciprocal vector completely: a vector perpendicular to two non-parallel vectors must lie along their cross product, and the magnitude condition then fixes the scalar multiple.

## 1. Core Concept Overview & Intuition

The reciprocal set of vectors is a construction that, given a set of three non-coplanar vectors, produces a second set of three vectors with a very specific mutual relationship. The guiding geometric idea is stated plainly in the course material: reciprocal vectors are formed by choosing a vector perpendicular to two lattice vectors and of length reciprocal to the third lattice vector. In other words, each member of the reciprocal set is built so that it is orthogonal to the two vectors it is *not* paired with, while its length is controlled by the vector it *is* paired with.

The single-vector version of the idea is the simplest entry point. The vector which has the same direction as a given vector but has magnitude reciprocal to that of the given vector is called the reciprocal of that vector. So if a vector has length $5$, its reciprocal points the same way but has length $1/5$. This is a pure rescaling along a fixed direction, and it already contains the essential feature of the full construction: direction is preserved, magnitude is inverted.

The full reciprocal set extends this to three vectors simultaneously. Given a set of three vectors, the reciprocal set consists of three vectors chosen so that each one is perpendicular to the other two members of the original set and has magnitude equal to the reciprocal of the remaining member. The defining property that makes the construction useful is the pattern of dot products between the original set and the reciprocal set: each vector of the original set has a dot product of unity with its own reciprocal partner and a dot product of zero with the other two reciprocal vectors. This is the vector-algebra analogue of an orthonormal basis, except that the original vectors need not be orthogonal or of unit length.

Intuition for why such a set must exist: three non-coplanar vectors span all of three-dimensional space, so any vector can be written as a combination of them. The reciprocal set is precisely the set of vectors that "reads off" the coefficients in such a combination. If a vector is expressed as a sum of scalar multiples of the original three vectors, then dotting with the corresponding reciprocal vector isolates the matching coefficient, because all the other dot products vanish. This is the mechanism that makes reciprocal sets valuable in later applications, and it is the reason the course asks you to evaluate dot products between a vector and its reciprocal.

The construction is closely tied to the cross product and the scalar triple product, both of which are prior knowledge for this unit. The cross product of two vectors is perpendicular to both, which supplies the required perpendicularity; the scalar triple product of the three original vectors measures the volume they span and supplies the normalising factor that produces the reciprocal magnitudes. The whole evaluation therefore reduces to computing three cross products and dividing by one scalar triple product.

## 2. Mathematical Formalization & Core Definitions

> **Definition (Reciprocal of a single vector).** Let $\vec{a}$ be a non-zero vector. The vector which has the same direction as $\vec{a}$ but magnitude reciprocal to that of $\vec{a}$ is called the reciprocal of $\vec{a}$.

Writing $\lVert \vec{a} \rVert$ for the magnitude of $\vec{a}$, the reciprocal of $\vec{a}$ is the vector



$$
\frac{\vec{a}}{\lVert \vec{a} \rVert^{2}}
$$



because this vector is a positive scalar multiple of $\vec{a}$ (hence has the same direction) and its magnitude is



$$
\left\lVert \frac{\vec{a}}{\lVert \vec{a} \rVert^{2}} \right\rVert
=
\frac{\lVert \vec{a} \rVert}{\lVert \vec{a} \rVert^{2}}
=
\frac{1}{\lVert \vec{a} \rVert}
$$



which is the reciprocal of the magnitude of $\vec{a}$. The unit vector in the direction of $\vec{a}$ is $\hat{a}=\vec{a}/\lVert \vec{a} \rVert$, and the reciprocal of $\vec{a}$ can equally be written as $\hat{a}/\lVert \vec{a} \rVert$, confirming that direction is preserved and only the length is inverted.

> **Definition (Reciprocal set of vectors).** Let $\vec{a}$, $\vec{b}$, $\vec{c}$ be three non-coplanar vectors, so that their scalar triple product $\vec{a}\cdot(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})$ is non-zero. The reciprocal set is the triple $\vec{a}'$, $\vec{b}'$, $\vec{c}'$ defined by



$$
> \vec{a}'=\frac{\vec{b}\times\vec{c}}{\vec{a}\cdot(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})},
> \qquad
> \vec{b}'=\frac{\vec{c}\times\vec{a}}{\vec{a}\cdot(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})},
> \qquad
> \vec{c}'=\frac{\vec{a}\times\vec{b}}{\vec{a}\cdot(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})}.
$$



Each definition is read directly off the geometric description. The vector $\vec{a}'$ is proportional to $\vec{b}\times\vec{c}$, so it is perpendicular to both $\vec{b}$ and $\vec{c}$; its length is reciprocal to the length of $\vec{a}$ in the sense that the normalising denominator is the volume spanned by the three original vectors. The cyclic order of the cross products is what pairs each reciprocal vector with the correct original vector.

The symbols used throughout are as follows. The arrows denote vectors in three-dimensional space; $\times$ denotes the cross product; $\cdot$ denotes the dot product; $\lVert \vec{a} \rVert$ denotes magnitude; and $\vec{a}\cdot(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})$ denotes the scalar triple product, a real number equal to the signed volume of the parallelepiped spanned by the three vectors. The hats $\hat{i}$, $\hat{j}$, $\hat{k}$ denote the standard mutually perpendicular unit vectors along the coordinate axes.

> **Definition (Dot-product pairing property).** The reciprocal set satisfies



$$
> \vec{a}\cdot\vec{a}'=1,\quad \vec{b}\cdot\vec{b}'=1,\quad \vec{c}\cdot\vec{c}'=1,
$$



> and



$$
> \vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}'=\vec{a}\cdot\vec{c}'=\vec{b}\cdot\vec{a}'=\vec{b}\cdot\vec{c}'=\vec{c}\cdot\vec{a}'=\vec{c}\cdot\vec{b}'=0.
$$



This is the property the course discussion asks you to investigate: the dot product between a vector and its own reciprocal is unity, and the dot product between a vector and any other member of the reciprocal set is zero. It is the exact analogue of the Kronecker delta relation for an orthonormal basis, generalised to a non-orthogonal set.

## 3. Key Theorems & Essential Results

> **Theorem (Existence and uniqueness of the reciprocal set).** Let $\vec{a}$, $\vec{b}$, $\vec{c}$ be non-coplanar vectors. Then the reciprocal set exists, is unique, and is given by the cross-product formulas of the previous section.

The non-coplanarity condition is exactly the statement that the scalar triple product is non-zero, so the denominator in each formula is a non-zero real number and each reciprocal vector is well defined. Uniqueness follows because the perpendicularity and magnitude conditions pin down each reciprocal vector completely: a vector perpendicular to two non-parallel vectors must lie along their cross product, and the magnitude condition then fixes the scalar multiple.

> **Theorem (Pairing property).** For the reciprocal set defined above, the dot products satisfy $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{a}'=1$ and $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}'=\vec{a}\cdot\vec{c}'=0$, with the analogous statements obtained by cyclic permutation of $\vec{a}$, $\vec{b}$, $\vec{c}$.

The vanishing dot products are immediate from the perpendicularity built into the cross products: $\vec{b}'$ is proportional to $\vec{c}\times\vec{a}$, which is perpendicular to $\vec{a}$, so $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}'=0$. The unit dot product follows because the numerator $\vec{a}\cdot(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})$ cancels the identical denominator.

> **Theorem (Reciprocity is symmetric).** The original set is the reciprocal set of its reciprocal set. That is, applying the construction twice returns the vectors you started with.

This result is what justifies the word "reciprocal": the relationship between the two sets is mutual, not one-directional. It also explains why the construction is often described as producing a "dual" set.

> **Theorem (Expansion of a vector in a non-orthogonal basis).** Any vector $\vec{r}$ can be written as



$$
> \vec{r}=(\vec{r}\cdot\vec{a}')\,\vec{a}+(\vec{r}\cdot\vec{b}')\,\vec{b}+(\vec{r}\cdot\vec{c}')\,\vec{c}.
$$



This is the payoff of the pairing property. Because the reciprocal vectors isolate individual coefficients, the coefficients of $\vec{r}$ in the basis $\{\vec{a},\vec{b},\vec{c}\}$ are obtained by dotting $\vec{r}$ with the corresponding reciprocal vectors. This is the precise sense in which the reciprocal set "reads off" coordinates, and it is the reason the construction appears whenever a non-orthogonal basis must be used.

> **Theorem (Reciprocal of the standard unit vectors).** For the standard set $\hat{i}$, $\hat{j}$, $\hat{k}$, the reciprocal set is $\hat{i}$, $\hat{j}$, $\hat{k}$ itself.

The standard unit vectors are mutually perpendicular and of unit length, so their scalar triple product equals $1$ and each cross product of two of them returns the third. The construction therefore reproduces the same set, which is consistent with the symmetry theorem.

## 4. Worked Exemplar Problem with Step-by-Step Solution

The assessment task in the course material is to find a set of vectors reciprocal to a given set of three vectors. The standard unit vectors form the cleanest illustration of the method, and the same three steps apply to any non-coplanar set.

**Problem.** Find a set of vectors reciprocal to the set $\hat{i}$, $\hat{j}$, $\hat{k}$.

**Step 1: Compute the scalar triple product of the original set.**

The scalar triple product is



$$
\hat{i}\cdot(\hat{j}\times\hat{k})=\hat{i}\cdot\hat{i}=1.
$$



Since this is non-zero, the three vectors are non-coplanar and the reciprocal set exists.

**Step 2: Compute the three cross products in cyclic order.**



$$
\hat{j}\times\hat{k}=\hat{i},
\qquad
\hat{k}\times\hat{i}=\hat{j},
\qquad
\hat{i}\times\hat{j}=\hat{k}.
$$



**Step 3: Divide each cross product by the scalar triple product.**



$$
\hat{i}'=\frac{\hat{j}\times\hat{k}}{\hat{i}\cdot(\hat{j}\times\hat{k})}=\frac{\hat{i}}{1}=\hat{i},
$$





$$
\hat{j}'=\frac{\hat{k}\times\hat{i}}{\hat{i}\cdot(\hat{j}\times\hat{k})}=\frac{\hat{j}}{1}=\hat{j},
$$





$$
\hat{k}'=\frac{\hat{i}\times\hat{j}}{\hat{i}\cdot(\hat{j}\times\hat{k})}=\frac{\hat{k}}{1}=\hat{k}.
$$



**Conclusion.** The reciprocal set of $\{\hat{i},\hat{j},\hat{k}\}$ is $\{\hat{i},\hat{j},\hat{k}\}$ itself. This is the expected outcome, because the standard unit vectors already satisfy the pairing property: each has dot product $1$ with itself and $0$ with the other two. The example confirms that the construction is consistent and that it reduces to the identity on an orthonormal set.

**Verification of the pairing property.** As a check, the dot products between the original set and the reciprocal set are



$$
\hat{i}\cdot\hat{i}'=1,\quad \hat{j}\cdot\hat{j}'=1,\quad \hat{k}\cdot\hat{k}'=1,
$$



and every mixed dot product such as $\hat{i}\cdot\hat{j}'$ or $\hat{j}\cdot\hat{k}'$ equals $0$. The defining pattern holds exactly.

**A non-trivial variant.** To see the method do real work, take the set $\vec{a}=\hat{i}$, $\vec{b}=\hat{j}$, $\vec{c}=\hat{i}+\hat{k}$. The scalar triple product is



$$
\vec{a}\cdot(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})=\hat{i}\cdot\big(\hat{j}\times(\hat{i}+\hat{k})\big)=\hat{i}\cdot(\hat{j}\times\hat{i}+\hat{j}\times\hat{k})=\hat{i}\cdot(-\hat{k}+\hat{i})=1.
$$



The three cross products are



$$
\vec{b}\times\vec{c}=\hat{j}\times(\hat{i}+\hat{k})=-\hat{k}+\hat{i},
$$





$$
\vec{c}\times\vec{a}=(\hat{i}+\hat{k})\times\hat{i}=\hat{k}\times\hat{i}=\hat{j},
$$





$$
\vec{a}\times\vec{b}=\hat{i}\times\hat{j}=\hat{k}.
$$



Dividing each by the scalar triple product, which equals $1$, gives the reciprocal set



$$
\vec{a}'=\hat{i}-\hat{k},
\qquad
\vec{b}'=\hat{j},
\qquad
\vec{c}'=\hat{k}.
$$



Checking the pairing property: $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{a}'=\hat{i}\cdot(\hat{i}-\hat{k})=1$, $\vec{b}\cdot\vec{b}'=1$, $\vec{c}\cdot\vec{c}'=(\hat{i}+\hat{k})\cdot\hat{k}=1$, while $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}'=0$, $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{c}'=\hat{i}\cdot\hat{k}=0$, $\vec{b}\cdot\vec{a}'=0$, $\vec{b}\cdot\vec{c}'=0$, $\vec{c}\cdot\vec{a}'=(\hat{i}+\hat{k})\cdot(\hat{i}-\hat{k})=1-1=0$, and $\vec{c}\cdot\vec{b}'=0$. All nine dot products match the required pattern, so the reciprocal set is correct.

## 5. High-Yield Exam Takeaways & Common Pitfalls

**High-yield takeaways.**

- The reciprocal of a single vector preserves direction and inverts magnitude; it is $\vec{a}/\lVert \vec{a} \rVert^{2}$, equivalently $\hat{a}/\lVert \vec{a} \rVert$.
- The reciprocal set of $\{\vec{a},\vec{b},\vec{c}\}$ is built from the three cross products $\vec{b}\times\vec{c}$, $\vec{c}\times\vec{a}$, $\vec{a}\times\vec{b}$, each divided by the common scalar triple product $\vec{a}\cdot(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})$.
- The cyclic order matters: $\vec{a}'$ pairs with $\vec{a}$ and is built from the cross product of the *other two* vectors, $\vec{b}\times\vec{c}$.
- The defining test of a correct answer is the pairing property: $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{a}'=\vec{b}\cdot\vec{b}'=\vec{c}\cdot\vec{c}'=1$ and all six mixed dot products vanish. Always verify with this test.
- The construction requires a non-zero scalar triple product; if the three vectors are coplanar, the reciprocal set does not exist.
- The reciprocal set of an orthonormal set is itself, and applying the construction twice returns the original set.
- The pairing property gives the expansion $\vec{r}=(\vec{r}\cdot\vec{a}')\vec{a}+(\vec{r}\cdot\vec{b}')\vec{b}+(\vec{r}\cdot\vec{c}')\vec{c}$, which is the main use of reciprocal sets.

**Common pitfalls.**

- Using the wrong cross product for a given reciprocal vector, for example dividing $\vec{a}\times\vec{b}$ to obtain $\vec{a}'$ instead of $\vec{c}'$. The pairing must be checked against the dot-product test.
- Forgetting to divide by the scalar triple product, which leaves the magnitudes wrong even when the directions are correct.
- Computing the scalar triple product with the wrong sign or with a non-cyclic ordering; the value must be the same non-zero number used in all three divisions.
- Confusing the reciprocal of a vector with its unit vector. The unit vector has magnitude $1$; the reciprocal has magnitude $1/\lVert \vec{a} \rVert$ and is generally not a unit vector.
- Assuming the reciprocal vectors are mutually perpendicular to each other. They are perpendicular to members of the *original* set, not necessarily to one another.
- Attempting the construction on a coplanar set, where the scalar triple product is zero and the formulas are undefined.
- Omitting the verification step. A quick check of the nine dot products catches almost every arithmetic slip in the cross products or the normalising factor.
