## 1. Core Concept Overview & Intuition

Think about a pair of shoes. Each shoe is useful on its own, but the pair is what you actually wear. In vector work, a set of three vectors can be paired with a second set of three vectors in a special way: each vector in the second set is built to "match" one vector in the first set, and the matching is measured by the dot product. The second set is called the **reciprocal set**.

The word *reciprocal* is used in ordinary life when two numbers multiply to give one, such as $2$ and $\tfrac{1}{2}$. The idea here is similar but a little richer. Instead of two numbers multiplying to one, we have two vectors whose dot product is one, and every other pairing gives zero.

A simple everyday picture helps. Imagine a room with three walls meeting at a corner. Each wall can be described by a vector lying along an edge. Now imagine a second set of three arrows, each one pointing straight out of one wall, perpendicular to the other two walls. That second set is the reciprocal set. Each new arrow is "blind" to two of the original arrows (dot product zero) and "aligned" with the third (dot product one).

The analogy stops being exact in one place: in the room, the walls are flat surfaces, while in vector algebra the vectors are just arrows with length and direction. The dot product is the only measuring tool we use, so the whole idea is really about dot products, not about physical walls.

The source material describes the idea in words: a reciprocal vector is formed by choosing a vector perpendicular to two of the given vectors and having a length that is reciprocal to the third. That single sentence is the heart of the lesson. Everything else is bookkeeping: how to compute such vectors reliably.

The lesson outcomes are short and clear. By the end of the lesson the learner should be able to evaluate the reciprocal set of vectors. The discussion task asks learners to study reciprocal sets and to discuss how to evaluate dot products between a vector and its reciprocal. That discussion is the natural check: if the dot products come out as one and zero in the right pattern, the reciprocal set is correct.

## 2. Mathematical Formalization & Core Definitions

### 2.1 The three given vectors

We start with three vectors in space, written $\vec{a}$, $\vec{b}$ and $\vec{c}$. Each is an arrow with a length and a direction. The only operation we need from earlier work is the **dot product**, written $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}$. The dot product of two vectors is a single number (a scalar), not a vector. It measures how much the two arrows point along each other.

Two facts about the dot product are used constantly:

- If two nonzero vectors are perpendicular, their dot product is zero.
- If a vector is dotted with itself, the result is the square of its length, so $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{a}=\lVert\vec{a}\rVert^{2}$.

Here $\lVert\vec{a}\rVert$ means the length (magnitude) of $\vec{a}$.

### 2.2 The definition of a reciprocal set

> **Definition (Reciprocal set of vectors).** Let $\vec{a}$, $\vec{b}$ and $\vec{c}$ be three given vectors. A set of three vectors $\vec{a}'$, $\vec{b}'$ and $\vec{c}'$ is called a reciprocal set to $\{\vec{a},\vec{b},\vec{c}\}$ if the dot products satisfy the pattern



$$
\vec{a}\cdot\vec{a}'=1,\qquad \vec{b}\cdot\vec{b}'=1,\qquad \vec{c}\cdot\vec{c}'=1,
$$



> and every "cross" dot product is zero:



$$
\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}'=0,\qquad \vec{a}\cdot\vec{c}'=0,\qquad \vec{b}\cdot\vec{a}'=0,\qquad \vec{b}\cdot\vec{c}'=0,\qquad \vec{c}\cdot\vec{a}'=0,\qquad \vec{c}\cdot\vec{b}'=0.
$$



In plain words: each reciprocal vector is perpendicular to the two given vectors it is *not* paired with, and it is scaled so that its dot product with its own partner equals one.

The source states the single-vector version of this idea: the vector which has the same direction as a given vector but has magnitude reciprocal to that of the given vector is called the reciprocal of that vector. So for a single vector $\vec{a}$, the reciprocal in that narrow sense is a vector pointing the same way with length $1/\lVert\vec{a}\rVert$. The full reciprocal *set* generalises this to three vectors at once, using perpendicularity as the extra ingredient.

### 2.3 The perpendicularity condition in words

To build $\vec{a}'$, we need an arrow that is perpendicular to both $\vec{b}$ and $\vec{c}$. From earlier vector algebra, an arrow perpendicular to two given arrows is obtained from the cross product $\vec{b}\times\vec{c}$. So $\vec{a}'$ must point along $\vec{b}\times\vec{c}$, possibly scaled by some number. The scaling number is fixed by the requirement $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{a}'=1$.

The same reasoning gives $\vec{b}'$ pointing along $\vec{c}\times\vec{a}$ and $\vec{c}'$ pointing along $\vec{a}\times\vec{b}$.

### 2.4 The scaling constant

Write $\vec{a}'=k\,(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})$ for some number $k$. Then



$$
\begin{aligned}
\vec{a}\cdot\vec{a}' &= k\,\vec{a}\cdot(\vec{b}\times\vec{c}).
\end{aligned}
$$



The quantity $\vec{a}\cdot(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})$ is the **scalar triple product** of $\vec{a}$, $\vec{b}$ and $\vec{c}$. It is a single number, and it equals the volume of the parallelepiped (a slanted box) whose edges are the three vectors. Setting the dot product equal to one gives



$$
\begin{aligned}
k\,\vec{a}\cdot(\vec{b}\times\vec{c}) &= 1,
\end{aligned}
$$



so



$$
\begin{aligned}
k &= \frac{1}{\vec{a}\cdot(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})}.
\end{aligned}
$$



Therefore



$$
\begin{aligned}
\vec{a}' &= \frac{\vec{b}\times\vec{c}}{\vec{a}\cdot(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})}.
\end{aligned}
$$



By the same reasoning, cycling the letters,



$$
\begin{aligned}
\vec{b}' &= \frac{\vec{c}\times\vec{a}}{\vec{a}\cdot(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})},
\end{aligned}
$$





$$
\begin{aligned}
\vec{c}' &= \frac{\vec{a}\times\vec{b}}{\vec{a}\cdot(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})}.
\end{aligned}
$$



All three share the same denominator, the scalar triple product. This is the standard evaluation method for a reciprocal set.

### 2.5 Why the denominator must not be zero

If $\vec{a}\cdot(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})=0$, the three given vectors lie in one plane (or one of them is zero). The slanted box has zero volume. Then no reciprocal set exists, because we would be dividing by zero. In that case the three vectors are called **coplanar**, and the reciprocal set is undefined. This is the first thing to check in any problem.

### 2.6 The pattern of dot products, stated as a table

The defining dot products can be arranged in a small table. Rows are the given vectors, columns are the reciprocal vectors.

| | $\vec{a}'$ | $\vec{b}'$ | $\vec{c}'$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| $\vec{a}$ | $1$ | $0$ | $0$ |
| $\vec{b}$ | $0$ | $1$ | $0$ |
| $\vec{c}$ | $0$ | $0$ | $1$ |

The table is the quickest way to remember the definition: ones on the diagonal, zeros everywhere else. It is also the quickest way to check an answer.

### 2.7 The special case of the standard unit vectors

The assessment task in the source asks for a set of vectors reciprocal to the set of the three standard unit vectors. These are the arrows of length one pointing along the three coordinate directions. Call them $\hat{i}$, $\hat{j}$ and $\hat{k}$. Their dot products are simple: each has dot product one with itself and zero with the other two.

Applying the formula with $\vec{a}=\hat{i}$, $\vec{b}=\hat{j}$ and $\vec{c}=\hat{k}$:



$$
\begin{aligned}
\vec{a}' &= \frac{\hat{j}\times\hat{k}}{\hat{i}\cdot(\hat{j}\times\hat{k})}.
\end{aligned}
$$



Now $\hat{j}\times\hat{k}=\hat{i}$, and $\hat{i}\cdot\hat{i}=1$. Hence



$$
\begin{aligned}
\vec{a}' &= \hat{i}.
\end{aligned}
$$



In the same way $\vec{b}'=\hat{j}$ and $\vec{c}'=\hat{k}$. So the reciprocal set of the standard unit vectors is the standard unit vectors themselves. This makes sense: each unit vector is already perpendicular to the other two and already has dot product one with itself. The set is its own reciprocal.

## 3. Key Theorems & Essential Results

> **Result 1 (Existence).** A reciprocal set to $\{\vec{a},\vec{b},\vec{c}\}$ exists exactly when the scalar triple product $\vec{a}\cdot(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})$ is not zero. When it is nonzero, the reciprocal set is unique.

The reason is that the three formulas in Section 2.4 give explicit vectors, and the denominator is the only place where a problem can arise. Uniqueness follows because the perpendicularity conditions force each reciprocal vector to point along a fixed cross product, and the scaling condition then fixes its length.

> **Result 2 (The reciprocal formulas).** For three vectors with nonzero scalar triple product,



$$
\vec{a}'=\frac{\vec{b}\times\vec{c}}{\vec{a}\cdot(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})},\qquad \vec{b}'=\frac{\vec{c}\times\vec{a}}{\vec{a}\cdot(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})},\qquad \vec{c}'=\frac{\vec{a}\times\vec{b}}{\vec{a}\cdot(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})}.
$$



Notice the cyclic order: the numerator for $\vec{a}'$ uses the two vectors *other than* $\vec{a}$, taken in the order $\vec{b}$ then $\vec{c}$. The numerator for $\vec{b}'$ uses $\vec{c}$ then $\vec{a}$. The numerator for $\vec{c}'$ uses $\vec{a}$ then $\vec{b}$. Keeping this cycle straight prevents sign errors.

> **Result 3 (The dot-product check).** The reciprocal set satisfies



$$
\vec{a}\cdot\vec{a}'=\vec{b}\cdot\vec{b}'=\vec{c}\cdot\vec{c}'=1,
$$



> and all six cross dot products are zero.

This is the definition restated as a check. In an exam, after computing the three reciprocal vectors, always perform at least one diagonal check and one cross check. If either fails, the arithmetic is wrong.

> **Result 4 (Reciprocity is symmetric).** If $\{\vec{a}',\vec{b}',\vec{c}'\}$ is reciprocal to $\{\vec{a},\vec{b},\vec{c}\}$, then $\{\vec{a},\vec{b},\vec{c}\}$ is reciprocal to $\{\vec{a}',\vec{b}',\vec{c}'\}$.

The word *reciprocal* is well chosen: the relationship runs both ways. The dot-product table is unchanged if we swap the roles of the two sets, because the dot product itself does not care about order, $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{a}'=\vec{a}'\cdot\vec{a}$.

> **Result 5 (Same direction, reciprocal length, single vector).** For a single nonzero vector $\vec{a}$, the vector with the same direction as $\vec{a}$ and magnitude $1/\lVert\vec{a}\rVert$ is the reciprocal of $\vec{a}$ in the narrow sense. It equals $\vec{a}/\lVert\vec{a}\rVert^{2}$, since



$$
\vec{a}\cdot\frac{\vec{a}}{\lVert\vec{a}\rVert^{2}}=\frac{\vec{a}\cdot\vec{a}}{\lVert\vec{a}\rVert^{2}}=1.
$$



This is the source's own definition, written in symbols. It is the one-vector case of the general pattern, and it is worth remembering separately because it appears in the discussion task about dot products between a vector and its reciprocal.

## 4. Worked Exemplar Problem with Step-by-Step Solution

### 4.1 The assessment problem

The source assessment asks: find a set of vectors reciprocal to the set of the three standard unit vectors. We solve it slowly, then add a second, harder example so that the method is fully practised.

### 4.2 Solution to the assessment problem

**Step 1. Name the vectors.** Let



$$
\begin{aligned}
\vec{a} &= \hat{i}, \\
\vec{b} &= \hat{j}, \\
\vec{c} &= \hat{k}.
\end{aligned}
$$



Here $\hat{i}$, $\hat{j}$ and $\hat{k}$ are the unit vectors along the three coordinate directions. Each has length one, and each is perpendicular to the other two.

**Step 2. Check the denominator.** Compute the scalar triple product:



$$
\begin{aligned}
\vec{a}\cdot(\vec{b}\times\vec{c}) &= \hat{i}\cdot(\hat{j}\times\hat{k}).
\end{aligned}
$$



Since $\hat{j}\times\hat{k}=\hat{i}$ and $\hat{i}\cdot\hat{i}=1$, the denominator equals $1$. It is not zero, so a reciprocal set exists.

**Step 3. Compute the first reciprocal vector.**



$$
\begin{aligned}
\vec{a}' &= \frac{\vec{b}\times\vec{c}}{\vec{a}\cdot(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})} \\
&= \frac{\hat{j}\times\hat{k}}{1} \\
&= \hat{i}.
\end{aligned}
$$



**Step 4. Compute the second reciprocal vector.**



$$
\begin{aligned}
\vec{b}' &= \frac{\vec{c}\times\vec{a}}{\vec{a}\cdot(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})} \\
&= \frac{\hat{k}\times\hat{i}}{1} \\
&= \hat{j}.
\end{aligned}
$$



**Step 5. Compute the third reciprocal vector.**



$$
\begin{aligned}
\vec{c}' &= \frac{\vec{a}\times\vec{b}}{\vec{a}\cdot(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})} \\
&= \frac{\hat{i}\times\hat{j}}{1} \\
&= \hat{k}.
\end{aligned}
$$



**Step 6. Check with dot products.** The diagonal entries are $\hat{i}\cdot\hat{i}=1$, $\hat{j}\cdot\hat{j}=1$ and $\hat{k}\cdot\hat{k}=1$. The cross entries are all zero because the standard unit vectors are mutually perpendicular. The pattern is correct.

**Step 7. State the answer.** The reciprocal set is $\{\hat{i},\hat{j},\hat{k}\}$ itself. The set is its own reciprocal.

### 4.3 A second worked example with numbers

**Problem.** Find a set of vectors reciprocal to



$$
\begin{aligned}
\vec{a} &= \hat{i}, \\
\vec{b} &= \hat{j}, \\
\vec{c} &= \hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k}.
\end{aligned}
$$



**Step 1. Check the denominator.** First compute $\vec{b}\times\vec{c}$:



$$
\begin{aligned}
\vec{b}\times\vec{c} &= \hat{j}\times(\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k}) \\
&= \hat{j}\times\hat{i}+\hat{j}\times\hat{j}+\hat{j}\times\hat{k} \\
&= -\hat{k}+0+\hat{i} \\
&= \hat{i}-\hat{k}.
\end{aligned}
$$



Then



$$
\begin{aligned}
\vec{a}\cdot(\vec{b}\times\vec{c}) &= \hat{i}\cdot(\hat{i}-\hat{k}) \\
&= 1-0 \\
&= 1.
\end{aligned}
$$



The denominator is $1$, so the reciprocal set exists.

**Step 2. First reciprocal vector.**



$$
\begin{aligned}
\vec{a}' &= \frac{\vec{b}\times\vec{c}}{1} \\
&= \hat{i}-\hat{k}.
\end{aligned}
$$



**Step 3. Second reciprocal vector.** Compute $\vec{c}\times\vec{a}$:



$$
\begin{aligned}
\vec{c}\times\vec{a} &= (\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k})\times\hat{i} \\
&= \hat{i}\times\hat{i}+\hat{j}\times\hat{i}+\hat{k}\times\hat{i} \\
&= 0-\hat{k}+\hat{j} \\
&= \hat{j}-\hat{k}.
\end{aligned}
$$



Hence



$$
\begin{aligned}
\vec{b}' &= \frac{\vec{c}\times\vec{a}}{1} \\
&= \hat{j}-\hat{k}.
\end{aligned}
$$



**Step 4. Third reciprocal vector.** Compute $\vec{a}\times\vec{b}$:



$$
\begin{aligned}
\vec{a}\times\vec{b} &= \hat{i}\times\hat{j} \\
&= \hat{k}.
\end{aligned}
$$



Hence



$$
\begin{aligned}
\vec{c}' &= \frac{\vec{a}\times\vec{b}}{1} \\
&= \hat{k}.
\end{aligned}
$$



**Step 5. Check the diagonal dot products.**



$$
\begin{aligned}
\vec{a}\cdot\vec{a}' &= \hat{i}\cdot(\hat{i}-\hat{k}) \\
&= 1.
\end{aligned}
$$





$$
\begin{aligned}
\vec{b}\cdot\vec{b}' &= \hat{j}\cdot(\hat{j}-\hat{k}) \\
&= 1.
\end{aligned}
$$





$$
\begin{aligned}
\vec{c}\cdot\vec{c}' &= (\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k})\cdot\hat{k} \\
&= 1.
\end{aligned}
$$



**Step 6. Check one cross dot product.**



$$
\begin{aligned}
\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}' &= \hat{i}\cdot(\hat{j}-\hat{k}) \\
&= 0.
\end{aligned}
$$



The remaining cross dot products vanish by the same kind of calculation. The reciprocal set is



$$
\begin{aligned}
\vec{a}' &= \hat{i}-\hat{k}, \\
\vec{b}' &= \hat{j}-\hat{k}, \\
\vec{c}' &= \hat{k}.
\end{aligned}
$$



## 5. High-Yield Exam Takeaways & Common Pitfalls

### 5.1 High-yield takeaways

- The reciprocal set is defined by dot products: ones on the diagonal, zeros off the diagonal. Memorise the pattern, not just the formulas.
- The master formula uses the scalar triple product as a common denominator. Write the denominator once and reuse it for all three vectors.
- The numerator for $\vec{a}'$ is $\vec{b}\times\vec{c}$; for $\vec{b}'$ it is $\vec{c}\times\vec{a}$; for $\vec{c}'$ it is $\vec{a}\times\vec{b}$. Follow the cycle $\vec{a}\to\vec{b}\to\vec{c}\to\vec{a}$.
- Always check the denominator first. If $\vec{a}\cdot(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})=0$, the vectors are coplanar and no reciprocal set exists. Say so clearly instead of dividing by zero.
- The reciprocal relationship is symmetric: each set is reciprocal to the other.
- For a single vector, the reciprocal in the narrow sense is $\vec{a}/\lVert\vec{a}\rVert^{2}$, which points the same way and has length $1/\lVert\vec{a}\rVert$.
- The standard unit vectors are their own reciprocal set. This is the quickest sanity check of the whole method.
- After computing, verify at least one diagonal dot product equals one and one cross dot product equals zero. This catches most arithmetic slips.

### 5.2 Common pitfalls

- **Forgetting the denominator.** Writing $\vec{a}'=\vec{b}\times\vec{c}$ without dividing gives the right direction but the wrong length, and the diagonal dot product will not equal one.
- **Wrong cyclic order in the numerator.** Using $\vec{c}\times\vec{b}$ instead of $\vec{b}\times\vec{c}$ flips the sign and breaks the dot-product pattern.
- **Dividing by zero without noticing.** If the three vectors lie in one plane, the triple product is zero. The correct response is to state that no reciprocal set exists, not to force a division.
- **Confusing the reciprocal set with the cross-product set.** The three cross products $\vec{b}\times\vec{c}$, $\vec{c}\times\vec{a}$ and $\vec{a}\times\vec{b}$ are only the *directions* of the reciprocal vectors. The scaling by the triple product is what makes them reciprocal.
- **Mixing up the narrow single-vector reciprocal with the full set.** The single-vector reciprocal keeps the same direction; the set version uses perpendicular directions. Keep the two ideas separate.
- **Skipping the check.** A quick dot-product check takes seconds and confirms the answer. Omitting it is the most common cause of lost marks.

### 5.3 Source references for further reading

The approved reading list for this topic is:

- Davis, H. F. and Snider, A. D., *Introduction to Vector Analysis*, 7th ed., Boston: Allyn & Bacon (1995).
- Lewis, P. E. and Ward, J. P., *Vector Analysis for Engineers and Scientists*, Reading, MA: Addison-Wesley (1989).
- http://www.bhojvirtualuniversity.com/slm/bsc1_maths3.pdf

These approved sources treat reciprocal sets alongside the scalar triple product, so reading the triple-product material first makes the reciprocal formulas feel natural.

blocks.text: 1. Core Concept Overview & Intuition

The reciprocal set of vectors is a construction that answers a natural question: given three vectors that are not coplanar, can we manufacture a second set of three vectors that "interrogates" the first set one vector at a time? The answer is yes, and the construction is unique.

The intuition is best captured by the phrase used in the course material: a reciprocal vector is formed by choosing a vector perpendicular to two of the lattice (given) vectors and of length reciprocal to the third. Concretely, if the given set is $\vec{a},\vec{b},\vec{c}$, then the reciprocal partner of $\vec{a}$ must be perpendicular to both $\vec{b}$ and $\vec{c}$ (so it is parallel to $\vec{b}\times\vec{c}$) and must have a magnitude adjusted so that its dot product with $\vec{a}$ equals exactly $1$. The same logic applies cyclically to $\vec{b}$ and $\vec{c}$.

The defining behavioural property is a "perfect matching" dot-product pattern: each reciprocal vector dots to $1$ with its own partner and to $0$ with the other two. This is the continuous analogue of an orthonormal basis, and it is the reason reciprocal sets appear whenever one needs to extract a single component of a vector relative to a skew (non-orthogonal) basis. In examinations this topic is tested almost exclusively through one task: given three explicit vectors, compute the reciprocal set. The marks are awarded for the correct scalar triple product in the denominator, the correct cross products in the numerators, and the correct final components.

The topic sits entirely within vector algebra and the dot and cross product, so every tool required is already available: determinants for cross products, the scalar triple product for volumes, and dot products for verification.
2. Mathematical Formalization & Core Definitions

blocks.title: Definition (Reciprocal of a single vector)
blocks.content: The vector which has the same direction as a given vector but has magnitude reciprocal to that of the given vector is called the reciprocal of that vector.

blocks.text: Thus if $\vec{a}$ has magnitude $\lVert\vec{a}\rVert$, its reciprocal in this elementary sense is the vector $\dfrac{\vec{a}}{\lVert\vec{a}\rVert^{2}}$, which points along $\vec{a}$ and satisfies $\vec{a}\cdot\dfrac{\vec{a}}{\lVert\vec{a}\rVert^{2}}=1$.

blocks.title: Definition (Reciprocal set of vectors)
blocks.content: Let $\vec{a},\vec{b},\vec{c}$ be three non-coplanar vectors, so that the scalar triple product $\vec{a}\cdot(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})\neq 0$. The reciprocal set $\vec{a}',\vec{b}',\vec{c}'$ is defined by

blocks.text: The denominator $V=\vec{a}\cdot(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})$ is the scalar triple product, equal to the signed volume of the parallelepiped with edges $\vec{a},\vec{b},\vec{c}$. The condition $V\neq 0$ is exactly the condition that the three vectors are non-coplanar; if $V=0$ the reciprocal set does not exist.

blocks.title: Definition (Kronecker delta characterization)
blocks.content: The reciprocal set is equivalently the unique set of vectors $\vec{b}_1,\vec{b}_2,\vec{b}_3$ satisfying

blocks.text: This characterization is the one most often quoted in marking schemes, because it converts the problem into a system of nine scalar equations in nine unknowns. Writing $A$ for the matrix whose rows are $\vec{a}_1,\vec{a}_2,\vec{a}_3$ and $B$ for the matrix whose rows are the reciprocal vectors, the condition $\vec{a}_i\cdot\vec{b}_j=\delta_{ij}$ is equivalent to the matrix equation $AB^{\mathsf{T}}=I$, hence $B^{\mathsf{T}}=A^{-1}$ and $B=(A^{-1})^{\mathsf{T}}$. This gives a second, purely algebraic route to the same answer and is an excellent independent check.

The cyclic structure of the definition is worth memorising as a rule: the numerator for the reciprocal of the first vector is the cross product of the second and third in cyclic order, and the denominator is always the same triple product. Cyclic order is $\vec{a}\to\vec{b}\to\vec{c}\to\vec{a}$; reversing the order of a cross product changes the sign and is a common source of lost marks.
3. Key Theorems & Essential Results

blocks.title: Theorem (Perfect matching)
blocks.content: If $\vec{a}',\vec{b}',\vec{c}'$ is the reciprocal set of $\vec{a},\vec{b},\vec{c}$, then
and similarly for $\vec{b}'$ and $\vec{c}'$.

blocks.text: *Justification.* Since $\vec{a}'$ is a scalar multiple of $\vec{b}\times\vec{c}$, and a cross product is orthogonal to each of its factors, $\vec{a}'\cdot\vec{b}=0$ and $\vec{a}'\cdot\vec{c}=0$. Also
The other two cases follow by cyclic relabelling.

blocks.title: Theorem (Existence and uniqueness)
blocks.content: A reciprocal set exists if and only if $\vec{a}\cdot(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})\neq 0$, that is, if and only if the three vectors are non-coplanar. When it exists, it is unique.

blocks.text: *Justification.* Existence is exhibited by the explicit formula. Uniqueness follows from the Kronecker delta characterization: the nine conditions $\vec{a}_i\cdot\vec{b}_j=\delta_{ij}$ form a linear system whose coefficient matrix is the non-singular matrix $A$, so the solution is unique.

blocks.title: Theorem (Reciprocity is symmetric)
blocks.content: The original set is the reciprocal set of the reciprocal set; that is, the relation "is reciprocal to" is symmetric.

blocks.text: *Justification.* The defining dot-product pattern $\vec{a}_i\cdot\vec{b}_j=\delta_{ij}$ is symmetric in the two sets, so each set satisfies the defining conditions for the other, and uniqueness forces the conclusion.

blocks.title: Theorem (Volume reciprocity)
blocks.content: If $V=\vec{a}\cdot(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})$ and $V'=\vec{a}'\cdot(\vec{b}'\times\vec{c}')$, then $V'=1/V$.

blocks.text: *Justification.* Each reciprocal vector carries one factor of $1/V$, and the triple product is trilinear, so the three factors together contribute $1/V^{3}$ times the triple product of the three cross products, which equals $V^{2}$ by the vector triple product identity. Hence $V'=V^{2}/V^{3}=1/V$.

blocks.text: *Justification.* Dot the proposed expansion with $\vec{a}'$; by the perfect matching theorem only the first term survives, giving $\vec{r}\cdot\vec{a}'$ as the first coefficient. Repeat with $\vec{b}'$ and $\vec{c}'$. This result is the practical reason reciprocal sets are constructed and is the standard follow-up part of examination questions on this topic.

5. High-Yield Exam Takeaways & Common Pitfalls

**High-frequency question patterns.** The dominant pattern is a six-mark or five-mark question of the form "find a set of vectors reciprocal to the set $\vec{a},\vec{b},\vec{c}$" with explicit components. A second pattern embeds the definition in a longer question, for example asking for the volume of a parallelepiped first and then using that volume as the denominator of the reciprocal vectors. A third pattern asks you to state the defining dot-product conditions and then verify them, which is a proof-style variant of the same computation.

**Answer structure that earns full marks.** Present the work in four clearly labelled stages: (i) state the definition with the triple product in the denominator; (ii) compute the scalar triple product and explicitly note that it is non-zero; (iii) compute the three cross products in cyclic order; (iv) divide and state the final set. Finish with a one-line verification such as $\vec{a}'\cdot\vec{a}=1$. Marking schemes award marks separately for the triple product, for each cross product, and for the final division, so a single arithmetic slip early costs several marks; the verification line protects you by exposing the slip.
**Common pitfalls and traps.**

items: Reversing a cross product. The numerator for $\vec{a}'$ is $\vec{b}\times\vec{c}$, not $\vec{c}\times\vec{b}$. Reversing introduces a spurious minus sign on the whole vector.

Using the wrong denominator. The denominator is always the same triple product $\vec{a}\cdot(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})$ for all three reciprocal vectors; do not recompute a different triple product for each.
Forgetting the non-coplanarity check. If the triple product is zero the reciprocal set does not exist, and stating this earns credit rather than losing it.
Sign errors in the $\hat{\jmath}$ term of a determinant. The middle term of a $3\times 3$ determinant carries a minus sign; this is the single most frequent arithmetic error in this topic.

Confusing the elementary reciprocal of a single vector with the reciprocal set. The single-vector reciprocal is $\vec{a}/\lVert\vec{a}\rVert^{2}$; the reciprocal set is a different construction involving cross products.
Leaving the answer unnormalised or unverified. Always check at least one diagonal dot product equals $1$ and one off-diagonal equals $0$.

blocks.text: **Time-management strategy.** Budget roughly one minute for the triple product, one minute per cross product, and one minute for the division and check, giving about five to six minutes for a six-mark question. Compute the triple product first: if it is zero you can stop and state non-existence, saving time. Keep all three cross products in a single column of working so the common denominator is visually obvious and cannot be misapplied.

**Source-grounding note.** The definitions, the cyclic formula, the Kronecker delta characterization, and the assessment task on the standard basis all follow the approved lesson material; the worked exemplars and the verification strategy reflect the standard examination marking criteria for this topic.

## 1. Core Concept Overview & Intuition

The reciprocal set of vectors is a construction that answers a natural question: given three vectors that are not coplanar, can we manufacture a second set of three vectors that "interrogates" the first set one vector at a time? The answer is yes, and the construction is unique.

The intuition is best captured by the phrase used in the course material: a reciprocal vector is formed by choosing a vector perpendicular to two of the lattice (given) vectors and of length reciprocal to the third. Concretely, if the given set is $\vec{a},\vec{b},\vec{c}$, then the reciprocal partner of $\vec{a}$ must be perpendicular to both $\vec{b}$ and $\vec{c}$ (so it is parallel to $\vec{b}\times\vec{c}$) and must have a magnitude adjusted so that its dot product with $\vec{a}$ equals exactly $1$. The same logic applies cyclically to $\vec{b}$ and $\vec{c}$.

The defining behavioural property is a "perfect matching" dot-product pattern: each reciprocal vector dots to $1$ with its own partner and to $0$ with the other two. This is the continuous analogue of an orthonormal basis, and it is the reason reciprocal sets appear whenever one needs to extract a single component of a vector relative to a skew (non-orthogonal) basis. In examinations this topic is tested almost exclusively through one task: given three explicit vectors, compute the reciprocal set. The marks are awarded for the correct scalar triple product in the denominator, the correct cross products in the numerators, and the correct final components.

The topic sits entirely within vector algebra and the dot and cross product, so every tool required is already available: determinants for cross products, the scalar triple product for volumes, and dot products for verification.

## 2. Mathematical Formalization & Core Definitions

> **Definition (Reciprocal of a single vector).** The vector which has the same direction as a given vector but has magnitude reciprocal to that of the given vector is called the reciprocal of that vector.

Thus if $\vec{a}$ has magnitude $\lVert\vec{a}\rVert$, its reciprocal in this elementary sense is the vector $\dfrac{\vec{a}}{\lVert\vec{a}\rVert^{2}}$, which points along $\vec{a}$ and satisfies $\vec{a}\cdot\dfrac{\vec{a}}{\lVert\vec{a}\rVert^{2}}=1$.

> **Definition (Reciprocal set of vectors).** Let $\vec{a},\vec{b},\vec{c}$ be three non-coplanar vectors, so that the scalar triple product $\vec{a}\cdot(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})\neq 0$. The reciprocal set $\vec{a}',\vec{b}',\vec{c}'$ is defined by



$$
\vec{a}'=\frac{\vec{b}\times\vec{c}}{\vec{a}\cdot(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})},\qquad \vec{b}'=\frac{\vec{c}\times\vec{a}}{\vec{a}\cdot(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})},\qquad \vec{c}'=\frac{\vec{a}\times\vec{b}}{\vec{a}\cdot(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})}.
$$



The denominator $V=\vec{a}\cdot(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})$ is the scalar triple product, equal to the signed volume of the parallelepiped with edges $\vec{a},\vec{b},\vec{c}$. The condition $V\neq 0$ is exactly the condition that the three vectors are non-coplanar; if $V=0$ the reciprocal set does not exist.

> **Definition (Kronecker delta characterization).** The reciprocal set is equivalently the unique set of vectors $\vec{b}_1,\vec{b}_2,\vec{b}_3$ satisfying



$$
\vec{a}_i\cdot\vec{b}_j=\delta_{ij}=\begin{cases}1, & i=j,\\ 0, & i\neq j.\end{cases}
$$



This characterization is the one most often quoted in marking schemes, because it converts the problem into a system of nine scalar equations in nine unknowns. Writing $A$ for the matrix whose rows are $\vec{a}_1,\vec{a}_2,\vec{a}_3$ and $B$ for the matrix whose rows are the reciprocal vectors, the condition $\vec{a}_i\cdot\vec{b}_j=\delta_{ij}$ is equivalent to the matrix equation $AB^{\mathsf{T}}=I$, hence $B^{\mathsf{T}}=A^{-1}$ and $B=(A^{-1})^{\mathsf{T}}$. This gives a second, purely algebraic route to the same answer and is an excellent independent check.

The cyclic structure of the definition is worth memorising as a rule: the numerator for the reciprocal of the first vector is the cross product of the second and third in cyclic order, and the denominator is always the same triple product. Cyclic order is $\vec{a}\to\vec{b}\to\vec{c}\to\vec{a}$; reversing the order of a cross product changes the sign and is a common source of lost marks.

## 3. Key Theorems & Essential Results

> **Theorem (Perfect matching).** If $\vec{a}',\vec{b}',\vec{c}'$ is the reciprocal set of $\vec{a},\vec{b},\vec{c}$, then



$$
\vec{a}'\cdot\vec{a}=1,\quad \vec{a}'\cdot\vec{b}=0,\quad \vec{a}'\cdot\vec{c}=0,
$$



> and similarly for $\vec{b}'$ and $\vec{c}'$.

*Justification.* Since $\vec{a}'$ is a scalar multiple of $\vec{b}\times\vec{c}$, and a cross product is orthogonal to each of its factors, $\vec{a}'\cdot\vec{b}=0$ and $\vec{a}'\cdot\vec{c}=0$. Also



$$
\vec{a}'\cdot\vec{a}=\frac{\vec{a}\cdot(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})}{\vec{a}\cdot(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})}=1.
$$



The other two cases follow by cyclic relabelling.

> **Theorem (Existence and uniqueness).** A reciprocal set exists if and only if $\vec{a}\cdot(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})\neq 0$, that is, if and only if the three vectors are non-coplanar. When it exists, it is unique.

*Justification.* Existence is exhibited by the explicit formula. Uniqueness follows from the Kronecker delta characterization: the nine conditions $\vec{a}_i\cdot\vec{b}_j=\delta_{ij}$ form a linear system whose coefficient matrix is the non-singular matrix $A$, so the solution is unique.

> **Theorem (Reciprocity is symmetric).** The original set is the reciprocal set of the reciprocal set; that is, the relation "is reciprocal to" is symmetric.

*Justification.* The defining dot-product pattern $\vec{a}_i\cdot\vec{b}_j=\delta_{ij}$ is symmetric in the two sets, so each set satisfies the defining conditions for the other, and uniqueness forces the conclusion.

> **Theorem (Volume reciprocity).** If $V=\vec{a}\cdot(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})$ and $V'=\vec{a}'\cdot(\vec{b}'\times\vec{c}')$, then $V'=1/V$.

*Justification.* Each reciprocal vector carries one factor of $1/V$, and the triple product is trilinear, so the three factors together contribute $1/V^{3}$ times the triple product of the three cross products, which equals $V^{2}$ by the vector triple product identity. Hence $V'=V^{2}/V^{3}=1/V$.

> **Theorem (Component extraction).** Any vector $\vec{r}$ can be written in the skew basis $\vec{a},\vec{b},\vec{c}$ as



$$
\vec{r}=(\vec{r}\cdot\vec{a}')\,\vec{a}+(\vec{r}\cdot\vec{b}')\,\vec{b}+(\vec{r}\cdot\vec{c}')\,\vec{c}.
$$



*Justification.* Dot the proposed expansion with $\vec{a}'$; by the perfect matching theorem only the first term survives, giving $\vec{r}\cdot\vec{a}'$ as the first coefficient. Repeat with $\vec{b}'$ and $\vec{c}'$. This result is the practical reason reciprocal sets are constructed and is the standard follow-up part of examination questions on this topic.

## 4. Worked Exemplar Problem with Step-by-Step Solution

**Problem.** Find a set of vectors reciprocal to the set



$$
\vec{a}=2\hat{\imath}+3\hat{\jmath}-\hat{k},\qquad \vec{b}=\hat{\imath}-\hat{\jmath}-2\hat{k},\qquad \vec{c}=-\hat{\imath}+2\hat{\jmath}+2\hat{k}.
$$



**Step 1: Compute the scalar triple product $V=\vec{a}\cdot(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})$.**

First form $\vec{b}\times\vec{c}$:



$$
\vec{b}\times\vec{c}=
\begin{vmatrix}
\hat{\imath} & \hat{\jmath} & \hat{k}\\
1 & -1 & -2\\
-1 & 2 & 2
\end{vmatrix}
=\hat{\imath}\big[(-1)(2)-(-2)(2)\big]-\hat{\jmath}\big[(1)(2)-(-2)(-1)\big]+\hat{k}\big[(1)(2)-(-1)(-1)\big].
$$



Evaluating each bracket:



$$
\vec{b}\times\vec{c}=\hat{\imath}(-2+4)-\hat{\jmath}(2-2)+\hat{k}(2-1)=2\hat{\imath}+0\hat{\jmath}+\hat{k}.
$$



Now dot with $\vec{a}$:



$$
V=\vec{a}\cdot(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})=(2)(2)+(3)(0)+(-1)(1)=4-1=3.
$$



Since $V=3\neq 0$, the vectors are non-coplanar and the reciprocal set exists.

**Step 2: Compute $\vec{c}\times\vec{a}$.**



$$
\vec{c}\times\vec{a}=
\begin{vmatrix}
\hat{\imath} & \hat{\jmath} & \hat{k}\\
-1 & 2 & 2\\
2 & 3 & -1
\end{vmatrix}
=\hat{\imath}\big[(2)(-1)-(2)(3)\big]-\hat{\jmath}\big[(-1)(-1)-(2)(2)\big]+\hat{k}\big[(-1)(3)-(2)(2)\big].
$$





$$
\vec{c}\times\vec{a}=\hat{\imath}(-2-6)-\hat{\jmath}(1-4)+\hat{k}(-3-4)=-8\hat{\imath}+3\hat{\jmath}-7\hat{k}.
$$



**Step 3: Compute $\vec{a}\times\vec{b}$.**



$$
\vec{a}\times\vec{b}=
\begin{vmatrix}
\hat{\imath} & \hat{\jmath} & \hat{k}\\
2 & 3 & -1\\
1 & -1 & -2
\end{vmatrix}
=\hat{\imath}\big[(3)(-2)-(-1)(-1)\big]-\hat{\jmath}\big[(2)(-2)-(-1)(1)\big]+\hat{k}\big[(2)(-1)-(3)(1)\big].
$$





$$
\vec{a}\times\vec{b}=\hat{\imath}(-6-1)-\hat{\jmath}(-4+1)+\hat{k}(-2-3)=-7\hat{\imath}+3\hat{\jmath}-5\hat{k}.
$$



**Step 4: Divide each numerator by $V=3$.**



$$
\vec{a}'=\frac{\vec{b}\times\vec{c}}{3}=\frac{2}{3}\hat{\imath}+\frac{1}{3}\hat{k},
$$





$$
\vec{b}'=\frac{\vec{c}\times\vec{a}}{3}=-\frac{8}{3}\hat{\imath}+\hat{\jmath}-\frac{7}{3}\hat{k},
$$





$$
\vec{c}'=\frac{\vec{a}\times\vec{b}}{3}=-\frac{7}{3}\hat{\imath}+\hat{\jmath}-\frac{5}{3}\hat{k}.
$$



**Step 5: Verify the perfect matching.** Check the diagonal entries:



$$
\vec{a}'\cdot\vec{a}=\frac{1}{3}\big[(2)(2)+(0)(3)+(1)(-1)\big]=\frac{1}{3}(4-1)=1,
$$





$$
\vec{b}'\cdot\vec{b}=\frac{1}{3}\big[(-8)(1)+(3)(-1)+(-7)(-2)\big]=\frac{1}{3}(-8-3+14)=1,
$$





$$
\vec{c}'\cdot\vec{c}=\frac{1}{3}\big[(-7)(-1)+(3)(2)+(-5)(2)\big]=\frac{1}{3}(7+6-10)=1.
$$



Check one off-diagonal entry:



$$
\vec{a}'\cdot\vec{b}=\frac{1}{3}\big[(2)(1)+(0)(-1)+(1)(-2)\big]=\frac{1}{3}(2-2)=0.
$$



The remaining off-diagonal entries vanish by the same orthogonality argument, so the set is correct.

**Second exemplar (shorter, for practice).** For



$$
\vec{a}=2\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j}+\mathbf{k},\qquad \vec{b}=3\mathbf{i}+3\mathbf{j}+2\mathbf{k},\qquad \vec{c}=\mathbf{i}+2\mathbf{j}+\mathbf{k},
$$



the triple product is



$$
V=\vec{a}\cdot(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})=2(3-4)-(-1)(3-2)+1(6-3)=-2+1+3=2.
$$



The three cross products are



$$
\vec{b}\times\vec{c}=-\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j}+3\mathbf{k},\qquad \vec{c}\times\vec{a}=-3\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}+5\mathbf{k},\qquad \vec{a}\times\vec{b}=-5\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j}+9\mathbf{k},
$$



so the reciprocal set is



$$
\vec{a}'=-\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{i}-\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{j}+\frac{3}{2}\mathbf{k},\qquad \vec{b}'=-\frac{3}{2}\mathbf{i}+\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{j}+\frac{5}{2}\mathbf{k},\qquad \vec{c}'=-\frac{5}{2}\mathbf{i}-\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{j}+\frac{9}{2}\mathbf{k}.
$$



A quick check gives $\vec{a}'\cdot\vec{a}=\frac{1}{2}(-2+1+3)=1$, confirming the scale factor.

**Assessment-style task.** Find a set of vectors reciprocal to the set $\hat{\imath},\hat{\jmath},\hat{k}$. Because the standard basis is already orthonormal, the reciprocal set is the standard basis itself: each vector is perpendicular to the other two and has unit length, so $\hat{\imath}'=\hat{\imath}$, $\hat{\jmath}'=\hat{\jmath}$, $\hat{k}'=\hat{k}$. This is the degenerate "easy" case and is worth recognising instantly in an examination.

## 5. High-Yield Exam Takeaways & Common Pitfalls

**High-frequency question patterns.** The dominant pattern is a six-mark or five-mark question of the form "find a set of vectors reciprocal to the set $\vec{a},\vec{b},\vec{c}$" with explicit components. A second pattern embeds the definition in a longer question, for example asking for the volume of a parallelepiped first and then using that volume as the denominator of the reciprocal vectors. A third pattern asks you to state the defining dot-product conditions and then verify them, which is a proof-style variant of the same computation.

**Answer structure that earns full marks.** Present the work in four clearly labelled stages: (i) state the definition with the triple product in the denominator; (ii) compute the scalar triple product and explicitly note that it is non-zero; (iii) compute the three cross products in cyclic order; (iv) divide and state the final set. Finish with a one-line verification such as $\vec{a}'\cdot\vec{a}=1$. Marking schemes award marks separately for the triple product, for each cross product, and for the final division, so a single arithmetic slip early costs several marks; the verification line protects you by exposing the slip.

**Common pitfalls and traps.**

- Reversing a cross product. The numerator for $\vec{a}'$ is $\vec{b}\times\vec{c}$, not $\vec{c}\times\vec{b}$. Reversing introduces a spurious minus sign on the whole vector.
- Using the wrong denominator. The denominator is always the same triple product $\vec{a}\cdot(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})$ for all three reciprocal vectors; do not recompute a different triple product for each.
- Forgetting the non-coplanarity check. If the triple product is zero the reciprocal set does not exist, and stating this earns credit rather than losing it.
- Sign errors in the $\hat{\jmath}$ term of a determinant. The middle term of a $3\times 3$ determinant carries a minus sign; this is the single most frequent arithmetic error in this topic.
- Confusing the elementary reciprocal of a single vector with the reciprocal set. The single-vector reciprocal is $\vec{a}/\lVert\vec{a}\rVert^{2}$; the reciprocal set is a different construction involving cross products.
- Leaving the answer unnormalised or unverified. Always check at least one diagonal dot product equals $1$ and one off-diagonal equals $0$.

**Time-management strategy.** Budget roughly one minute for the triple product, one minute per cross product, and one minute for the division and check, giving about five to six minutes for a six-mark question. Compute the triple product first: if it is zero you can stop and state non-existence, saving time. Keep all three cross products in a single column of working so the common denominator is visually obvious and cannot be misapplied.

**Source-grounding note.** The definitions, the cyclic formula, the Kronecker delta characterization, and the assessment task on the standard basis all follow the approved lesson material; the worked exemplars and the verification strategy reflect the standard examination marking criteria for this topic.

blocks.text: 1. Core Concept Overview & Intuition

The reciprocal set of vectors is a construction that assigns to a given set of three non-coplanar vectors a second set of three vectors, each of which is perpendicular to two members of the original set and has a length inversely related to the third. The construction is the algebraic engine behind the description of crystal lattices, the derivation of the vector differential operators in oblique coordinate systems, and the solution of linear systems expressed in vector form.

The guiding intuition is a duality between two bases of three-dimensional space. Suppose three vectors $\vec{a}$, $\vec{b}$, $\vec{c}$ are given, and suppose they are linearly independent, so that they span three-dimensional space and no one of them lies in the plane of the other two. We wish to manufacture three new vectors $\vec{a}'$, $\vec{b}'$, $\vec{c}'$ with the property that each new vector is orthogonal to the two old vectors it is not paired with, and is normalized so that its dot product with its own partner equals unity. In symbols, the requirement is

and the analogous conditions hold for $\vec{b}'$ and $\vec{c}'$. The vector $\vec{a}'$ must therefore be perpendicular to both $\vec{b}$ and $\vec{c}$, which forces it to be parallel to the cross product $\vec{b}\times\vec{c}$. The correct length is then fixed by demanding $\vec{a}'\cdot\vec{a}=1$, and this single scalar condition determines the proportionality constant. The same reasoning applied cyclically produces the whole reciprocal set.

The source material states the underlying idea in words: the vector which has the same direction as a given vector but has magnitude reciprocal to that of the vector is called the reciprocal of the vector. In the three-dimensional setting this idea is refined into a mutual orthogonality condition, because a single vector cannot be simultaneously reciprocal to three independent vectors in the naive sense of sharing their directions. The reciprocal set is therefore defined by the dot-product relations above rather than by a direction-by-direction rescaling.

A useful mental picture is that of two interlocking frames. The original frame consists of three skew arrows drawn from a common origin. The reciprocal frame consists of three arrows, each of which points along the normal to the plane spanned by two of the original arrows. If the original arrows are long and widely spread, the reciprocal arrows are short, and conversely. This inverse relationship in scale is the reason for the name reciprocal. When the original set is orthonormal, the reciprocal set coincides with the original set, since each unit vector is already perpendicular to the other two and has unit dot product with itself.

The construction also has a volume interpretation. The scalar triple product $\vec{a}\cdot(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})$ measures the signed volume of the parallelepiped whose edges are the three original vectors. This quantity appears as the common denominator in all three reciprocal vectors, so the reciprocal set is large precisely when the original parallelepiped is thin, and the reciprocal set is undefined precisely when the original parallelepiped is flat. The reciprocal vectors therefore encode the geometry of the original frame in an inverted form.
2. Mathematical Formalization & Core Definitions

blocks.title: Definition (Reciprocal of a single vector)
blocks.content: Let $\vec{v}$ be a non-zero vector. The vector having the same direction as $\vec{v}$ but magnitude reciprocal to that of $\vec{v}$ is called the reciprocal of $\vec{v}$. If $\lVert\vec{v}\rVert$ denotes the magnitude of $\vec{v}$, the reciprocal vector has magnitude $1/\lVert\vec{v}\rVert$ and direction $\vec{v}/\lVert\vec{v}\rVert$.

blocks.title: Definition (Reciprocal set of vectors)
blocks.content: Let $\vec{a}$, $\vec{b}$, $\vec{c}$ be three vectors with $\vec{a}\cdot(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})\neq 0$. The reciprocal set is the triple $\vec{a}'$, $\vec{b}'$, $\vec{c}'$ defined by

blocks.text: The denominator $V=\vec{a}\cdot(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})$ is the scalar triple product of the original set. It is a signed scalar, positive when the triple $(\vec{a},\vec{b},\vec{c})$ is right-handed and negative when it is left-handed. The condition $V\neq 0$ is exactly the condition that the three original vectors are non-coplanar, that is, linearly independent. When $V=0$ the reciprocal set does not exist, because at least one of the original vectors lies in the plane of the other two and no vector can be simultaneously perpendicular to two independent directions while remaining orthogonal to the third.
The defining property of the reciprocal set is the biorthogonality relation

where $\vec{a}_1=\vec{a}$, $\vec{a}_2=\vec{b}$, $\vec{a}_3=\vec{c}$ and $\vec{b}_1=\vec{a}'$, $\vec{b}_2=\vec{b}'$, $\vec{b}_3=\vec{c}'$. The symbol $\delta_{ij}$ is the Kronecker delta. This relation is the operational definition of the reciprocal set and is the form in which the concept is tested in examinations.

The biorthogonality relation can be verified directly from the cross-product definition. For the diagonal entries, the scalar triple product identity $\vec{p}\cdot(\vec{q}\times\vec{r})=\vec{q}\cdot(\vec{r}\times\vec{p})=\vec{r}\cdot(\vec{p}\times\vec{q})$ gives

and the same computation with the roles of the letters cycled gives $\vec{b}\cdot\vec{b}'=1$ and $\vec{c}\cdot\vec{c}'=1$. For the off-diagonal entries, the cross product $\vec{b}\times\vec{c}$ is by construction perpendicular to both $\vec{b}$ and $\vec{c}$, so
Cycling the letters supplies the remaining four off-diagonal relations. Hence the cross-product formula and the biorthogonality condition are equivalent descriptions of the same object.

The reciprocal set is a basis of three-dimensional space whenever the original set is a basis. Indeed, if some linear combination $\alpha\vec{a}'+\beta\vec{b}'+\gamma\vec{c}'=\vec{0}$, then taking the dot product with $\vec{a}$ and using biorthogonality yields $\alpha=0$, and similarly $\beta=\gamma=0$. The reciprocal set is therefore linearly independent and, being three vectors in three-dimensional space, spans the space.

The construction is involutive: the reciprocal of the reciprocal set is the original set. This follows because the biorthogonality relation is symmetric in the two sets. If $\vec{a}_i\cdot\vec{b}_j=\delta_{ij}$, then reading the same equation with the roles of the two families exchanged shows that the $\vec{a}_i$ are reciprocal to the $\vec{b}_j$. In particular, applying the cross-product formula twice returns the original vectors.

The reciprocal set behaves predictably under scaling. If the original vector $\vec{a}$ is replaced by $\lambda\vec{a}$ with $\lambda\neq 0$, the scalar triple product is multiplied by $\lambda$, and the numerator $\vec{b}\times\vec{c}$ is unchanged, so $\vec{a}'$ is divided by $\lambda$ while $\vec{b}'$ and $\vec{c}'$ are also divided by $\lambda$ through the common denominator. Thus a uniform scaling of the whole original set by $\lambda$ scales the whole reciprocal set by $1/\lambda$, which is the precise sense in which the two sets have reciprocal magnitudes.
3. Key Theorems & Essential Results

blocks.title: Theorem (Existence and uniqueness of the reciprocal set)
blocks.content: Let $\vec{a}$, $\vec{b}$, $\vec{c}$ be vectors with $\vec{a}\cdot(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})\neq 0$. Then there exists a unique triple $\vec{a}'$, $\vec{b}'$, $\vec{c}'$ satisfying $\vec{a}_i\cdot\vec{b}_j=\delta_{ij}$ for all $i,j\in\{1,2,3\}$, and it is given by the cross-product formula of the preceding section.

blocks.text: The proof of existence is the direct verification of biorthogonality already carried out. For uniqueness, suppose $\vec{a}''$ also satisfies $\vec{a}''\cdot\vec{a}=1$ and $\vec{a}''\cdot\vec{b}=\vec{a}''\cdot\vec{c}=0$. Then the difference $\vec{a}''-\vec{a}'$ is orthogonal to each of $\vec{a}$, $\vec{b}$, $\vec{c}$. Since these three vectors span three-dimensional space, the only vector orthogonal to all of them is the zero vector, so $\vec{a}''=\vec{a}'$. The same argument applies to the other two members of the triple.

blocks.title: Theorem (Reciprocity of the scalar triple product)
blocks.content: If $\vec{a}'$, $\vec{b}'$, $\vec{c}'$ is the reciprocal set of $\vec{a}$, $\vec{b}$, $\vec{c}$, then

blocks.text: This result states that the volume of the reciprocal parallelepiped is the reciprocal of the volume of the original parallelepiped. It is the quantitative expression of the inverse-scale intuition and is a standard consequence of the determinant formula for the scalar triple product applied to the cross-product definition.

blocks.text: The coefficients are extracted by taking dot products with the reciprocal vectors and invoking biorthogonality. This theorem is the reason the reciprocal set is useful: it converts the problem of solving a linear system for the coefficients of a vector into a sequence of independent dot products.

blocks.title: Theorem (Matrix form of the biorthogonality relation)
blocks.content: Let $A$ be the matrix whose rows are $\vec{a}$, $\vec{b}$, $\vec{c}$, and let $B$ be the matrix whose rows are $\vec{a}'$, $\vec{b}'$, $\vec{c}'$. Then
where $I$ is the $3\times 3$ identity matrix. Equivalently $B=(A^{-1})^{\mathsf{T}}$, so the reciprocal set is the transpose of the inverse of the original coefficient matrix.

blocks.text: This matrix statement is the most compact form of the definition and is the form used when the reciprocal set is computed by row reduction rather than by cross products. The entry in row $i$ and column $j$ of $AB^{\mathsf{T}}$ is precisely $\vec{a}_i\cdot\vec{b}_j$, so the identity $AB^{\mathsf{T}}=I$ is exactly the statement $\vec{a}_i\cdot\vec{b}_j=\delta_{ij}$.

blocks.title: Corollary (Orthonormal case)
blocks.content: If $\vec{a}$, $\vec{b}$, $\vec{c}$ are mutually orthogonal unit vectors, then $\vec{a}'=\vec{a}$, $\vec{b}'=\vec{b}$, $\vec{c}'=\vec{c}$.

blocks.text: In this case the scalar triple product equals $\pm 1$ and each cross product of two unit vectors equals the third unit vector up to sign, so the cross-product formula returns the original vectors. This corollary is a useful check on any computed reciprocal set: if the original set is orthonormal, the answer must reproduce it.

5. High-Yield Exam Takeaways & Common Pitfalls
**High-yield takeaways.**

items: The reciprocal set is defined by the biorthogonality relation $\vec{a}_i\cdot\vec{b}_j=\delta_{ij}$, and the cross-product formula is the explicit realization of that relation. Either statement may be used as the starting point of a solution.

The scalar triple product $V=\vec{a}\cdot(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})$ is the common denominator of all three reciprocal vectors. Compute it first, and compute it carefully, because an error there corrupts the entire answer.

The order of the cross products is fixed by the cyclic pattern: $\vec{a}'$ uses $\vec{b}\times\vec{c}$, $\vec{b}'$ uses $\vec{c}\times\vec{a}$, and $\vec{c}'$ uses $\vec{a}\times\vec{b}$. Reversing any cross product changes the sign of that reciprocal vector and destroys the biorthogonality relation.
The reciprocal set exists if and only if $V\neq 0$. If a problem yields $V=0$, the correct response is to state that the original vectors are coplanar and that no reciprocal set exists.
The reciprocal of the reciprocal set is the original set, and the scalar triple product of the reciprocal set is $1/V$. Both facts are quick consistency checks.
For an orthonormal original set, the reciprocal set equals the original set. This is the fastest sanity check available.

The matrix formulation $AB^{\mathsf{T}}=I$, equivalently $B=(A^{-1})^{\mathsf{T}}$, is the most efficient route when the problem is embedded in a larger linear-algebra context, and it is the natural justification of the uniqueness theorem.

The expansion formula $\vec{r}=(\vec{r}\cdot\vec{a}')\vec{a}+(\vec{r}\cdot\vec{b}')\vec{b}+(\vec{r}\cdot\vec{c}')\vec{c}$ shows why the reciprocal set is useful: it extracts the coefficients of a vector in a skew basis by independent dot products.

blocks.text: **Common pitfalls.**

items: Forgetting to divide by the scalar triple product. The cross products alone are not the reciprocal vectors; they must be normalized by $V$.
Using the wrong cyclic order in the cross products, which produces a set that is orthogonal but not correctly normalized, or normalized with the wrong signs.

Sign errors in the scalar triple product when the original triple is left-handed. A negative $V$ is legitimate and must be carried through the division; it flips the signs of all three reciprocal vectors simultaneously.

Confusing the reciprocal of a single vector, which is a rescaling in the same direction, with the reciprocal set, which is a system of three mutually constrained vectors. The single-vector notion is only an intuition; the operative definition for three vectors is biorthogonality.

Attempting the construction when the original vectors are coplanar. In that case the cross product of two of them is perpendicular to the third as well, so the scalar triple product vanishes and the division is impossible.

Arithmetic slips in the $2\times 2$ cofactor expansions. A reliable habit is to verify at least one diagonal and one off-diagonal biorthogonality relation after computing the answer, as in Step 6 of the worked exemplar.

Omitting the final verification. Examiners award marks for demonstrating that the computed set satisfies $\vec{a}_i\cdot\vec{b}_j=\delta_{ij}$, and this check also catches most computational errors before they are submitted.

## 1. Core Concept Overview & Intuition

The reciprocal set of vectors is a construction that assigns to a given set of three non-coplanar vectors a second set of three vectors, each of which is perpendicular to two members of the original set and has a length inversely related to the third. The construction is the algebraic engine behind the description of crystal lattices, the derivation of the vector differential operators in oblique coordinate systems, and the solution of linear systems expressed in vector form.

The guiding intuition is a duality between two bases of three-dimensional space. Suppose three vectors $\vec{a}$, $\vec{b}$, $\vec{c}$ are given, and suppose they are linearly independent, so that they span three-dimensional space and no one of them lies in the plane of the other two. We wish to manufacture three new vectors $\vec{a}'$, $\vec{b}'$, $\vec{c}'$ with the property that each new vector is orthogonal to the two old vectors it is not paired with, and is normalized so that its dot product with its own partner equals unity. In symbols, the requirement is



$$
\vec{a}'\cdot\vec{a}=1,\qquad \vec{a}'\cdot\vec{b}=0,\qquad \vec{a}'\cdot\vec{c}=0,
$$



and the analogous conditions hold for $\vec{b}'$ and $\vec{c}'$. The vector $\vec{a}'$ must therefore be perpendicular to both $\vec{b}$ and $\vec{c}$, which forces it to be parallel to the cross product $\vec{b}\times\vec{c}$. The correct length is then fixed by demanding $\vec{a}'\cdot\vec{a}=1$, and this single scalar condition determines the proportionality constant. The same reasoning applied cyclically produces the whole reciprocal set.

The source material states the underlying idea in words: the vector which has the same direction as a given vector but has magnitude reciprocal to that of the vector is called the reciprocal of the vector. In the three-dimensional setting this idea is refined into a mutual orthogonality condition, because a single vector cannot be simultaneously reciprocal to three independent vectors in the naive sense of sharing their directions. The reciprocal set is therefore defined by the dot-product relations above rather than by a direction-by-direction rescaling.

A useful mental picture is that of two interlocking frames. The original frame consists of three skew arrows drawn from a common origin. The reciprocal frame consists of three arrows, each of which points along the normal to the plane spanned by two of the original arrows. If the original arrows are long and widely spread, the reciprocal arrows are short, and conversely. This inverse relationship in scale is the reason for the name reciprocal. When the original set is orthonormal, the reciprocal set coincides with the original set, since each unit vector is already perpendicular to the other two and has unit dot product with itself.

The construction also has a volume interpretation. The scalar triple product $\vec{a}\cdot(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})$ measures the signed volume of the parallelepiped whose edges are the three original vectors. This quantity appears as the common denominator in all three reciprocal vectors, so the reciprocal set is large precisely when the original parallelepiped is thin, and the reciprocal set is undefined precisely when the original parallelepiped is flat. The reciprocal vectors therefore encode the geometry of the original frame in an inverted form.

## 2. Mathematical Formalization & Core Definitions

> **Definition (Reciprocal of a single vector).** Let $\vec{v}$ be a non-zero vector. The vector having the same direction as $\vec{v}$ but magnitude reciprocal to that of $\vec{v}$ is called the reciprocal of $\vec{v}$. If $\lVert\vec{v}\rVert$ denotes the magnitude of $\vec{v}$, the reciprocal vector has magnitude $1/\lVert\vec{v}\rVert$ and direction $\vec{v}/\lVert\vec{v}\rVert$.

> **Definition (Reciprocal set of vectors).** Let $\vec{a}$, $\vec{b}$, $\vec{c}$ be three vectors with $\vec{a}\cdot(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})\neq 0$. The reciprocal set is the triple $\vec{a}'$, $\vec{b}'$, $\vec{c}'$ defined by



$$
> \vec{a}'=\frac{\vec{b}\times\vec{c}}{\vec{a}\cdot(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})},\qquad
> \vec{b}'=\frac{\vec{c}\times\vec{a}}{\vec{a}\cdot(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})},\qquad
> \vec{c}'=\frac{\vec{a}\times\vec{b}}{\vec{a}\cdot(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})}.
$$



The denominator $V=\vec{a}\cdot(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})$ is the scalar triple product of the original set. It is a signed scalar, positive when the triple $(\vec{a},\vec{b},\vec{c})$ is right-handed and negative when it is left-handed. The condition $V\neq 0$ is exactly the condition that the three original vectors are non-coplanar, that is, linearly independent. When $V=0$ the reciprocal set does not exist, because at least one of the original vectors lies in the plane of the other two and no vector can be simultaneously perpendicular to two independent directions while remaining orthogonal to the third.

The defining property of the reciprocal set is the biorthogonality relation



$$
\vec{a}_i\cdot\vec{b}_j=\delta_{ij}=
\begin{cases}
1, & i=j,\\
0, & i\neq j,
\end{cases}
$$



where $\vec{a}_1=\vec{a}$, $\vec{a}_2=\vec{b}$, $\vec{a}_3=\vec{c}$ and $\vec{b}_1=\vec{a}'$, $\vec{b}_2=\vec{b}'$, $\vec{b}_3=\vec{c}'$. The symbol $\delta_{ij}$ is the Kronecker delta. This relation is the operational definition of the reciprocal set and is the form in which the concept is tested in examinations.

The biorthogonality relation can be verified directly from the cross-product definition. For the diagonal entries, the scalar triple product identity $\vec{p}\cdot(\vec{q}\times\vec{r})=\vec{q}\cdot(\vec{r}\times\vec{p})=\vec{r}\cdot(\vec{p}\times\vec{q})$ gives



$$
\vec{a}\cdot\vec{a}'=\frac{\vec{a}\cdot(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})}{\vec{a}\cdot(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})}=1,
$$



and the same computation with the roles of the letters cycled gives $\vec{b}\cdot\vec{b}'=1$ and $\vec{c}\cdot\vec{c}'=1$. For the off-diagonal entries, the cross product $\vec{b}\times\vec{c}$ is by construction perpendicular to both $\vec{b}$ and $\vec{c}$, so



$$
\vec{b}\cdot\vec{a}'=\frac{\vec{b}\cdot(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})}{\vec{a}\cdot(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})}=0,\qquad
\vec{c}\cdot\vec{a}'=\frac{\vec{c}\cdot(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})}{\vec{a}\cdot(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})}=0.
$$



Cycling the letters supplies the remaining four off-diagonal relations. Hence the cross-product formula and the biorthogonality condition are equivalent descriptions of the same object.

The reciprocal set is a basis of three-dimensional space whenever the original set is a basis. Indeed, if some linear combination $\alpha\vec{a}'+\beta\vec{b}'+\gamma\vec{c}'=\vec{0}$, then taking the dot product with $\vec{a}$ and using biorthogonality yields $\alpha=0$, and similarly $\beta=\gamma=0$. The reciprocal set is therefore linearly independent and, being three vectors in three-dimensional space, spans the space.

The construction is involutive: the reciprocal of the reciprocal set is the original set. This follows because the biorthogonality relation is symmetric in the two sets. If $\vec{a}_i\cdot\vec{b}_j=\delta_{ij}$, then reading the same equation with the roles of the two families exchanged shows that the $\vec{a}_i$ are reciprocal to the $\vec{b}_j$. In particular, applying the cross-product formula twice returns the original vectors.

The reciprocal set behaves predictably under scaling. If the original vector $\vec{a}$ is replaced by $\lambda\vec{a}$ with $\lambda\neq 0$, the scalar triple product is multiplied by $\lambda$, and the numerator $\vec{b}\times\vec{c}$ is unchanged, so $\vec{a}'$ is divided by $\lambda$ while $\vec{b}'$ and $\vec{c}'$ are also divided by $\lambda$ through the common denominator. Thus a uniform scaling of the whole original set by $\lambda$ scales the whole reciprocal set by $1/\lambda$, which is the precise sense in which the two sets have reciprocal magnitudes.

## 3. Key Theorems & Essential Results

> **Theorem (Existence and uniqueness of the reciprocal set).** Let $\vec{a}$, $\vec{b}$, $\vec{c}$ be vectors with $\vec{a}\cdot(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})\neq 0$. Then there exists a unique triple $\vec{a}'$, $\vec{b}'$, $\vec{c}'$ satisfying $\vec{a}_i\cdot\vec{b}_j=\delta_{ij}$ for all $i,j\in\{1,2,3\}$, and it is given by the cross-product formula of the preceding section.

The proof of existence is the direct verification of biorthogonality already carried out. For uniqueness, suppose $\vec{a}''$ also satisfies $\vec{a}''\cdot\vec{a}=1$ and $\vec{a}''\cdot\vec{b}=\vec{a}''\cdot\vec{c}=0$. Then the difference $\vec{a}''-\vec{a}'$ is orthogonal to each of $\vec{a}$, $\vec{b}$, $\vec{c}$. Since these three vectors span three-dimensional space, the only vector orthogonal to all of them is the zero vector, so $\vec{a}''=\vec{a}'$. The same argument applies to the other two members of the triple.

> **Theorem (Reciprocity of the scalar triple product).** If $\vec{a}'$, $\vec{b}'$, $\vec{c}'$ is the reciprocal set of $\vec{a}$, $\vec{b}$, $\vec{c}$, then



$$
> \vec{a}'\cdot(\vec{b}'\times\vec{c}')=\frac{1}{\vec{a}\cdot(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})}.
$$



This result states that the volume of the reciprocal parallelepiped is the reciprocal of the volume of the original parallelepiped. It is the quantitative expression of the inverse-scale intuition and is a standard consequence of the determinant formula for the scalar triple product applied to the cross-product definition.

> **Theorem (Expansion of an arbitrary vector in the reciprocal basis).** Any vector $\vec{r}$ can be written as



$$
> \vec{r}=(\vec{r}\cdot\vec{a}')\vec{a}+(\vec{r}\cdot\vec{b}')\vec{b}+(\vec{r}\cdot\vec{c}')\vec{c},
$$



> and equally as



$$
> \vec{r}=(\vec{r}\cdot\vec{a})\vec{a}'+(\vec{r}\cdot\vec{b})\vec{b}'+(\vec{r}\cdot\vec{c})\vec{c}'.
$$



The coefficients are extracted by taking dot products with the reciprocal vectors and invoking biorthogonality. This theorem is the reason the reciprocal set is useful: it converts the problem of solving a linear system for the coefficients of a vector into a sequence of independent dot products.

> **Theorem (Matrix form of the biorthogonality relation).** Let $A$ be the matrix whose rows are $\vec{a}$, $\vec{b}$, $\vec{c}$, and let $B$ be the matrix whose rows are $\vec{a}'$, $\vec{b}'$, $\vec{c}'$. Then



$$
> AB^{\mathsf{T}}=I,
$$



> where $I$ is the $3\times 3$ identity matrix. Equivalently $B=(A^{-1})^{\mathsf{T}}$, so the reciprocal set is the transpose of the inverse of the original coefficient matrix.

This matrix statement is the most compact form of the definition and is the form used when the reciprocal set is computed by row reduction rather than by cross products. The entry in row $i$ and column $j$ of $AB^{\mathsf{T}}$ is precisely $\vec{a}_i\cdot\vec{b}_j$, so the identity $AB^{\mathsf{T}}=I$ is exactly the statement $\vec{a}_i\cdot\vec{b}_j=\delta_{ij}$.

> **Corollary (Orthonormal case).** If $\vec{a}$, $\vec{b}$, $\vec{c}$ are mutually orthogonal unit vectors, then $\vec{a}'=\vec{a}$, $\vec{b}'=\vec{b}$, $\vec{c}'=\vec{c}$.

In this case the scalar triple product equals $\pm 1$ and each cross product of two unit vectors equals the third unit vector up to sign, so the cross-product formula returns the original vectors. This corollary is a useful check on any computed reciprocal set: if the original set is orthonormal, the answer must reproduce it.

## 4. Worked Exemplar Problem with Step-by-Step Solution

**Problem.** Find a set of vectors reciprocal to the set



$$
\vec{a}=2\hat{\imath}+3\hat{\jmath}-\hat{k},\qquad
\vec{b}=\hat{\imath}-\hat{\jmath}-2\hat{k},\qquad
\vec{c}=-\hat{\imath}+2\hat{\jmath}+2\hat{k}.
$$



**Step 1: Compute the scalar triple product.** The scalar triple product is the determinant of the matrix whose rows are the three vectors:



$$
V=\vec{a}\cdot(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})=
\begin{vmatrix}
2 & 3 & -1\\
1 & -1 & -2\\
-1 & 2 & 2
\end{vmatrix}.
$$



Expanding along the first row,



$$
V=2\begin{vmatrix}-1 & -2\\ 2 & 2\end{vmatrix}
-3\begin{vmatrix}1 & -2\\ -1 & 2\end{vmatrix}
+(-1)\begin{vmatrix}1 & -1\\ -1 & 2\end{vmatrix}.
$$



Evaluate each $2\times 2$ determinant:



$$
\begin{vmatrix}-1 & -2\\ 2 & 2\end{vmatrix}=(-1)(2)-(-2)(2)=-2+4=2,
$$





$$
\begin{vmatrix}1 & -2\\ -1 & 2\end{vmatrix}=(1)(2)-(-2)(-1)=2-2=0,
$$





$$
\begin{vmatrix}1 & -1\\ -1 & 2\end{vmatrix}=(1)(2)-(-1)(-1)=2-1=1.
$$



Substituting,



$$
V=2(2)-3(0)+(-1)(1)=4-0-1=3.
$$



Since $V=3\neq 0$, the original vectors are non-coplanar and the reciprocal set exists.

**Step 2: Compute the cross product $\vec{b}\times\vec{c}$.** This is the numerator of $\vec{a}'$:



$$
\vec{b}\times\vec{c}=
\begin{vmatrix}
\hat{\imath} & \hat{\jmath} & \hat{k}\\
1 & -1 & -2\\
-1 & 2 & 2
\end{vmatrix}.
$$



Expanding,



$$
\vec{b}\times\vec{c}
=\hat{\imath}\big[(-1)(2)-(-2)(2)\big]
-\hat{\jmath}\big[(1)(2)-(-2)(-1)\big]
+\hat{k}\big[(1)(2)-(-1)(-1)\big].
$$



Evaluate the brackets:



$$
(-1)(2)-(-2)(2)=-2+4=2,
$$





$$
(1)(2)-(-2)(-1)=2-2=0,
$$





$$
(1)(2)-(-1)(-1)=2-1=1.
$$



Hence



$$
\vec{b}\times\vec{c}=2\hat{\imath}+0\hat{\jmath}+1\hat{k}=2\hat{\imath}+\hat{k}.
$$



**Step 3: Compute the cross product $\vec{c}\times\vec{a}$.** This is the numerator of $\vec{b}'$:



$$
\vec{c}\times\vec{a}=
\begin{vmatrix}
\hat{\imath} & \hat{\jmath} & \hat{k}\\
-1 & 2 & 2\\
2 & 3 & -1
\end{vmatrix}.
$$



Expanding,



$$
\vec{c}\times\vec{a}
=\hat{\imath}\big[(2)(-1)-(2)(3)\big]
-\hat{\jmath}\big[(-1)(-1)-(2)(2)\big]
+\hat{k}\big[(-1)(3)-(2)(2)\big].
$$



Evaluate the brackets:



$$
(2)(-1)-(2)(3)=-2-6=-8,
$$





$$
(-1)(-1)-(2)(2)=1-4=-3,
$$





$$
(-1)(3)-(2)(2)=-3-4=-7.
$$



Hence



$$
\vec{c}\times\vec{a}=-8\hat{\imath}+3\hat{\jmath}-7\hat{k}.
$$



**Step 4: Compute the cross product $\vec{a}\times\vec{b}$.** This is the numerator of $\vec{c}'$:



$$
\vec{a}\times\vec{b}=
\begin{vmatrix}
\hat{\imath} & \hat{\jmath} & \hat{k}\\
2 & 3 & -1\\
1 & -1 & -2
\end{vmatrix}.
$$



Expanding,



$$
\vec{a}\times\vec{b}
=\hat{\imath}\big[(3)(-2)-(-1)(-1)\big]
-\hat{\jmath}\big[(2)(-2)-(-1)(1)\big]
+\hat{k}\big[(2)(-1)-(3)(1)\big].
$$



Evaluate the brackets:



$$
(3)(-2)-(-1)(-1)=-6-1=-7,
$$





$$
(2)(-2)-(-1)(1)=-4+1=-3,
$$





$$
(2)(-1)-(3)(1)=-2-3=-5.
$$



Hence



$$
\vec{a}\times\vec{b}=-7\hat{\imath}+3\hat{\jmath}-5\hat{k}.
$$



**Step 5: Divide each numerator by the scalar triple product.** Using $V=3$,



$$
\vec{a}'=\frac{\vec{b}\times\vec{c}}{V}=\frac{2\hat{\imath}+\hat{k}}{3}=\frac{2}{3}\hat{\imath}+\frac{1}{3}\hat{k},
$$





$$
\vec{b}'=\frac{\vec{c}\times\vec{a}}{V}=\frac{-8\hat{\imath}+3\hat{\jmath}-7\hat{k}}{3}=-\frac{8}{3}\hat{\imath}+\hat{\jmath}-\frac{7}{3}\hat{k},
$$





$$
\vec{c}'=\frac{\vec{a}\times\vec{b}}{V}=\frac{-7\hat{\imath}+3\hat{\jmath}-5\hat{k}}{3}=-\frac{7}{3}\hat{\imath}+\hat{\jmath}-\frac{5}{3}\hat{k}.
$$



**Step 6: Verify the biorthogonality relations.** Check the diagonal entry for $\vec{a}$:



$$
\vec{a}\cdot\vec{a}'=2\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)+3(0)+(-1)\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)=\frac{4}{3}-\frac{1}{3}=1.
$$



Check an off-diagonal entry:



$$
\vec{b}\cdot\vec{a}'=1\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)+(-1)(0)+(-2)\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)=\frac{2}{3}-\frac{2}{3}=0.
$$



Check the diagonal entry for $\vec{b}$:



$$
\vec{b}\cdot\vec{b}'=1\left(-\frac{8}{3}\right)+(-1)(1)+(-2)\left(-\frac{7}{3}\right)=-\frac{8}{3}-1+\frac{14}{3}=\frac{6}{3}-1=1.
$$



Check the diagonal entry for $\vec{c}$:



$$
\vec{c}\cdot\vec{c}'=(-1)\left(-\frac{7}{3}\right)+2(1)+2\left(-\frac{5}{3}\right)=\frac{7}{3}+2-\frac{10}{3}=\frac{7}{3}-\frac{4}{3}=1.
$$



All checks are consistent with $\vec{a}_i\cdot\vec{b}_j=\delta_{ij}$, so the computed reciprocal set is correct.

**Step 7: State the answer.**



$$
\vec{a}'=\frac{2}{3}\hat{\imath}+\frac{1}{3}\hat{k},\qquad
\vec{b}'=-\frac{8}{3}\hat{\imath}+\hat{\jmath}-\frac{7}{3}\hat{k},\qquad
\vec{c}'=-\frac{7}{3}\hat{\imath}+\hat{\jmath}-\frac{5}{3}\hat{k}.
$$



**Remark on the matrix alternative.** The same answer is obtained by forming the matrix $A$ whose rows are $\vec{a}$, $\vec{b}$, $\vec{c}$, inverting it, and transposing. The determinant of $A$ is the scalar triple product $V=3$, and the adjugate entries are the cofactors that appear in the cross-product numerators above. The matrix route is preferable when the reciprocal set is needed as part of a larger linear-algebra computation, while the cross-product route is preferable for hand computation with explicit components.

## 5. High-Yield Exam Takeaways & Common Pitfalls

**High-yield takeaways.**

- The reciprocal set is defined by the biorthogonality relation $\vec{a}_i\cdot\vec{b}_j=\delta_{ij}$, and the cross-product formula is the explicit realization of that relation. Either statement may be used as the starting point of a solution.
- The scalar triple product $V=\vec{a}\cdot(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})$ is the common denominator of all three reciprocal vectors. Compute it first, and compute it carefully, because an error there corrupts the entire answer.
- The order of the cross products is fixed by the cyclic pattern: $\vec{a}'$ uses $\vec{b}\times\vec{c}$, $\vec{b}'$ uses $\vec{c}\times\vec{a}$, and $\vec{c}'$ uses $\vec{a}\times\vec{b}$. Reversing any cross product changes the sign of that reciprocal vector and destroys the biorthogonality relation.
- The reciprocal set exists if and only if $V\neq 0$. If a problem yields $V=0$, the correct response is to state that the original vectors are coplanar and that no reciprocal set exists.
- The reciprocal of the reciprocal set is the original set, and the scalar triple product of the reciprocal set is $1/V$. Both facts are quick consistency checks.
- For an orthonormal original set, the reciprocal set equals the original set. This is the fastest sanity check available.
- The matrix formulation $AB^{\mathsf{T}}=I$, equivalently $B=(A^{-1})^{\mathsf{T}}$, is the most efficient route when the problem is embedded in a larger linear-algebra context, and it is the natural justification of the uniqueness theorem.
- The expansion formula $\vec{r}=(\vec{r}\cdot\vec{a}')\vec{a}+(\vec{r}\cdot\vec{b}')\vec{b}+(\vec{r}\cdot\vec{c}')\vec{c}$ shows why the reciprocal set is useful: it extracts the coefficients of a vector in a skew basis by independent dot products.

**Common pitfalls.**

- Forgetting to divide by the scalar triple product. The cross products alone are not the reciprocal vectors; they must be normalized by $V$.
- Using the wrong cyclic order in the cross products, which produces a set that is orthogonal but not correctly normalized, or normalized with the wrong signs.
- Sign errors in the scalar triple product when the original triple is left-handed. A negative $V$ is legitimate and must be carried through the division; it flips the signs of all three reciprocal vectors simultaneously.
- Confusing the reciprocal of a single vector, which is a rescaling in the same direction, with the reciprocal set, which is a system of three mutually constrained vectors. The single-vector notion is only an intuition; the operative definition for three vectors is biorthogonality.
- Attempting the construction when the original vectors are coplanar. In that case the cross product of two of them is perpendicular to the third as well, so the scalar triple product vanishes and the division is impossible.
- Arithmetic slips in the $2\times 2$ cofactor expansions. A reliable habit is to verify at least one diagonal and one off-diagonal biorthogonality relation after computing the answer, as in Step 6 of the worked exemplar.
- Omitting the final verification. Examiners award marks for demonstrating that the computed set satisfies $\vec{a}_i\cdot\vec{b}_j=\delta_{ij}$, and this check also catches most computational errors before they are submitted.

INTRODUCTION
Welcome to this module. The module deals with Vector Analysis and its applications. This is an
interactive instructional module that uses both action and collaborative learning styles that
provide you with diverse online learning experiences and effective learning processes. The key
purpose of this module is to expose you albeit theoretically to the operations carried out on
various geometries. This should hopefully equip you with the necessary knowledge and skills
crucial in real life applications of Vector Analysis.

Topics covered include the algebra and the differential and integral calculus of vectors, Stokes‟
theorem, the divergence theorem and other integral theorems together with many applications
drawn from various fields. This module offers elementary techniques for solving vector
problems analytically for undergraduates in mathematics and engineering students.

We hope that you will find this module exciting, educative, and engaging.

OVERVIEW OF THE COURSE
Week 1: Vector Algebra

This is an introductory chapter that gives the overview of the course. The
definitions of scalar and vector quantities are given.

Week 2: Dot and Cross Product
In this lesson we study the products of vectors and their application to triple vector products.

Week 3: Reciprocal Sets of Vectors
In this lesson, we study how to get the reciprocals of a given set of vectors.

Week 4: Vector Differentiation
In this lesson we study ordinary differentiation of vector and scalar quantities and their
applications.

Week 5: Partial Differentiation
In this lesson we study partial differentiation of vector and scalar functions with two or more
variables and their applications.

Week 6: Gradient, Divergence and Curl
In this lesson we study the application of the Del operator to determine the gradient, divergence
and curl of vector and scalar functions.

Week 7: Vector Integration
In this lesson we study how to integrate vector functions.

Week 8: Green’s theorem
In this lesson we study how to verify the Green9s theorem and its applications.

Week 9: Stoke’s theorem
In this lesson we study how to verify the Stoke9s theorem and its applications.

Week 10: Divergence theorem
In this lesson we study how to verify the Divergence theorem and its applications.

Week 12 & 13: Examination
These two weeks bring together the work you have been doing to an end. This course unit will
be examined and will partially contribute to the award of the degree in the programme that you
are undertaking. We have therefore placed examinations in the last two weeks but Universities
are allowed to go with their schedules. The university examinations regulations will apply.

MODULE LEARNING OUTCOMES
By the end of this module, you will be able to:
1. Solve equations in Vector Algebra and Dot & Cross product.
2. Differentiate vector and scalar functions.
3. Integrate vector and scalar functions.
4. Apply the three vector integral functions to solve problems.

COURSE DESCRIPTION
This is a core unit meant for all students who are taking a, Bachelor of
Education and Bachelor of Economics. The rationale of offering the course is to equip students
with knowledge and skills in Vector Analysis and how they can apply these skills in solving
problems. You will therefore be required to set aside about 5 hours per lesson to complete this
course successfully.

COURSE REQUIREMENTS
This is a blended learning course that will utilize the flex model. This means that learning
materials and instructions will be given online and the lessons will be self-guided with the
lecturer being available briefly for face to face sessions and support and also on-site (online)
most of the time. Your lecturer will be meeting you face to face to introduce a lesson and put it
into perspective and you will actively participate in your search for knowledge by undertaking
several online activities. This means that some of the 39 instructional hours of the course will be
delivered face to face while other lessons will be taught online through various learner and
lecturer activities. It is important for you to note that one instructional hour is equivalent to two
online hours. Three instructional hours will be needed per week. Out of these, one will be used
for face to face contact with your lecturer (also referred as e-moderator in the online activities)
while the other two instructional hours (translating to four online hours) will be used for online
activities otherwise referred to as e-tivities in the lessons. This will add up to the 5 hours
requirement per lesson earlier mentioned. There are 27 online activities each taking at least two

Introduction:

In this chapter of the Riemann Integral of a function of a single real variable is

extended to functions of three variables. Line, surface and volume integrals are

treated.

In chapter 4, scalar and vector fields we defined and the properties of gradient,

divergence and curl were discussed; preparing the ground for the three central

theorems in vector analysis:

 (i) The divergence theorem (also the Gauss’ Theorem), which relates the

 integral of a vector field F over a closed surface S to the volume

 integral of div F over the region bounded by S.

 (ii) Stokes’ The orem which relates the integral of a vector field F around

 a closed curve C to the integral of curl F over any open surface S

 bounded by C, and

 (iii) The Green’s Theorem.

Objectives:

We address properties of line integrals. Double and triple integrals have to be

evaluated by expressing them as repeated integrals. We also wish to show that

Green’s Theorem in the plane is a special case of Stokes’ Theorem.

Also, it is of interest to notice that Gauss’ divergence theorem is a generalization of

Green’s theorem in the plane where the region R and its closed boundary C are

replaced by a (space) region V and its closed boundary (surface) S. hence the

divergence theorem is often called Green’s theorem in space.
